title: Penalties were a big factor in Buffalo vs. Houston
summary: For those of you new to the site (and I hope there are many of you), here’s the gist; every week I review the penalties from the Bills game. We talk the rules, what was a big deal. What wasn’t. This week will be a bit shortened just like the game week. Standard and Advanced […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills looks to pass the ball during the first quarter of the game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images) | Getty Images For those of you new to the site (and I hope there are many of you), here’s the gist; every week I review the penalties from the Bills game. We talk the rules, what was a big deal. What wasn’t. This week will be a bit shortened just like the game week. Standard and Advanced Metrics Penalty Counts This is where most traditional penalty analysis lives and breathes. For us it’s just the journey. The league averages are likely a good deal higher now than they will be at the end of the season, but this is where things stand right now. Buffalo was significantly higher than average while Houston was right around it. The easy conclusion is that the Bills had the rougher day, but that’s not necessarily true. Let’s keep going. For yards called on the field, both teams had a very rough go of it. And here the script is flipped. At least on the assessed yards. Here’s where we diverge from traditional analysis. On the right side are “true yards” which count yards impacted/negated by flags as well. And when they’re added in, it’s a dead heat. Penalty harm Buffalo Bills I apologize as I have a time crunch this week so I won’t go through all the flags or have GIFs but look for those next week. The short version for any new readers is that “Harm” factors in not just the assessed yards of a flag, but those negated by penalty as well. It also counts lost downs, points negated, etc. For an example of the calculation, Christian Benford’s defensive pass interference call was assessed for 21 yards which is 2.1 harm (yards x 0.1) but also gave up a free down from second. That adds in 1.0 harm for the total of 3.1. Davison Igbinosun has a “negative” harm on his defensive holding as the Texans had gained seven yards on the play but gave that up for the free five to retain the down. It’s a rare quirk in the formula. It happens, but not enough to drastically revise the whole thing. Overall I felt the penalties were warranted on Buffalo. The too many men on the field which negated what should have been an easy conversion was in my opinion the most egregious one. I know this is brief, so let me know if you have any questions/thoughts/concerns in the comments. The Bills had 13.2 harm for this game total. 10.0 is a good enough divider between a good day and bad, so it’s safe to say the yellow laundry had an impact on Buffalo. Houston Texans The Texans by count looked much better off than Buffalo, but a closer look at impact says otherwise. The Texans had two flags over 4.0 Harm. Kamari Lassiter was called for defensive pass interference and that is all assessed yards. This occurred in the end zone, putting the ball on the one-yard line and was a true field flipper. David Montgomery was called for a chop block and this was more complex. The flag itself was 15 yards. It also wiped out a six-yard gain on 3rd & 5. That negated a first down or, put differently, impacted two downs for another 2.0 Harm. The Texans had 14.2 total harm. While not by much, despite the lower counts compared to the Bills, the Texans had the worse day.

title: Carolina Panthers 2027 NFL Draft Prospect Profile: Kyngstonn Viliamu-Asa
summary: The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the […]
full_text: SOUTH BEND, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 12: Kyngstonn Viliamu-Asa #27 of the Notre Dame Fighting Irish celebrates recovering a fumble during the second quarter against the Rice Owls at Notre Dame Stadium on September 12, 2026 in South Bend, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In this series, we’ll only be looking at prospects the Panthers could seriously consider. This week our profile will focus on Notre Dame Fighting Irish linebacker Kyngstonn Viliamu-Asa. Bio Viliamu-Asa (6’3”, 230 lbs.) was a five star recruit coming out of Bellflower, CA. After an ACL tear near the end of his freshman season in high school, he returned his junior year and dominated, earning the CIF Defensive Player of the Year on route to a MaxPreps National Championship. His senior year saw his dominance continue as he was named LA Times Player of the Year and was a Butkus Award finalist. Viliamu-Asa played in all 14 games for Notre Dame his true freshman season but didn’t really thrive until last season when he took over the starting role. Through the first 11 games of the season, he had accrued 48 tackles, 7.5 tackles for loss, three sacks, an interception, and a fumble recovery. Unfortunately, his season was once again cut short this time by tearing the ACL in his other knee. Viliamu-Asa did come back healthy in time for the season opener this year, logging five tackles and a fumble recovered in a 52-0 romp over Rice. Strengths/Weaknesses Viliamu-Asa has an incredible feel for the game, especially against the run. He diagnoses plays well and is a force when moving downhill towards the ballcarrier. He is also an accomplished blitzer, relying on impeccable timing to disrupt run and pass plays. While his athleticism won’t set records, he has the speed to make plays sideline to sideline and match well in pass coverage. Teams will also value his versatility: he has effectively lined up in the box, on the line, and in the slot for the Fighting Irish. The biggest question mark for Viliamu-Asa will be the medicals. He has torn the ACL in both knees at this point, and any lingering damage might scare teams away. He is also a little on the lighter side for an off-ball linebacker in the NFL. He’ll need to add some weight and strength to handle power backs at the next level consistently. Projection Viliamu-Asa will be a coveted player based on his run defense alone, but he has shown the ability to perform well against the pass. His positional versatility and overall impact is something teams covet at the linebacker position, especially as teams prioritize the running game more and more. If the medicals check out in the spring, he could definitely hear his name called on the first night of the Draft. With the poor defensive showing against the Bears, especially in the run game, the Panthers could be one of the many teams interested in Viliamu-Asa’s services next year. Pairing another do-it-all linebacker with Devin Lloyd could really help beef up the middle of the defense in Carolina. What do you think, Panthers fans? If Kyngstonn Viliamu-Asa is available when the Panthers select in the 2027 NFL Draft, should they take him? Sound off in the comments!

title: Panthers go into Week 2 mostly healthy
summary: The Carolina Panthers played in a shootout against the Chicago Bears on Sunday. I guess the upside of neither team playing defense is that the Panthers came out relatively unscathed. There are only four players on the injury report for Week 2. One is just a rest day, and two were already hurt before Week […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - NOVEMBER 16: A Carolina Panthers football helmet during the NFL game between the Carolina Panthers and the Atlanta Falcons on November 16th, 2025 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Carolina Panthers played in a shootout against the Chicago Bears on Sunday. I guess the upside of neither team playing defense is that the Panthers came out relatively unscathed. There are only four players on the injury report for Week 2. One is just a rest day, and two were already hurt before Week 1. Panthers Injury Report Patrick Jones – DNP – Back Bobby Brown III – DNP – Back Darren Waller – DNP – Rest Jalen Coker – LP – Ankle Bobby Brown left the Bears game twice. but it seems like the only thing ailing him on the injury report is the same back issue that kept him out of practice last Wednesday. He was able to return to the practice field later in the week and toughed it out on Sunday. Patrick Jones continues to nurse a back issue of his own. He seems unlikely to play at this point unless there’s a change to his practice status. Darren Waller is old and needs days off. That’s all it is. Jalen Coker came up a little gimpy early in the Bears game, but he got his ankle taped up and went on to have the best game of his career. He was wearing a walking boot after the game but said it was just precautionary. It seems he was telling the truth. The fact that he’s already back at practice on Wednesday, even if just in a limited fashion, would imply he’ll be good to go on Sunday. Falcons Injury Report Chris Lindstrom – DNP – Concussion Tua Tagovailoa – DNP – Oblique AJ Terrell – DNP – Shoulder Michael Penix – FP – Knee Cooper Rush – FP – Back Billy Bowman Jr. – FP – Achilles The Falcson might be down a couple of starters from Week 1, for better or worse. Starting right guard Chris Lindstrom is dealing with a concussion, and it’s rare in today’s NFL for players to make it back in time for the next game after sustaining one. Starting corner AJ Terrell is dealing with a shoulder injury, but the Panthers might be rooting for him to make it back healthy based on how he played against the Steelers. All three of the Falcons quarterbacks are on the injury report. Tagovailoa got the starting nod for Week 1 but then injured himself out of it. Micahel Penix is back practicing fully, but he and the team are still being cautious as he makes his way back from his third ACL tear. If he doesn’t go, Cooper Rush and his janky back will get the start.

title: Chicago Bears Pass Protection Analysis on the Sacks Allowed vs Panthers
summary: Welcome to another season of Sackwatch! My 16th year writing this weekly in-season column! Shout-out to WCG O.G. Kev H. for suggesting I write it to show that not every sack allowed deserves fans screaming at the offensive linemen. Back then, there wasn’t a sacks-are-a-quarterback-stat discourse or much understanding among fans of how nuanced an […]
full_text: Sep 13, 2026; Charlotte, North Carolina, USA; Carolina Panthers linebacker Jaelan Phillips (5) sacks Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams (18) in the second quarter at Bank of America Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Jim Dedmon-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Welcome to another season of Sackwatch ! My 16th year writing this weekly in-season column! Shout-out to WCG O.G. Kev H. for suggesting I write it to show that not every sack allowed deserves fans screaming at the offensive linemen. Back then, there wasn’t a sacks-are-a-quarterback-stat discourse or much understanding among fans of how nuanced an offense’s pass protection was. Back then, it was: Jay Cutler is sacked, blame J’Marcus Webb! Okay, fine, Webb deserved his fair share of blame, but not when Cutler took a 7-step drop, worked through a few reads, stepped up, scrambled around, then ran into Webb’s guy, who shook free once Jay tried to sneak past. Pass protection is the five big guys working together up front, with the tight ends and running backs also playing a part. Sometimes that part is a chip to redirect, and other times it’s being locked up on a defender. It’s also the quarterback knowing where every possible pressure could come from, who is responsible for it, and when no one is, that responsibility falls on him to either evade it or, more likely, hit his hot read. The wide receivers, backs, or tight ends in the pattern need to know when they are the hot read and whether they need to deviate from the called play and be ready sooner for the ball. The offensive play caller needs to know when his tackle has a hard time with a speedy EDGE that he better get him some help on occasion. And sometimes the opposition just has the perfect play called at the right time to beat an offense, because the defense gets paid to make plays too. The Chicago Bears allowed 2 sacks to the Carolina Panthers on Sunday, so let’s take a closer look at what happened. SACK 1: 2nd Quarter: 1-10-CHI 20 (2:31) (Shotgun) C.Williams sacked at CHI 14 for -6 yards (J.Phillips) This looked like a zone read, but I think it was a play-action pass all the way. Panthers’ outside linebacker Jaelan Phillips (#5) was lined up outside tight end Cole Kmet, and after one step with Cole, he fired across towards Caleb Williams. The hope is the playside EDGE on this call is influenced by the play action, but Phillips played pass all the way, so he either read it or keyed on something in prep that had him ready when he saw this look. My guess is that Kmet was the clear out, and they were going to hit TE3 Sam Roush coming under the line and popping out into the right flat. But Phillips was on Caleb so fast, taking away the throwing window, so the right play was to protect the ball and brace for the sack. Good call by the Panthers and good play by Phillips, so this is a sacks happen. SACK 2: 3rd Quarter: 3-7-CHI 23 (12:09) (Shotgun) C.Williams sacked at CHI 21 for -2 yards (P.Umanmielen) Outside linebacker Princely Umanmielen (#3) cleaned up the play, but it was a right-place, right-time sack as Williams ran into him after the spin. What forced him into scramble mode was the stunt in front of him. Chicago center Garrett Bradbury stayed with Carolina defensive tackle Derrick Brown (#95) too long, and also turned his shoulders too far, creating a gap. He was in no position to pick up the stunting Devin Lloyd (#55) coming back around. Brown quickly crossed Bradbury’s face into the opposite A-gap and set a pick on right guard Jonah Jackson, giving Lloyd a free run. Had Bradbury not opened up so much, he may have been able to get Lloyd, so this one is on him. Here’s the individual Sackwatch tally after one week: Garrett Bradbury – 1 Sacks happen – 1 And here are the total Bears sacks allowed in Week 1, going all the way back to the Mike Martz era: 2010 Sacks – 4 (Martz) 2011 Sacks – 5 (Martz) 2012 Sacks – 2 (Tice) 2013 Sacks – 0 (Trestman) 2014 Sacks – 2 (Trestman) 2015 Sacks – 2 (Gase) 2016 Sacks – 5 (Loggains) 2017 Sacks – 4 (Loggains) 2018 Sacks – 4 (Nagy) 2019 Sacks – 5 (Nagy) 2020 Sacks – 1 (Nagy) 2021 Sacks – 3 (Nagy) 2022 Sacks – 2 (Getsy) 2023 Sacks – 4 (Getsy) 2024 Sacks – 2 (Waldron) 2025 Sacks – 2 (Johnson) 2026 Sacks – 2 (Johnson) OMG! #Bears fans, my guys at BreakingT did the shirt!Caleb Williams & Luther Burden III: Never Let It RestGet yours here at this link: breakingt.com/products/cal… — Lester A. title: Ben Johnson Expects the Unexpected Against Brian Flores and the Vikings
summary: With Week 1 in the rearview, the Chicago Bears have turned the page to their home opener, with the Minnesota Vikings coming to Soldier Field for a divisional matchup Sunday. Bears head coach Ben Johnson has faced Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores numerous times throughout his coaching career, but that familiarity doesn’t make Flores […]
full_text: With Week 1 in the rearview, the Chicago Bears have turned the page to their home opener, with the Minnesota Vikings coming to Soldier Field for a divisional matchup Sunday. Bears head coach Ben Johnson has faced Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores numerous times throughout his coaching career, but that familiarity doesn’t make Flores any easier to game plan for. “You’d like to think he’s put everything he could possibly do on tape until you play him next and you realize he hasn’t yet,” Johnson told the media on Wednesday. “So it’ll be something new. There always is with him, and that’s what makes him such a good coordinator. It’s a great challenge. It really is.” That challenge is evident in Flores’ approach, particularly when it comes to his use of pressure. “It comes from all over the place,” Johnson said, describing Flores’ blitz packages. “He’ll hit you in the A gap, he’ll hit you from outside the tackles. He likes to bring zero more than any other coordinator in this league. In any situation, normal downs, second-and-long, third-downs, redzone, it really doesn’t matter. He keeps you on your toes.” Last week, Flores blitzed the Green Bay Packers on 55 of 67 plays (82.1%). The Vikings blitzed on 55 of 67 plays in Week 1 😳 pic.twitter.com/DOk17n50UP — PFF (@PFF) September 15, 2026 Brian Flores is insane pic.twitter.com/HnfEPV3Dvi — Warren Sharp (@SharpFootball) September 14, 2026 Despite Flores’ heavy use of the blitz in Week 1, Johnson knows each gameplan is specific to the week and the opponent. Last season, Flores’ blitz rate differed significantly between his two games against Johnson and the Bears. Brian Flores blitzed Jordan Love on 87.1% of dropbacks, per PFF on Sunday. Will he continue that against Caleb Williams? Flores has faced Williams four previous times: 2024 Week 12: 44.4% 2024 Week 15: 60.0% 2025 Week 1: 40.9% 2025 Week 11: 77.8% The two games under 50%? At… — Tyler Forness (@TheRealForno) September 14, 2026 That unpredictability is part of what makes the Vikings such a challenge, and it means the Bears will have to prepare for a variety of possibilities heading into Sunday. However, Johnson believes the team’s approach to its weekly preparation, regardless of the opponent, helps set them up for success. “For our players, they have to dedicate themselves over the course of the week to have success on game day. Fortunately I do think that our guys, the way we train them, is very demanding and very detailed, with teams like this in mind,” Johnson said. title: Will the Vikings’ Dallas Turner stop the Bears in their tracks?
summary: The chatter around the Chicago Bears’ offense has hit a new zenith. The laughter around Ben Johnson’s assertion of being the “highest-scoring offense of all time” has quieted significantly after hanging 59 points on a defense with legitimate talent. Still, the Bears offense faces a daunting challenge in Week 2 as they face off against […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MN - SEPTEMBER 13: Minnesota Vikings linebacker Dallas Turner (15) celebrates his strip sack of Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love (10) during the fourth quarter of a NFL game between the Minnesota Vikings and Green Bay Packers on September 13, 2026, at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis MN. (Photo by Nick Wosika/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The chatter around the Chicago Bears’ offense has hit a new zenith. The laughter around Ben Johnson’s assertion of being the “highest-scoring offense of all time” has quieted significantly after hanging 59 points on a defense with legitimate talent. Still, the Bears offense faces a daunting challenge in Week 2 as they face off against the Minnesota Vikings and Brian Flores. Flores, as many of you already know, has developed quite the reputation for causing chaos for other teams’ offenses, mixing up exotic blitz packages that frequently confuse quarterbacks. I expect no different from Flores this Sunday as he aims to stymie the Caleb Williams-led attack. In fact, Brian Flores blitzed Jordan Love on 78.3% of dropbacks, per Next Gen Stats, resulting in a pressure rate above 50% and 4 sacks. An absolute manic. Still, Flores has an emerging weapon who may let him drop more into coverage — Dallas Turner. Turner, in his third season, had nine pressures, seven QB hits, one sack, and one forced fumble in the first game of the season. For those keeping track at home, seven is a lot of QB hits to have in one game. This would suggest that Turner is continuing to build on the improvements he made last season, jumping from three sacks as a rookie in 2024 to eight, and with the departure of Jonathan Greenard, Turner is now the feature EDGE on a defense that relies on having good DEs. Turner primarily lines up on the right side of the line, across from the LT, which means that he will likely lock horns with Braxton Jones. This matchup will be crucial for both sides. It is well documented that Jones relies primarily on his athleticism to stay with quicker DEs, while he struggles to anchor against bigger/stronger DEs. Turner is a smaller EDGE at 6’-3” and 247 lbs who relies on his speed and bend to beat opposing OLs. This is a strength-against-strength matchup, as the Bears will rely heavily on Jones’ quick feet to neutralize Turner. While struggling on a handful of pass sets against Trevis Gipson, Jones looked relatively sharp against a deep DL in Carolina, only surrendering 2 pressures on the day. While Caleb Williams has a tendency to bail out his OL at times, especially on the blindside, Jones will still need to keep the speedy Turner in front of him to keep Williams clean. Love showed that it is possible to beat the Brian Flores blitz in the first three quarters of the game, with a 60% completion, 227 yards passing, and 2 TD passes against it. The blitz eventually overwhelmed him and the Packers’ OL in the 4th quarter, leading to 1 INT, 2 FFs, and 3 sacks. With that said, if Flores is concerned about Ben Johnson’s ability to scheme pass catchers open quickly, he could rely on Turner to beat Jones outright. If this is the case, Braxton Jones’ ability to withstand the pressure will be critical to a Bears win.

title: Caleb Williams Week 1 QB Grade: Bears @ Panthers Film Breakdown
summary: Note: As you may recall, I like to do select play breakdowns from each week. However, this week I’m away from my usual editing setup, so I won’t be able to put those together. Instead, I’ll be linking to breakdowns of some plays I’d like to highlight from a few of my favorite Bears and […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Carolina Panthers during the first half of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Note: As you may recall, I like to do select play breakdowns from each week. However, this week I’m away from my usual editing setup, so I won’t be able to put those together. Instead, I’ll be linking to breakdowns of some plays I’d like to highlight from a few of my favorite Bears and football content creators. People, it feels so good to be back. The long hibernation from Chicago Bears football is finally over, and boy did we wake up with a roar. In a game that featured very little defense, the Chicago Bears took down the Carolina Panthers 59-37. I’m sure many of you have already heard some of the gaudy numbers and records put up by a Bears offense led by Caleb Williams and coached by offensive guru Ben Johnson, but for those who may have missed a few of them, let’s do a quick recap. It was the highest-scoring season opener in NFL history, with both teams combining for 96 points , breaking the previous mark of 88 set by the Buccaneers and Saints in 2018. The 59 points scored by Chicago set a franchise record for the most points in a season opener. They were also the most points the Bears have scored in any game since December 7, 1980, when they absolutely smoked the Green Bay Packers 61-7. And the records didn’t stop there. Chicago racked up 552 yards of total offense, the most the franchise has ever produced in a season opener and tied for the seventh-most in Bears history. It was also the second time in Ben Johnson’s tenure that Chicago has eclipsed 500 yards of offense, joining the ridiculous 576-yard performance against Cincinnati last season. Among those 552 yards, the Bears saw both D’Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai rush for more than 100 yards, marking the second time in just seven regular-season games that the duo has accomplished the feat. Before Swift and Monangai first did it against Philadelphia last November, you had to go all the way back to 1985, when Walter Payton and Matt Suhey each rushed for more than 100 yards against the Lions. Not to be outdone, or left out of the record book, Caleb Williams set a Bears franchise mark of his own. With another two touchdown passes against Carolina, Williams has now thrown for at least two touchdowns in eight consecutive games, including the playoffs. The streak dates all the way back to December 7 against the Packers at Lambeau Field and is now the longest such streak by a quarterback in Bears history. And somehow, after scoring 59 points and piling up 552 yards, the prevailing feeling inside the Bears locker room was that they still left points on the board . That might be the craziest part of all of this. For me personally, it was one of the most memorable opening games to a Bears season since 2012, when Chicago kicked off the year with a 41-21 win over the Indianapolis Colts. For more information including scoring key, game-by-game grading sheets, weekly grading scorecards, and an overall look at his 2026 season, you can view Caleb’s entire season workbook here . Benchmarks Stat Formatting Key: (Last Season totals are underlined , Last Season averages in Italics , and this week’s stats appear in regular text.) C/A: 330/568 (58.1%) | 19.4/33.4 (58.1%) | 21/29 72.4% Yards: 3942 | 231.9 | 269 Touchdowns: 31 | 1.8 | 4 Turnovers: 8 | 0.5 | 0 QB at Fault Sacks: 1 3 | 0.8 | 0 aDOT: 8.9 | 10.7 Passer Rating: 90.1 | 124.1 True Passer Rating : 125. 8 | 173.6 Time to Throw: 3.00s | 3.04s Time to Pressure: 2.67s | 2.56s Pressure Rate: 30.84% | 41.46% On-Target Rate: 67.6% | 84.0% Poor Play Rate / Big Play Rate: 9.0 % PPR / 7.6% BPR | 4.7% PPR / 11.6% BRP EPA per dropback: +0.11 | +0.54 ANY/A : 6.8 | 9.7 Game Scorecard The full grading sheet for each play can be found here. Game Notes Note: Last year, I included PFF grades in these breakdowns. With PFF continuing to expand its use of AI across its platform, and with my confidence in how accurately its grades reflect quarterback performance declining, I’ve decided to move away from them this season. In their place, I’ll be using PFN’s Impact Score , which will be notated as PFN on grading sheets moving forward. NFL Passer Rating / True Passer Rating / PFN:IS: 124.1 / 173.6 / 87.7 The average NFL passer rating through Week 1 of the 2026 season sits at 95.3 , putting Williams’ 124.1 NFL Passer Rating well above the league average and firmly in the range of a very good to near elite performance based off that metric. A 173.6 TPR represents an elite game in my model, with 100 serving as the baseline for “Average.” Caleb had just one start during the 2025 season north of a 170 TPR, when he posted a 187.7 against the Dallas Cowboys in Week 3. He has now already matched that total in one game. On the PFN scale, where 75 represents an average qualifying quarterback and 90 represents elite territory, Williams’ 87.7 Impact Score was one of the best performances of Week 1. His 87.7 ranked third among all quarterbacks for the week. Williams averaged a 74.9 Impact Score during the 2025 season, which ranked 20th among quarterbacks. Needless to say, he’s off to a much hotter start in that metric this year. On-Target Throws: 2025 Season Average: 67.6% | Week 1 vs. Panthers: 84.0% Reminder: Completion percentage ≠ On-Target Percentage. On-target throws are only measured on aimed passes, meaning throwaways, spikes and passes deflected at the line of scrimmage are excluded. Drops, however, can still count as on-target throws. Short-Level Passing (Behind LOS–9 yards): 15/15 | 100.0% On-Target Deep-Level Passing (10–20+ yards): 6/10 | 60.0% On-Target Williams had just one start during the 2025 season in which he topped an 80.0% On-Target Rate: Week 15 against the Cleveland Browns, when he also finished at 84.0% . One start into the 2026 season, and he has already matched his best mark from a year ago. It also represents a massive improvement from where he started last season. Against the Minnesota Vikings in Week 1 of 2025, Williams posted just a 41.7% On-Target Rate . One year later, he more than doubled that number in his season debut. Poor Play Rate / Big Play Rate: 4.7% PPR / 11.6% BPR Williams averaged a 9.0% Poor Play Rate in 2025 compared to a 7.6% Big Play Rate . He’s off to a much better start in both categories this season, recording just two poor plays across 43 graded plays while producing five big plays against Carolina. The best of the bunch was his 22-yard touchdown throw to Cole Kmet, a perfectly placed ball with linebacker Devin Lloyd draped over Kmet in coverage. Time to Throw: 3.19 seconds Williams posted a 3.19-second Time to Throw, 0.19 seconds higher than his 2025 season mark. As we know by now, that number can be somewhat deceiving with Williams. A portion of it is inflated by his uncanny ability to extend plays, escape pressure and keep his eyes downfield rather than simply taking what would otherwise be a dead play. Under Pressure: +0.66 EPA per dropback Williams was particularly dangerous when pressured against Carolina, leading all quarterbacks in Week 1 in EPA per dropback while under pressure , according to PFN using TruMedia data, at +0.66 EPA/dropback . Using the same pressure charting for a more traditional look at his performance, Williams completed 4 of 8 passes for 96 yards and a touchdown, good for a 133.3 passer rating. And that doesn’t account for what he did with his legs, where he added two rushing touchdowns on scrambles. A Tale of Two Halfs?: Well, not really. Despite a pretty jarring difference between the scores for each half (6.60 vs. -0.30) Caleb was tasked to do less within the second half, sticking to underneath routes that focused on moving the chains while the ground game took over. 6 of his 9 second half…

title: Beyond the Box Score: Say what you want about Zac Taylor, but he’s striking the right chords so far this season
summary: Just before training camp got underway in late July, Bengals head coach Zac Taylor wrote on a board during a team meeting: The Bengals’ 2025 record— 6-11. Even after a great offseason on the field and from the front office that, from a fan’s perspective, put last season’s disaster in the rearview mirror, Taylor pushed […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - SEPTEMBER 13: Joe Burrow #9 of the Cincinnati Bengals celebrates 33-27 win against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers with fans after the game at Paycor Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Jeff Dean/Getty Images) | Getty Images Just before training camp got underway in late July, Bengals head coach Zac Taylor wrote on a board during a team meeting: The Bengals’ 2025 record— 6-11. Even after a great offseason on the field and from the front office that, from a fan’s perspective, put last season’s disaster in the rearview mirror, Taylor pushed the right button by reminding the players that last season wasn’t good enough. Let’s not forget that while a lot of players from last year aren’t here, a lot of last year’s team still is. That created the sense of urgency we saw throughout the offseason and training camp. That sense of urgency carried into the preseason and Week 1, when the Bengals beat the Buccaneers 33-27 to start the season 1-0. Some say Week 1 is a liar, and that may be true. However, I put a lot of stock in Week 1. It’s the first game of the season, and it sets the tone. Tampa Bay came into Sunday with five straight season-opening wins, the second-longest streak in the NFL behind the Philadelphia Eagles. Baker Mayfield had thrown nine touchdowns in Week 1 over his first three seasons with the Buccaneers. On Sunday, the Bengals became the first team since Week 16 of 2018 to have a scoop-and-score against the Buccaneers, snapped Tampa Bay’s five-game winning streak in Week 1, and held Baker Mayfield without a touchdown pass. They also forced and recovered three fumbles from Mayfield and recovered a fourth fumble from the Buccaneers. Zac Taylor had the Bengals ready to play. The Bengals’ defense, much-maligned over the last three years, was all over the field for the entire 60 minutes. They didn’t force a punt, but they forced four turnovers. That makes up for not forcing a punt. Before training camp, Taylor also challenged his coordinators to make sure they’re using their great talent accordingly. On Sunday, Al Golden’s defense sacked Mayfield four times and recovered four fumbles. They also held Tampa Bay to two field goals, including on a promising first drive for the Buccaneers. They even held the Bucs to just 282 total yards. They held just two teams under 300 yards last year: The 5-12 Cleveland Browns and the 3-14 Arizona Cardinals. The Bengals’ defense will also improve, and their leaders will make sure of it. For what it’s worth, the Bengals only punted once, and their offense, after a three-and-out on their first drive, scored on five of their next seven drives. One of those drives ran out the clock in the fourth quarter. After the Bengals’ first preseason game, Zac Taylor said in the locker room that they had to get better at finishing games with their four-minute offense. On Sunday, the Bengals ran out the final 3:14 of the clock on offense. They were aggressive, headlined by Burrow’s dart to a leaping Tee Higgins over the middle, and efficient, facing only one third down, which came when they were already in the red zone. Evan McPherson was named a captain on the Monday before the season started. On Sunday, McPherson made four field goals, including three in the second half. Two of those field goals were from at least 55 yards, including a 58-yarder at the start of the fourth quarter. Those two 55+ yard field goals accounted for six points. The Bengals won the game by six points. McPherson earned Week 1 AFC Special Teams Player of the Week for his performance. Taylor has his imprint all over this team. He called a great game on Sunday, has command of the locker room, holds his coordinators accountable, and has let go of any arrogance he may have had the last three years. Success can affect people in different ways. The Bengals got so close to winning the Super Bowl in 2021 and 2022. That may have given Taylor and the front office the impression they were set for the next several seasons. What followed, of course, was two straight 9-8 seasons with a playoff berth, but Taylor and the front office may have thought they had gotten unlucky with injuries and just needed to change a few things to get back into contention. Then 2025 happened. That humbled Taylor, the front office, and Joe Burrow, not to mention everybody on the roster who went through last year. What followed was an offseason that felt different. Zac Taylor sounded different. He sounded more urgent, recognizing the front office went all-in this offseason and sent a message: win this year, or maybe this is it for the Bengals’ head coach. Sunday after the game, Taylor gave Bengals’ director of player personnel Duke Tobin a game ball for his 200th win as a member of the Bengals. That shows respect and that there is alignment within the organization not seen since… maybe ever in the franchise’s history. This is a confident Bengals team, but it’s not an arrogant Bengals team. In 2021 and 2022, they went about business as a confident group, but arrogance eventually may have seeped in. That’s why this offseason offered the opportunity for a complete reset, and Zac Taylor looks and sounds like he did just that. Taylor is striking the right chords as a leader, and the players, including Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, Tee Higgins, and Dexter Lawrence, are rallying around him. Urgency is at an all-time high, and the steady-handed, positive identity and culture Taylor created from the moment he arrived are driving it. Like the Bengals did this offseason, Taylor evolved as a leader, and it’s already paying dividends.

title: Bengals Film Room: Turnovers lead the way for revamped defense vs. Bucs
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals defeated the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 33-27 in a matchup between two teams desperate to return to the playoffs in 2026. The Bengals forced and recovered four fumbles on Sunday. Each play led to the Bengals putting points on the board. On the Bengals’ first forced fumble, they trailed 3-0, fresh off an […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals defeated the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 33-27 in a matchup between two teams desperate to return to the playoffs in 2026. The Bengals forced and recovered four fumbles on Sunday. Each play led to the Bengals putting points on the board. On the Bengals’ first forced fumble, they trailed 3-0, fresh off an offense that went 3-and-out to start the game. Initial pressure from Boye Mafe forced Baker Mayfield to step up into secondary pressure from Barrett Carter. As Carter got Mayfield in his grasp, Myles Murphy came from behind to hit Baker. The hit jarred the ball loose, and Demetrius Knight Jr. picked it up for the scoop-and-score. That play electrified the crowd and gave the Bengals an early 7-3 lead. A fantastic play from every angle pic.twitter.com/d7MnzfbWPX — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) September 14, 2026 The Bengals’ second forced fumble and recovery came on the Buccaneers’ very next possession. Bryan Cook came up and hit Bucky Irving, knocking the ball out. Boye Mafe combined with Cook on that hit, and Cook also had the awareness to recover the fumble. That play set the Bengals up in their own territory to begin the next drive. Ultimately, leading to a two-yard Mike Gesicki touchdown reception. Bryan Cook was feeling himself here, as he should. Great awareness from Mafe to recover the fumble. pic.twitter.com/GeEFJXg7Ff — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) September 14, 2026 The Buccaneers bounced back by driving down the field on their next possession. However, they would turn it over for a third straight time near the end zone. Dexter Lawrence pushed the guard directly into Baker Mayfield’s lap, nearly coming up with his first sack as a Bengal. A holding penalty went uncalled, and Mayfield escaped Lawrence’s grasp and took off toward the goal line. This time, Barrett Carter made the play, knocking the ball out of Baker Mayfield’s hands before he could score the touchdown. Bryan Cook recovered it in the end zone. The Bengals then went on a 12-play, 80-yard touchdown drive capped by a Chase Brown run. While we were robbed of a Sexy Dexy celebration, we will take the third turnover of the first half all day long. pic.twitter.com/nL3Ak1RWhO — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) September 14, 2026 The Bengals’ fourth and final forced fumble and recovery came in the fourth quarter. Holding a 10-point lead, Boye Mafe was able to get the sack-fumble on Mayfield. TJ Slaton came up with the fumble recovery, which ultimately led to another Evan McPherson field goal. The Bengals 4th forced fumble and recovery of the day was caused by Boye Mafe. Mafe was highly impressive generating pressure throughout the game on Sunday. pic.twitter.com/yi25Q1gVuS — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) September 14, 2026 Just an impressive performance by the Bengals defense overall. Playing opportunistic defense, making the hustle plays to create turnovers, and players having the awareness to recover each one of them shows a defense that has the talent to keep improving throughout the season. A great debut for the revamped defense on Sunday.

title: Bengals Film Room: Amarius Mims dominates at right tackle
summary: I have been banging the drum all summer that Amarius Mims has the potential to take the leap into being an All-Pro tackle this season for the Cincinnati Bengals. Mims was the Bengals’ first-round pick in the 2024 NFL Draft. I thought he was incredible for Cincinnati last season. With the expectation that he could […]
full_text: I have been banging the drum all summer that Amarius Mims has the potential to take the leap into being an All-Pro tackle this season for the Cincinnati Bengals . Mims was the Bengals’ first-round pick in the 2024 NFL Draft. I thought he was incredible for Cincinnati last season. With the expectation that he could become more consistent this season, it feels like the sky is the limit for what he can be at tackle in the league. Mims is a massive human being. He is every bit of the 6’8” and 350 pounds he is listed at. Even more impressive is how smoothly he moves at that size. He is quick out of his stance in pass protection, flies up to the second level as a run blocker, and also gets out in space to lead the way for big plays, as he did on Sunday for Chase Brown on a nice first-down carry. Mims getting out in space to lead the way for the Chase Brown first down is a thing of beauty. pic.twitter.com/jdXRodHiTB — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) September 14, 2026 Mims did not allow a pressure against Tampa Bay on Sunday. He was tasked with matching up with Rueben Bain Jr. for the majority of the day. He shut down the rookie all day long. Mims will be asked to do it all again with an even tougher opponent in Will Anderson for the Texans. Anderson is arguably the best pass rusher in the NFL currently. Anderson finished the 2024 season with 11 sacks and added another 12 sacks in 2025. Mims will have his hands full with Anderson, but if he plays as well as he did on Sunday, he should be able to at least keep him from completely wrecking the game. If Mims completely shuts him down, that All-Pro talk grows even louder going forward. Here is an expanded sample of how well Mims performed on Sunday versus Bain and the rest of the Buccaneers’ defense. Amarius Mims vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers pic.twitter.com/ehyW38iwIP — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) September 14, 2026 Mims earned an 84.5 pass-blocking grade from PFF on Sunday, the highest of his career. If he keeps this up over a 17-game regular season, it will be hard to keep him off one of the All-Pro teams when it’s time for postseason honors.

title: Evan McPherson named AFC Special Teams Player of the Week after historic performance
summary: Cincinnati Bengals kicker Evan McPherson has been named the AFC Special Teams Player of the Week after helping his team score a 33-27 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 1. McPherson converted all four field-goal attempts and three extra points, accounting for 15 of Cincinnati’s 33 points. He led all NFL kickers in […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals kicker Evan McPherson talks with Tampa Bay Buccaneers Evan Deckers before the opening of NFL regular season at Paycor Stadium on September 13, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Cincinnati Bengals kicker Evan McPherson has been named the AFC Special Teams Player of the Week after helping his team score a 33-27 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 1. McPherson converted all four field-goal attempts and three extra points, accounting for 15 of Cincinnati’s 33 points. He led all NFL kickers in Week 1 scoring, and his four field goals led all AFC kickers. McPherson’s kicks came from 20, 55, 58, and 32 yards. He became the first player in Bengals history to make multiple field goals from 55+yards in a game, and his 58-yarder tied for the fourth-longest kick in team history. That kick also came in the fourth quarter of a game the Bengals ultimately won by just six points. McPherson has now made 123 career field goals, surpassing former kicker Horst Muhlmann (120) for fifth in Bengals history. Money Mac also extended his streak of made field goals to 16, dating back to Week 11 of last season. That marks the third-most consecutive field goals in team history, trailing 21 by former kicker Shayne Graham in 2007 and 17 by Graham from 2005-06. This is McPherson’s fifth career AFC Special Teams Player of the Week award. He previously received the honor in Weeks 1 and 11 of the 2021 season, Week 4 of the 2022 campaign, and Week 13 of 2025.

title: Bengals vs. Buccaneers: The Good, The Bad and The Ugly
summary: The Bengals opened the 2026 season with a win, and for once, the defense had a lot to do with it. There were some familiar warts along the way, but Cincinnati made enough plays to hold off Tampa Bay, 33-27, at Paycor Stadium. Whew. A Week 1 game that actually ended with the Bengals on the happy side of things. Here are the best and worst from Cincinnati’s season-opening win. The Good […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow (9) checks in with head coach Zac Taylor between plays in the second quarter of the NFL Week 1 game between the Cincinnati Bengals and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati on Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Bengals opened the 2026 season with a win, and for once, the defense had a lot to do with it. There were some familiar warts along the way, but Cincinnati made enough plays to hold off Tampa Bay, 33-27, at Paycor Stadium. Whew. A Week 1 game that actually ended with the Bengals on the happy side of things. Here are the best and worst from Cincinnati’s season-opening win. The Good The defense came to play Well, hello there. After everything we heard about Cincinnati’s rebuilt defense during the offseason, we finally got to see it against an actual NFL offense. And the unit immediately made its presence felt. The Bengals forced fumbles on three consecutive Tampa Bay possessions in the first half. Myles Murphy strip-sacked Baker Mayfield, and Demetrius Knight Jr. scooped it up and returned it 27 yards for a touchdown. Then Bryan Cook forced a fumble from Bucky Irving, with Boye Mafe recovering. A few plays later, Joe Burrow found Mike Gesicki for a touchdown. On the next Tampa possession, Barrett Carter forced another Mayfield fumble near the goal line, and Cook recovered it in the end zone. Three straight possessions. Three turnovers. Cincinnati eventually forced four fumbles and recovered all four, while also sacking Mayfield four times. The Bengals turned those takeaways into 24 points. That’s a pretty good way to start a new defensive era. Mike Gesicki was exactly what Cincinnati needed Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins weren’t exactly having their usual Sunday. So, naturally, Mike Gesicki decided to have a day. Gesicki caught five passes for 78 yards and a touchdown on seven targets, leading Cincinnati in receiving. He also came up big late in the first half, catching three passes for 52 yards on the drive that ended with an Evan McPherson field goal. The Bucs spent plenty of attention on Chase and Higgins, and Burrow simply went somewhere else with the football. That’s what makes this offense so interesting. If defenses want to take away Cincinnati’s two star receivers, there are going to be opportunities for guys like Gesicki to make them pay. Chase Brown and the run game This was not the old-school Bengals running the ball 40 times and winning 17-13. But it was a much more balanced attack. Cincinnati ran the ball 27 times and threw it 35 times, and Chase Brown finished with 16 carries for 56 yards and a touchdown. He also caught five passes for 23 yards. More importantly, the Bengals showed a willingness to use the run as something other than a change of pace. Brown’s five-yard touchdown run capped an 80-yard, 12-play drive in the second quarter and pushed Cincinnati’s lead to 21-3. If Dan Pitcher’s offense really is going to lean into a more balanced approach in 2026, Sunday was a pretty encouraging first look. Money Mac is back Evan McPherson had himself a day. Four field goals. Four makes. Twenty yards. Thirty-two yards. Fifty-five yards. Fifty-eight yards. Those last two are particularly important because Tampa Bay had started to make things uncomfortable. Cincinnati wasn’t consistently finishing drives with touchdowns, but McPherson kept adding points. He accounted for 12 of the Bengals’ 33 points and gave Cincinnati some breathing room when the offense wasn’t quite clicking. Oh, and the 58-yarder was just ridiculous. It’s nice having that in your back pocket again. The offensive line quietly did its job This probably won’t generate nearly as many headlines as a scoop-and-score or a 58-yard field goal, but it might be one of the more important things to come out of this game. Joe Burrow was sacked just once. He finished 25-of-35 for 254 yards, one touchdown and one interception, while completing passes to nine different receivers. There were still some issues, but Burrow generally had enough time to work through his reads. Considering how much of Cincinnati’s success ultimately depends on keeping No. 9 upright, that’s a pretty significant development. Sometimes the best thing an offensive line can do is make you forget it’s there. Sunday was one of those days. The Bad Joe Burrow’s pick-six There’s no way around this one. Burrow had a pretty solid afternoon overall, but his third-quarter interception was brutal. With Cincinnati leading 27-13, Burrow tried to hit Andrei Iosivas, and Tampa Bay linebacker Josiah Trotter stepped in front of the pass and took it 27 yards for a touchdown. Just like that, a 14-point game became a seven-point game. It wasn’t the kind of mistake that cost Cincinnati the game, but it absolutely gave Tampa Bay life when the Bucs needed it. Burrow finished with 254 yards and a touchdown, so this wasn’t some disaster of a performance. But that interception was a bad one, and he’ll know it. The good news? The Bengals responded. The defense still missed too many tackles Four forced fumbles and four sacks will get you a lot of attention. But this wasn’t a flawless defensive performance. Cincinnati missed tackles, and Tampa Bay was able to move the football despite the turnovers. The Bengals also committed multiple offsides penalties, which is the kind of self-inflicted stuff that can become a real problem against better teams. That’s the tradeoff with an aggressive defense. You want guys flying around trying to make plays. You also need them to know where the line is. Cincinnati found that line a few times Sunday—and stepped over it. Ja’Marr Chase was basically a decoy Two catches. Twelve yards. Four targets. That’s it for Ja’Marr Chase. Obviously, this isn’t going to happen every week. Tampa Bay made a concerted effort to take Chase away, and Burrow responded by distributing the ball elsewhere. That’s actually a positive development. Still, there’s a difference between taking Chase away and simply not getting him involved. The Bengals didn’t need Chase to win this game. But there will be Sundays when they absolutely will. The offense left some points out there Cincinnati scored 33 points, so complaining about the offense feels a little ridiculous. Still, there were stretches where the Bengals had opportunities to put Tampa Bay away and couldn’t quite do it. The Bengals went 2-for-5 in the red zone, according to the game statistics. That’s an area that could come back to bite them against a team that doesn’t hand them four turnovers. The offense did enough. But it didn’t exactly leave the Bucs’ defense picking up the pieces. The Ugly That pick-six made this way too interesting This is where things got uncomfortable. Cincinnati was up 27-13. Tampa Bay had struggled to protect the football. The Bengals’ defense was flying around. Then Burrow threw the pick-six. Suddenly it was 27-20. The Buccaneers had momentum, the crowd had gotten a little quieter, and everybody watching was thinking the same thing: Please don’t do this. Fortunately, McPherson answered with a 58-yard field goal, and the defense eventually forced its fourth turnover of the afternoon. But Cincinnati turned what could have been a comfortable fourth quarter into a game that required some actual late-game execution. Tampa Bay wouldn’t go away Credit to the Bucs. After falling behind 24-10 at halftime, Tampa Bay kept hanging around. The Buccaneers cut the lead to seven in the third quarter, and Baker Mayfield eventually ran for an eight-yard touchdown with 3:19 left to make it 33-27. That’s when Cincinnati finally got the kind of close-out drive it has been looking for. The Bengals possessed the ball for the final 3:19 and didn’t give Tampa Bay another opportunity. So, yes, it got ugly. But Cincinnati actually finished the job. And honestly, after some of the fourth-quarter endings Bengals fans have endured over the years, I’ll take an ugly close-out over another…

title: Bengals Week 1 awards from 33-27 win vs. Buccaneers
summary: The Bengals are 1-0. That’s a pretty good place to start. Cincinnati opened the 2026 season with a 33-27 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and while there were certainly some things that need cleaning up, there were also plenty of individual performances worth recognizing. The new-look defense stole the show, Evan McPherson reminded everyone […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals center Ted Karras (64) celebrates with place kicker Evan McPherson (2) after McPherson made a field goal in the 4th quarter over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Paycor Stadium on September 13, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Bengals are 1-0. That’s a pretty good place to start. Cincinnati opened the 2026 season with a 33-27 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and while there were certainly some things that need cleaning up, there were also plenty of individual performances worth recognizing. The new-look defense stole the show, Evan McPherson reminded everyone why they call him “Money Mac,” and a few guys who probably weren’t at the top of anyone’s bingo card made some big plays. So, without further ado, let’s get into this week’s award nominees. Most Valuable Player (MVP) Criteria: This award goes to the player whose performance had the greatest direct impact on securing the victory. Nominee 1: Demetrius Knight Jr. — Linebacker Stats / Moments: Knight Jr. opened Cincinnati’s scoring with a 27-yard fumble return touchdown after Myles Murphy forced a Baker Mayfield fumble. Why MVP-worthy: Talk about making an entrance. Knight’s defensive touchdown gave the Bengals their first points of the season and immediately gave the new-look defense some life. He wasn’t just in the right place at the right time, either. Knight was flying around all afternoon and looked very comfortable in his first regular-season game with a much larger role. When you’re trying to change the identity of a defense, plays like this are exactly what you’re looking for. Nominee 2: Evan McPherson — Kicker Stats / Moments: McPherson connected on all four of his field-goal attempts, including kicks from 55 and 58 yards. He finished with 12 points. Why MVP-worthy: When the offense couldn’t quite finish drives, McPherson did. The 58-yarder in the fourth quarter was especially important. Tampa Bay had just cut Cincinnati’s lead to seven, and the Bengals needed something to stop the momentum. Enter Money Mac. That kick pushed the lead back to 10 and gave the defense a little more breathing room. Four-for-four with two 50-plus yarders is a pretty strong way to start the year. Nominee 3: Bryan Cook — Safety Stats / Moments: Cook forced a fumble and recovered a Tampa Bay fumble, which was Baker Mayfield’s goal-line gaffe in the first half. Why MVP-worthy: Cook was simply around the football. His fumble recovery came after Mayfield coughed the ball up near the goal line, preventing Tampa Bay from potentially coming away with points. He also forced another Buccaneers fumble, helping Cincinnati maintain control of a game that ultimately became much closer than it looked at halftime. After spending the offseason talking about what Cook could bring to a revamped secondary, Bengals fans got a pretty good first taste. Nominee 4: Mike Gesicki — Tight End Stats / Moments: Gesicki caught five passes for 78 yards and a touchdown on seven targets, leading Cincinnati in receiving. Why MVP-worthy: When Tampa Bay made it difficult to get Ja’Marr Chase involved, Burrow went elsewhere. Gesicki was the primary beneficiary. His two-yard touchdown reception gave Cincinnati its first offensive touchdown of the season, and he consistently found ways to move the chains. You don’t necessarily need your biggest stars to dominate every week. Sometimes you need the guys underneath them to make the defense pay for all that attention. Gesicki did exactly that. Unsung Hero of the Week Criteria: Awarded to a player whose efforts were significant yet flew under the radar, often stepping up in a rotational role, making an impact that doesn’t necessarily show up in the box score, or taking advantage of an opportunity created by injuries. Nominee 1: Dexter Lawrence II — Defensive Tackle Why Unsung-worthy: The stat sheet doesn’t really tell the story here. Lawrence didn’t need a bunch of sacks or splash plays to make his presence felt. He consistently affected what Tampa Bay wanted to do up front and helped create opportunities for the players around him. Nuggets from #Bengals PFF grading data: -Dexter Lawrence with 11 true pass set rushes. His win rate was 36%. That's best in the NFL among all DI (min. 10 attempts). – CBs did a nice job tackling in run game, Jalen Davis and Dax Hill, both graded out 84+. Hill with 2 stops. -… — Paul Dehner Jr. (@pauldehnerjr) September 14, 2026 And that’s exactly why Cincinnati went and got him. The Bengals invested heavily in their defensive front this offseason, and Lawrence’s Week 1 performance was one of those games where the tape was more impressive than the box score. Not exactly a bad debut in stripes. Nominee 2: Barrett Carter — Linebacker Stats / Moments: Carter finished with a team-high eight tackles, recorded a half-sack, and forced a fumble at the goal line. Why Unsung-worthy: Knight Jr. gets the highlight-reel touchdown, but Carter was everywhere. The goal-line forced fumble was enormous. Tampa Bay was threatening to turn a Bengals defensive stop into points, and Carter simply took the football away. Eight tackles, a half-sack and a forced fumble is a pretty busy afternoon. And unlike the defensive touchdown, this is the kind of production that can get lost when one side of the ball generates four turnovers. Nominee 3: Boye Mafe — EDGE Stats / Moments: Mafe recovered a fumble after Bucky Irving lost the ball and was part of a defensive front that helped force four Tampa Bay turnovers. Why Unsung-worthy: Mafe wasn’t necessarily the guy getting all the headlines, but he was involved in the chaos up front. The Bengals wanted a more aggressive, deeper defensive line rotation in 2026, and Mafe’s ability to contribute in that rotation is going to matter. Recovering a fumble isn’t glamorous. It is, however, extremely useful. Nominee 4: Chase Brown — Running Back Stats / Moments: Brown carried the ball 16 times for 56 yards and a touchdown while adding five receptions for 23 yards. Why Unsung-worthy: Brown wasn’t spectacular statistically, but he was steady. His five-yard touchdown run extended Cincinnati’s lead to 21-3 in the second quarter, and he was involved throughout an offense that ran 27 times compared with 35 pass attempts. More importantly, the Bengals didn’t abandon the running game when things weren’t perfect. Brown is going to be a major part of that balance if Cincinnati sticks with this approach. Play of the Game Criteria: The single most impactful or memorable moment that significantly shifted the game in Cincinnati’s favor. Nominee 1: Demetrius Knight Jr.’s Scoop-and-Score Myles Murphy knocked the ball loose from Baker Mayfield, and Knight Jr. picked it up and raced 27 yards for the touchdown. It’s hard to beat a defensive touchdown for this award. It was Cincinnati’s first score of the season and the first big statement from a defense that has spent the offseason trying to change its reputation. Something poetic about Demetrius Knight Jr. being the first to score a touchdown for the Bengals this year. After getting a ton of hate last year & this offseason, nice to see him get his moment. If you believe in omens, this’d be a great one for his sophomore year… pic.twitter.com/QKY2PbonmF — Bengalscentre (@benga1scentre) September 14, 2026 Nominee 2: Bryan Cook’s Goal-Line Fumble Recovery Mayfield lost the football near the Cincinnati goal line, and Cook recovered it in the end zone. Tampa Bay was knocking on the door. Instead of seven points—or at minimum a field goal—the Bengals walked away with the football. That’s the kind of play that can completely change a game. Bryan Cook with a great debut for the Bengals. Flies all around the field, is physical, and made some huge splash plays with a forced fumble and a fumble recovery on two separate plays. pic.twitter.com/YUCHzyKULl — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) September 15, 2026 Nominee 3: Evan McPherson’s 58-Yard Field Goal With Tampa Bay having cut Cincinnati’s lead to 27-20, McPherson drilled…

full_text: BEREA, OHIO - JUNE 11: Teven Jenkins #78 of the Cleveland Browns talks with Zak Zinter #70 and Zion Johnson #77 during the Cleveland Browns Mandatory Minicamp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on June 11, 2026 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images The Cleveland Browns began practice preparations for Week 2 versus Baker Mayfield and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers as big underdogs on the road . While it is not anyone’s expectation, it might take Deshaun Watson throwing for “400 yards and five touchdowns” for the Browns to overcome the Bucs, with both teams coming off Week 1 losses. Injuries always play a role in the NFL, including Cleveland being without their top backup running back, Dylan Sampson , for at least four weeks . title: TE Dae’Quan Wright will not return to the Browns, NFL this year as league puts its foot down
summary: While many predicted chaos as NIL and more money (legally now) entered college football, no one could have predicted the wild turns surrounding a tight end fighting for a backup or practice squad spot on an NFL roster. Yet, here we are with former Cleveland Browns TE Dae’Quan Wright, as well as DT Zxavian Harris. […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - AUGUST 22: Dae'Quan Wright #88 of the Cleveland Browns warms up prior to a preseason game against the Buffalo Bills at Huntington Bank Field on August 22, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images While many predicted chaos as NIL and more money (legally now) entered college football, no one could have predicted the wild turns surrounding a tight end fighting for a backup or practice squad spot on an NFL roster. Yet, here we are with former Cleveland Browns TE Dae’Quan Wright , as well as DT Zxavian Harris . A quick catch-up for everyone who hasn’t been following the story: The Cleveland Browns added Wright in mid-August after the Philadelphia Eagles waived him Wright was mostly away from the Browns for the first week he was on the roster, then came news that he was part of a lawsuit attempting to return to college Cleveland then waived Wright , which opened up his chance to return to college Given his plan to return to school, no other NFL team claimed Wright Lawsuits went back and forth , including the SEC making it a rule that schools would face punishment if they rostered players who had declared for and/or signed a professional contract. Another lawsuit said that wasn’t acceptable. Then most of us got lost in the legalese of it all Wright and Zxavian Harris were not placed on LSU’s roster for their game against Clemson , despite reportedly enrolling and practicing LSU officially filled their roster, leaving no chance for Wright and Harris to play for them this year At the end of the last linked piece in the list above, we asked Browns fans whether they would want Wright back, likely on the practice squad, now that he wasn’t going to be playing for LSU. As preparations began for Week 2 of the NFL season, the league made it very clear to teams that Wright and Harris were not welcome this season: Today’s full NFL memo, clarifying that Zxavian Harris and Dae’Quan Wright are barred from visiting, trying out with or being signed by NFL clubs during the 2026 NFL season. https://t.co/mhYoCGBd9T pic.twitter.com/TikNSW1nus — Tom Pelissero (@TomPelissero) September 16, 2026 Likely, the NFL is setting a precedent to make sure players do not attempt to circumvent the NFL draft and other player acquisition processes and mechanisms. The league also doesn’t like players controlling their own destiny in ways that are different than the ones the NFL sets. Given that Wright and Harris have gone through a number of legal battles already, it is likely this action by the league could create another. Then again, even if a court overturns the NFL’s ruling, will a team go against the league’s wishes and sign a backup, practice squad player? Join the conversation! title: Browns QB Deshaun Watson believes media sets unrealistic expectations for him
summary: When it comes to self-awareness, Cleveland Browns QB Deshaun Watson seems to be lacking, as his infamous press conference proved. On top of that, his play on the field has been even worse, including Week 1’s destruction at the hands of the Jacksonville Jaguars. Now, rarely does one player cause a loss or create a […]
full_text: BEREA, OHIO - JUNE 07: Deshaun Watson #4 of the Cleveland Browns speaks during a press conference after the Cleveland Browns mandatory veteran minicamp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on June 7, 2023 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images When it comes to self-awareness, Cleveland Browns QB Deshaun Watson seems to be lacking, as his infamous press conference proved . On top of that, his play on the field has been even worse, including Week 1’s destruction at the hands of the Jacksonville Jaguars. Now, rarely does one player cause a loss or create a win. When it happens, it is often the quarterback who can pull it off. Right or wrong, the head coach and quarterback tend to get the heavy end of the blame and credit for a team’s performance. HC Todd Monken and Watson earned the fans’ ire after Week 1, which was only added to when Monken backed his starting quarterback . According to Watson, continuing to show a lack of self-awareness, a lot of that is because the media sets unrealistic expectations for him: #Browns Deshaun Watson on if he needs to have a big game to get the nod at home and also build up goodwill for the return to Huntington Bank Field: pic.twitter.com/aA37LoCgpr — Mary Kay Cabot (@MaryKayCabot) September 16, 2026 As pretty much everyone who responded said, at this point fans are just hoping for adequate or average play from the quarterback. Forget 400 yards and five touchdowns. Forget living up to his contract. Forget not being the primary reason the team lost. Average. Adequate. The sunk cost of the trade and the contract, on top of moving on from Baker Mayfield , is water under the bridge at this point. Fans and media would just like to see Watson look like he belongs as one of the best 32 quarterbacks in the NFL, even if it is among the bottom 10. Instead, Cleveland fans rightfully are wishing for a variety of other backup quarterbacks, including their own, because Watson cannot reach that low, low expectation on the field. title: Browns legend Joe Thomas: Team’s failures broke him one year, Manning’s wild request
summary: When Cleveland Browns Hall of Famer Joe Thomas spoke to DBN’s Barry Shuck a couple of years ago, he was open and honest about how difficult it was to play for a losing team. Thomas, like former Browns DE Myles Garrett, put on great performances on the field only to see their team lose over […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OH - NOVEMBER 27, 2016: Left tackle Joe Thomas #73 of the Cleveland Browns kneels during timeout in the second quarter of a game against the New York Giants on November 27, 2016 at FirstEnergy Stadium in Cleveland, Ohio. New York won 27-13. (Photo by: Nick Cammett/Diamond Images/Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images When Cleveland Browns Hall of Famer Joe Thomas spoke to DBN’s Barry Shuck a couple of years ago , he was open and honest about how difficult it was to play for a losing team. Thomas, like former Browns DE Myles Garrett , put on great performances on the field only to see their team lose over and over again. Thomas and Garrett are locked together as the best modern-day Cleveland players , who both rarely saw any chance of winning championships in the orange and brown. While Garrett was moved in a trade, Thomas continues to talk about the Browns, including comments on Baker Mayfield and, recently, Deshaun Watson . Most of the time, Thomas has presented a measured approach to talking about his career and football. This video, talking about how Cleveland’s struggles broke him after one game, was less measured and spoke to what many Browns fans have also felt, while not actually playing at an all-time great level: Joe Thomas says he cried after playing a perfect game in a 30 point loss to Tom Brady and realized he had spent 10 years fooling himself into believing the Browns were a Super Bowl team before each season “The way I entered every season was like, if I need to get the most out of… pic.twitter.com/i9ksUFXIby — dank (@cptdankkk) September 15, 2026 Later in the interview, Thomas talked about a phone call he received from QB Peyton Manning when the Denver Broncos were trying to trade for him . The Hall of Famer noted he was happy in Cleveland, even if he was broken by the team’s performance, so he would not demand a trade. Manning then had a much more extreme idea: Peyton Manning wanted Joe Thomas to take a 💩 on the GM’s desk so he would get traded 😂 pic.twitter.com/lhu7IlXe2E — Bussin' With The Boys (@BussinWTB) September 15, 2026 Putting the two videos together, you have to wonder if Thomas now regrets not asking for the trade when he could have joined a Super Bowl-caliber team. From a heartfelt, sad statement about how he felt after playing a “perfect” game but losing by 30 to a discussion about defecating on GM Ray Farmer’s desk, the Joe Thomas experience. Plus, he dives into the thought process of the entire team after their season-opening loss. An unusual offensive showing by the Dallas Cowboys helped to torpedo their potential to put up points in their narrow 28-20 loss to the New York Giants in Week 1. And with another division opponent, the Washington Commanders, heading their way, the urgency is there to avoid starting the 2026 season with an 0-2 record in the NFC East. “It’s definitely urgent, because it’s [another] division game, such as the Giants was,” said All-Pro receiver George Pickens after Wednesday’s practice. “We definitely need to nail down our Ps and Qs. The discourse du jour on Wednesday at the Cowboys’ team facility was, ironically, about defensive communication. It was lacking in a 28-20 season-opening loss to the Giants on Sunday , much to the surprise of the team’s coaching staff. Locke wanted people to consider something. “Communication is an ongoing thing,” Locke said. “It doesn’t just stop. You just don’t get good at it. You’ve got to keep improving it. Last season, he had a Pro Football Focus (PFF) grade of 57.4 overall with a pass-blocking grade under 50. His PFF grade for Sunday was 70.2 overall. title: Cowboys playoff tracker: How loss to Giants affects Cowboys’ playoff chances
summary: After every Cowboys game this season, we will try to post a playoff tracker in which we look at the Cowboys’ latest playoff chances. And we will continue doing this until a playoff berth is secured – or until they are eliminated from playoff contention. With the season opener out of the way, the Giants […]
full_text: Football: NFC Playoffs: Dallas Cowboys fan in stands holding up sign during game vs Detroit Lions at AT&T Stadium. Arlington, TX 1/4/2015 CREDIT: Greg Nelson (Photo by Greg Nelson /Sports Illustrated via Getty Images) (Set Number: X159116 TK1 ) After every Cowboys game this season, we will try to post a playoff tracker in which we look at the Cowboys’ latest playoff chances. And we will continue doing this until a playoff berth is secured – or until they are eliminated from playoff contention. With the season opener out of the way, the Giants are undefeated and the Cowboys are winless. Does that mean the Cowboys should immediately go into tank mode to secure the No. 1 draft pick? And should the undefeated Giants start resting their starters for the playoffs? Not so fast. The NFL expanded the playoff field to 14 teams in 2020, with seven teams from each conference now qualifying. Since then, 84 teams have made the playoffs over six seasons. More importantly for the Cowboys, 27% of teams that started 0-1 from 2020 through 2025 eventually made the playoffs. Teams that started 1-0 made the playoffs 61% of the time. So all is not lost for the Cowboys. But their historical playoff rate certainly didn’t improve with Sunday’s loss. The graphic below shows how often teams with each W/L record after each of their first nine games eventually made the playoffs from 2020 through 2025. The numbers illustrate why an 0-1 start creates some urgency. The brevity of the NFL season means that if you follow up a season-opening loss with more losses, you’ll be out of the playoff race pretty fast. In other words, next week’s game against Washington is already approaching must-win territory: Start the season 0-2 and your historical playoff rate drops to just 15%; three consecutive losses to start the season and that historical playoff rate drops to just 4%, and for all intents and purposes, your season is over. The Cowboys lost their opener and are now looking at a 27% historical playoff rate. If they had won, they’d be sitting pretty with a 61% historical playoff rate. But let’s not get ahead of ourselves. The good news is that getting back to .500 already changes the picture considerably. Historically, teams sitting at 1-1 after two games made the playoffs 43% of the time. Win the next two, and the Cowboys would be 2-1 — a record that historically translated into a 62% playoff rate. So there’s no reason to panic after one game. But there is reason to pay attention. We’ll try to keep tracking the numbers every week. Hopefully, the next update starts with a 1-1 record.
