title: How to fix the Cowboys Sunday night defensive disaster
summary: The Dallas Cowboys’ defense on Sunday night was an absolute sieve. It was especially disappointing, considering the elevated expectations we placed on this new group from the multitude of big changes the team made over the last several months. The New York Giants made this unit look silly as the defense failed to do the […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - SEPTEMBER 13: Malik Nabers #1 of the New York Giants runs after the catch during the third quarter of the game against the Dallas Cowboys on September 13, 2026 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys’ defense on Sunday night was an absolute sieve. It was especially disappointing, considering the elevated expectations we placed on this new group from the multitude of big changes the team made over the last several months. The New York Giants made this unit look silly as the defense failed to do the simplest of things. It’s one thing to lose, but how it all went down has created doubt about just how effective the 2026 “new and improved” defensive group can be this year. For a better sense of what went wrong, we’re going to take a closer look at this defensive apocalypse and examine what mistakes are fixable and what are legitimate concerns. Read option readiness The problem: Edge defenders took the bait and completely abandoned their lane responsibilities Offensive coordinator Matt Nagy didn’t need to be sneaky, as the Cowboys defense wasn’t fooled by masked intentions. Instead, it was just sheer overaggressiveness and their inability to control themselves. Again and again, the Cowboys edge rushers crashed inside, attacking a ball-less Cam Skattebo, while Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart took off in another direction. By the time the defense figured out what happened, Dart was already several yards downfield. The linebackers were slow to scrape over, turning basic option runs into continuous chunk yardage plays. Fixability: Easy The good news is this isn’t a physical limitation. The defense just needs better discipline. The coaches must instill the importance of holding their assignment and stop trying to be the hero on every play. It’s concerning that so many got caught and hints that the group as a whole is too amped up, but it’s totally correctable. Coming up flat on the flat The problem: Complete lack of spatial awareness and closing speed on underneath routes The flat turned out to be the safe zone for the Giants offense, especially down the stretch. The Cowboys’ linebackers and safeties were so focused on managing traffic over the middle that they were hanging too far back and couldn’t react quickly enough to make plays in the flat. Swing passes that should have been minimal gains turned into chunkier plays because the nearest reactor had too far to go. Fixability: Moderate While the read-option problem is a player discipline issue, defending the flat is shared by the player and coaches. It requires a schematic adjustment to stop conceding the underneath so easily, but it also requires quicker reaction from defenders to get on the move before the ball leaves the quarterback’s hand. The players have the quickness, so the limiter isn’t athleticism, but more cerebral. Soft coverage The problem: Allowing receivers to sneak into soft spots in coverage Far too often, the Giants’ pass-catchers were left unattended in the secondary with no defender anywhere close. It almost seemed effortless for receivers to sneak behind the linebackers and find space. Again, the Cowboys were more concerned about giving up the big play, to the point where they allowed too much cushion on short and intermediate stuff. The soft zone coverage had too many holes, and it really wasn’t all that difficult for Dart to lob throws to his targets. Fixability: Moderate Better communication and quicker reaction can tighten up some of these creases, but there’s a fine line between trusting the players to make the changes and considering adjusting the scheme. The Cowboys must figure out which is more pertinent because if they stubbornly employ a coverage scheme that isn’t working, it will be a slow death this year compared to the fast one last year, but a death no less. Free chances The problem: Too many penalties at the worst possible time In a game where possessions were scarce, the Cowboys could ill afford to give the Giants freebies, but that’s exactly what they did. The penalties in this game came in many forms and on both sides of the ball. They had two offside penalties from anxious defenders, both coming on short-yardage plays. They had a late hit out of bounds and a facemask penalty from players caught in the heat of the moment. And there was the taunting penalty, where a player was showboating late in the game despite being down two scores. All these infractions gave the Giants free yards and extra chances. Fixability: Hard Penalties usually stem from poor technique from desperate players in recovery mode, while others are just mental miscues. The Cowboys’ penalties fall into the latter category, and while those are easier to correct, Brian Schottenheimer’s track record with the team isn’t inspiring. Last year, the Cowboys had 133 accepted penalties, the most in the NFL. Showing such a lack of discipline right out of the gate suggests more of these mistakes are coming. The Cowboys’ performance Sunday night has fans backpedaling their excitement for the season, and that’s fair. But it would be more concerning if the root cause is a lack of talent rather than things that can be corrected. The coaching staff has their work cut out for them and must help the players carry out their plan. If they can’t bridge the gap quickly, they could dig themselves an early hole that they might not be able to crawl out of.

title: 2026 NFL Week 2: Dallas Cowboys vs. Washington Commanders
summary: Welcome to Week 2 of the Dallas Cowboys season. For the first, and hopefully last, time the Cowboys are looking to bounce back from a loss. This past Sunday was a humbling experience for the Cowboys as they had an enormous amount of positivity heading into the season opener, but football is a meritocracy and […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - DECEMBER 25: Jayden Daniels #5 of the Washington Commanders and Dak Prescott #4 of the Dallas Cowboys after Dallas' 30-23 victory at Northwest Stadium on December 25, 2025 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by G Fiume/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to Week 2 of the Dallas Cowboys season. For the first, and hopefully last, time the Cowboys are looking to bounce back from a loss. This past Sunday was a humbling experience for the Cowboys as they had an enormous amount of positivity heading into the season opener, but football is a meritocracy and the New York Giants earned the right to win that game. This week the Cowboys will have to out work and out earn another division rival in the Washington Commanders. Like Dallas, Washington lost in Week 1 to a division rival in the Philadelphia Eagles. This means that the loser of this game is going to be sitting at 0-2 overall and within the NFC East. Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, Javonte Williams and the rest of Brian Schottenheimer’s “GOTI” offense are going to have to be more consistent if they want to change the team’s fortunes. What’s more is that the defense is going to need more than Caleb Downs to shine. Quinnen Williams, Donovan Ezeriuaku, DaRon Bland, and specifically Christian Parker are going to have to make sure last week was an aberration. This post will serve as our story stream for the week. All articles related to the game will cycle through. Here we go. title: Cowboys vs. Commanders: Matchups to watch in Week 2
summary: After last week’s embarrassing performance against the New York Giants, the Dallas Cowboys return home this week to take on another division foe, the Washington Commanders. Hopefully playing in front of their hometown crowd will light the fire inside everyone that look to be lacking last week, because they can’t afford to start 0-2, especially […]
full_text: After last week’s embarrassing performance against the New York Giants, the Dallas Cowboys return home this week to take on another division foe, the Washington Commanders. Hopefully playing in front of their hometown crowd will light the fire inside everyone that look to be lacking last week, because they can’t afford to start 0-2, especially with the division. To help secure the “W” this week the Cowboys would be wise to try to exploit certain matchups to help sway the game in their favor. We’ve identified the ones we believe could help the Cowboys secure the victory this week against the Commanders. Hopefully it pays off with their first win of the season. WR George Pickens vs. Commanders’ secondary George Pickens didn’t have his best season debut last week against the Giants, dropping several passes, but has a chance to rebound in a big way this week against the Commanders secondary. It’s somewhat of a patchwork unit right now with Trey Amos sidelined and the Cowboys would be wise to exploit that. Targeting Pickens early and often should help rebuild his confidence as well as help get the entire offense back on track after a ho-hum performance last week. OLB Donovan Ezeiruaku vs. LT Brandon Coleman The Cowboys traded for Rashan Gary and drafted Malachi Lawrence in the hopes of upgrading their pass rush along with second-year OLB Donovan Ezeiruaku, but you couldn’t tell from their Week 1 performance. The pass rush was pretty much nonexistent last week, allowing Giants QB Jaxon Dart to pick them apart. Expect that to change this week in the head-to-head battle between Ezeiruaku and Brandon Coleman, who is filling in at LT for an injured Laremy Tunsil. LB Jaishawn Barham vs. RB Jacory Croskey-Merritt Barham, the Cowboys third-round pick this year, will play a much bigger role for the next few weeks while DeMarvion Overshown is out with a hamstring injury. Hopefully his physical play will help improve what was an abysmal performance against the run last week against the Giants. Jacory Croskey-Merritt doesn’t run with the same type of physicality as Cam Skattebo, but he has the potential to be dangerous nonetheless. Hopefully No. 55 can help contain him.

title: The Parker Report: How the Cowboys defense fared in week 1
summary: With NFL Week 1 in the books, lets take a look at how first-year defensive coordinator Christian Parker and his revamped defense looked against the Giants. Team stats allowed In their first week of action, the Cowboys defense gave up 394 total yards, 29 first downs, and allowed an 82% third down conversion rate (9/11). […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - SEPTEMBER 13: Cam Skattebo #44 of the New York Giants runs against three Dallas Cowboys defenders during the game on September 13, 2026 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images With NFL Week 1 in the books, lets take a look at how first-year defensive coordinator Christian Parker and his revamped defense looked against the Giants. Team stats allowed In their first week of action, the Cowboys defense gave up 394 total yards, 29 first downs, and allowed an 82% third down conversion rate (9/11). The team recorded two sacks and took advantage of one turnover on a forced fumble. The real gut punch here is the quantity of turnover worthy plays on defense (five) while only walking away with just the one. The main storyline is of the game, however, is time of possession. The Giants offense was also their best defense, as they controlled the ball for over 36 minutes. The inability of the Cowboys defense to get off the field kept Dak and the high powered offense on the sideline, seeing the field just twice in the second half. Individual stat leaders Second-year edge Donovan Ezeiruaku had one of the better nights on defense. He led the team with ten tackles, had a half sack, two hits on the quarterback, and one forced fumble. Caleb Downs was the only player to finish with a full sack on the stat sheet. The quarterback takedown came on a well disguised slot blitz. The devastating blind side hit forced a Jaxson Dart fumble, conveniently landing in the waiting arms of a Giants offensive lineman. This was exactly the playmaking ability Downs showcased throughout his time at Alabama and Ohio State. Speaking of fumbles, the team forced four of them but only recovered one. Donovan Ezeiruaku, Caleb Downs, Cobie Durant and Quinnen Williams each had their turn jarring the ball loose. The lone fumble recovery came on the Quinnen Williams punchout, which bounced right into Shavon Revel’s lap. Advanced analytics The Cowboys rolled out their 3-4 base on 28 snaps (41.2%), allowing 112 yards. They lined up in nickel on 24 snaps (35.3%) but allowed a whopping 215 yards. It’s interesting to see that the extra DB is what spurred the leaky defense. The coverage split was 77.8% zone and 22.2% man. Dallas lived in a two-high or three-deep zone structure throughout most of the day. The Cowboys blitzed at the seventh highest rate in week one, but that translated to just the 21st ranking in pressures. And when Dallas rushed only four, Jaxson Dart went 17-of-19 for 200 yards and two touchdowns. Dallas bit hard on the play-action. Dart was 5-of-7, had a touchdown, and ran for 26 yards on off the play fake. The young edges consistently crashed hard, opening outside lanes for Dart on the rollout pass or to take off and run. How’d the rookies look? Caleb Downs played nearly every snap on defense. The young star made his presence known with a huge hit on Jaxson Dart, forcing a fumble that was recovered by the Giants. His final stat line would read eight tackles, one sack, one forced fumble, and one QB hit. Where he could improve would be his pass coverage win rate. Great start for the rookie, but there is still much improvement to be had. Malachi Lawrence was not good enough. He was involved in more than one negative big play on Sunday night. Too many times we saw him bite on play fakes, crashing down while leaving a huge void to the outside. His pass rush was nearly non-existent. Lawrence ended the night as the fourth lowest rated player on defense against the Giants. Jaishawn Barham finished the night with six tackles as a rotational linebacker. He had one noticeable hit in the backfield, but outside of that was somewhat forgettable. There were questions about his effort late in the game as the Giants connected in the flat multiple plays in a row on their way to a game sealing touchdown. With Overshown potentially missing up to two weeks , we should see more of Barham against the Commanders and Ravens. LT Overton played a small role Sunday night but did finish with one tackle and one pass breakup at the line. With a strong preseason and a solid first game with limited snaps, expect to see his role grow as the season continues. Final grade: D- The Cowboys came into MetLife Stadium with high expectations surrounding a fresh start on a rebuilt defense. What the Cowboys got was more of the same. There is no nice way to put this: this team was dominated on the defensive side of the ball. While they limited the explosive plays of over 15 yards, they allowed the Giants offense to methodically work their way down the field for touchdowns while chewing up so much clock that their own offense saw the field just twice in the second half. We witnessed large voids in coverage more than once, resulting in touchdowns and first downs. Some mental mistakes are to be expected for a new defense, but too many of the same misses can be seen on film. Dallas will need to get this corrected in a hurry if they want to keep pace in the NFC. The only reason this defense doesn’t get an F is because they forced four fumbles. The law of averages did not apply as the ball seemed magnetized to Giants players after being stripped on more than one occasion. If the Cowboys can tighten up but also keep their intensity around punchouts and strip sacks, the football will bounce their way and win them some games. The Cowboys have a ton of work to do on the defensive side of the ball. Their next test comes at home against the Washington Commanders this Sunday. Jaxson Dart’s mobility was crucial for the Giants victory and Dallas faces another one coming to town in Jayden Daniels. It’s imperative this defense doesn’t overcommit to the inside play fakes because Daniels will take the run option every single time. We’ll see if Parker will make the proper adjustments in week two.
author: Dyllan Rivers

title: Cowboys opponent: A look at the Commanders for Week 2
summary: The Dallas Cowboys dropped their Week 1 game and are looking to bounce back. They don’t have to wait long for another NFC East opponent. After opening the season with a 28-20 loss to the New York Giants, Dallas returns home Sunday to face the Washington Commanders, who are also coming off a one-score loss […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - DECEMBER 25: Jacory Croskey-Merritt #22 of the Washington Commanders runs the ball against the Dallas Cowboys in the third quarter of a game at Northwest Stadium on December 25, 2025 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Greg Fiume/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys dropped their Week 1 game and are looking to bounce back. They don’t have to wait long for another NFC East opponent. After opening the season with a 28-20 loss to the New York Giants, Dallas returns home Sunday to face the Washington Commanders, who are also coming off a one-score loss in Week 1. Washington fell 24-22 to the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday, but the final score doesn’t tell the entire story. The Commanders showed some promising things in their first game under a new offensive coordinator and with a revamped defense, including some impressive physicality on special teams. This may be the greatest punt coverage you’ll ever see from a gunner 😤 pic.twitter.com/SmYgIV9A2g — Footballism (@FootbaIIism) September 14, 2026 They also showed some of the issues that helped produce a 5-12 record last season. Now, Washington heads to Arlington for its first road game of 2026. Here’s what Cowboys fans need to know. A lot changed in Washington this offseason The Commanders spent the offseason rebuilding a team that finished 5-12 in 2025. The biggest changes came on defense, at the behest of former Cowboys DC Dan Quinn. Washington brought in several new pieces and entered the season with a revamped unit under new defensive coordinator Daronte Jones. The Commanders also added to their offense including veteran receiver Stefon Diggs, giving quarterback Jayden Daniels another established weapon alongside Terry McLaurin. The Commanders’ offense also has a new play caller. David Blough took over as offensive coordinator, meaning Daniels is operating in his third offensive system in three seasons. That transition looked uneven in Week 1. Washington also added rookie linebacker Sonny Styles with the seventh overall pick. He immediately made an impact in Week 1, recording a sack against Philadelphia. Sonny Styles NFL Debut vs Eagles. 4 TKL, 2 TFL, 1 SACK, 1 QBH. https://t.co/ma4aR4UFim pic.twitter.com/jZH8wB8udC — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) September 14, 2026 Jayden Daniels is back, but he wasn’t quite himself yet This is still Jayden Daniels’ team. After an injury-plagued 2025 season, Daniels returned to regular-season action Sunday, September 13, against Philadelphia and finished 18-of-34 for 164 yards and two touchdowns, adding 31 yards on five rushing attempts. The numbers weren’t spectacular, but the fourth quarter offered a glimpse of what Washington hopes its offense can become. Daniels threw touchdown passes to Diggs and rookie Antonio Williams as the Commanders scored 13 fourth-quarter points and turned a 24-9 deficit into a two-point game. The problem was everything that came before it. Washington had just 50 yards on its seven non-scoring drives, struggling to sustain drives for long stretches. That’s something Dallas’ defense will have to account for Sunday: Which Washington offense shows up for four quarters? And can they make enough plays to keep the Commanders’ offense off-balance? Washington can run the football If there was one thing the Commanders did consistently against Philadelphia, it was run the football. Washington finished with 132 rushing yards on 32 attempts, averaging 4.1 yards per carry. Jacory Croskey-Merritt led the way with 63 yards and a touchdown on 16 carries. Rachaad White added 22 yards on seven carries, while Daniels contributed another 31 yards. If Week 1 was a sign of things to come, this is obviously a cause for concern for Dallas. The Cowboys just watched the Giants control the game on the ground and through time of possession in Week 1. New York ran 68 offensive plays to Dallas’ 52, held the ball for more than 36 minutes in the 28-20 victory, and, as many have pointed out, limited the Cowboys to two possessions in the second half. If the Commanders can establish their running game, they can keep Daniels out of obvious passing situations while pressuring a Dallas defense that allowed 394 total yards to New York in Week 1. Stefon Diggs is already involved One of Washington’s biggest offseason additions made an immediate impact. Diggs caught four passes for 55 yards and a touchdown against Philadelphia. He also drew attention for a costly unsportsmanlike conduct penalty after his touchdown celebration, a mistake that affected Washington’s late-game two-point strategy. Still, his presence gives Daniels something the quarterback didn’t have for much of last season: another veteran receiver capable of winning matchups outside of McLaurin. McLaurin caught only two passes for 14 yards in Week 1, but one came during Washington’s fourth-quarter comeback. The combination of McLaurin and Diggs will be one of the things to watch on Sunday whenever Washington’s offense takes the field. The defense looked better in spots Washington’s defense had a respectable opening week against Philadelphia. The Commanders held the Eagles to 318 total yards, including 203 passing yards and 136 rushing yards. Washington generated three sacks, and the pressure came from multiple places. Frankie Luvu, Odafe Oweh and rookie Sonny Styles each recorded a sack. The defense also did a good job limiting Philadelphia’s offense for long stretches. But the Commanders gave up several explosive plays and struggled with communication in the secondary. That’s where the matchup with Dallas will be interesting. The Cowboys struggled to generate sustained offense against New York, producing just 244 total yards and 20 points. Dak Prescott threw for 175 yards, while Dallas averaged only 3.8 yards per rushing attempt. So, Week 2 presents a straightforward question for the Cowboys. Can Dallas create more explosive plays against a Washington defense that has also shown it can give up opportunities in the secondary? Antonio Williams is worth knowing Keep an eye on Antonio Williams. The rookie receiver wasn’t even listed as one of Washington’s three starting receivers on the team’s initial depth chart. Still, he led the Commanders in receiving against Philadelphia, catching four passes for 64 yards and a touchdown. His touchdown was part of Washington’s fourth-quarter comeback. Williams also fits the profile of the young players Washington is trying to develop around Daniels. The Commanders have praised his route-running ability and his versatility to play both inside and outside. After one game, he has already given Washington another name for opposing defenses to account for, and could be part of a suddenly deep Washington receiving corps with the potential to damage any defense. Jayden Daniels to the rookie, Antonio Williams, for a TD ‼️ WASvsPHI on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/rznfyftIjU — NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026 This is a different Washington team than Dallas saw last year The Cowboys swept the Commanders last season, winning the final matchup 30-23 at Washington, but this year’s Commanders look different. There’s a new offensive coordinator, a revamped defense, a healthy Daniels and a new veteran weapon in Diggs. Washington is also trying to establish a more balanced offense built around its quarterback’s ability to threaten defenses with both his arm and legs. So far, returns are mixed, but it’s just Week 2. The Commanders moved the ball for 295 yards against Philadelphia but converted only 5 of 15 third downs. They scored 22 points despite producing only 20 first downs. Both teams are 0-1. Both have new questions after Week 1, and both have already seen enough of their new-look teams to know that some changes need to be made. The Cowboys and Commanders will meet Sunday at AT&T Stadium, with both teams looking to put their first loss of 2026 behind them.

title: 3 things we learned about the Cowboys in Week 1 loss
summary: The Dallas Cowboys kicked off the season against the New York Giants, and it gave them a shot to get a big win in the NFC East. Many thought it would happen due to the Cowboys dominance against the Giants over the last decade, but things didn’t turn out that way. For the game, Dallas […]
full_text: Sep 13, 2026; East Rutherford, New Jersey, USA; Dallas Cowboys running back Javonte Williams (33) carries the ball for a touchdown against the New York Giants during the fourth quarter at MetLife Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Dallas Cowboys kicked off the season against the New York Giants, and it gave them a shot to get a big win in the NFC East. Many thought it would happen due to the Cowboys dominance against the Giants over the last decade, but things didn’t turn out that way. For the game, Dallas only amassed 244 total yards and they held the ball for just over 23 minutes. The running game was virtually nonexistent as the Cowboys gained a pedestrian 69 yards while averaging only 3.8 yards per carry. Defensively, the gave up nine conversions on eleven third down plays by the Giants. Not ideal at all. The Cowboys have a lot to clean up before playing the Washington Commanders this Sunday in their home opener. Before that takes place, let’s dive into three things we learned about Dallas in Week 1. It’s going to take time for Christian Parker’s defense to gel One of the additions to the Cowboys that had people the most excited during the offseason was defensive coordinator Christian Parker. However, many forgot the fact that although he has a great football mind, Sunday night was his first time calling plays for a defense in a real game, and it showed. Parker was thoroughly out coached by Giants offensive coordinator Matt Nagy, and the most alarming part was the lack of adjustments he made when things weren’t going well. It’s only the first game for Parker in this role, which does give him some grace. Plus, there’s a ton of new players and his system is also new, and running it in training camp and the preseason isn’t the same as when the regular season starts. So, Parker has to get back to the drawing board before Week 2, and even if they do play better, it will take some time to get everything flowing the way he wants it to. Penalties are still an issue In 2025, the Cowboys lead the NFL with 133 penalties and they were second in most yards penalized with 1,136. They didn’t get off to a good start this season in that regard as they were called for nine penalties against the Giants which totaled 90 yards. This is glaring issue that somehow keeps plaguing Dallas regardless of who the coach has been over the last decade. The biggest, and without question the most costly penalty, came late in the fourth quarter when running back Javonte Williams got a taunting penalty after he scored a touchdown which led to a missed extra point by kicker Brandon Aubrey. The Cowboys had planned to go for a two-point conversion there, but the penalty changed their minds. Head coach Brian Schottenheimer has got to find a way to get this problem rectified. Lack of pass rush is concerning Dallas simply could not make life difficult for Jaxson Dart on Sunday night. The rushed him with four players on 20 plays, but the only generated two pressures. Whenever they decided to blitz him, he either made plays with his legs or found wide open targets. It routinely happened as the Giants carved the Cowboys up third down which led to over 36 minutes of time of possession. This issue is one that the Cowboys will have a hard time overcoming because they don’t have the talent up front defensively to consistently get pressure although they have Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark on the interior. They have time to make improvements, but how much they can do so without the right type of players is the question. This will likely be a season long thing.

title: Cowboys positional rankings reveal where accountability needs to start
summary: For me it’s quite simple: Because the expectations for the offense and defense were quite high, and both units were outcoached and outplayed by the Giants, the accountability falls squarely on Brian Schottenheimer and Christian Parker. Alas, if only simple answers were the right answers – they almost never are. One of the team captains, […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - SEPTEMBER 13: Brian Schottenheimer head coach of the Dallas Cowboys during the third quarter of the game against the New York Giants on September 13, 2026 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images For me it’s quite simple: Because the expectations for the offense and defense were quite high, and both units were outcoached and outplayed by the Giants, the accountability falls squarely on Brian Schottenheimer and Christian Parker. Alas, if only simple answers were the right answers – they almost never are. The Cowboys went from two red-flag performances retained from the entire 2025 season to 12 in one game . And perhaps even more strikingly, the team went from 13 starter-quality performances retained or acquired from 2025 to just four against the Giants . This wasn’t simply a bad game. It was a remarkable concentration of bad individual performances . One of the team captains, Quinnen Williams, has spoken up and announced the team would take accountability . I think the takeaway is this: Quinnen wanted to make sure he said certain things into a microphone, and a lot of it centered around the idea of the team embracing criticism this week. That doesn't mean things will get better, but it means they aren't delusional about last night. https://t.co/hwe1E4RZca — Bobby Belt (@BobbyBeltTX) September 14, 2026 The idea today is to look at positional rankings (or percentile rankings) to identify which players and units need to take a little more constructive criticism than others. We’ve covered positional rankings extensively this offseason, go here if you need a quick primer . The idea is that instead of using a player’s raw PFF Grade, we look at where a given player is ranked relative to the other players in the league at his position. Relative positional performance gives us a way to separate the players who actually hurt the Cowboys from those who merely looked bad because the team lost. Example: Jalen Thompson has a 43.7 Grade for the season opener, which suggests he had a slightly below-average game. But he ranks 71 out of 84 qualifying safeties, which would give him a positional ranking (1 – position rank / total qualifying players) * 100 of just 15, an indication of a red flag or bottom 20 performance. title: NFL picks and predictions: Broncos vs. Jaguars and the rest of Week 2
summary: Welcome back to the second installment of Hart’s Picks for the 2026 NFL regular season. For Week 1, I was 11-5 with my predictions. Not too shabby, but a few of the outcomes were a bit of a surprise—but that is what makes football fun. Let’s see how I do with my Week 2 slate […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - AUGUST 14: Denver cornerback Pat Surtain II (2) waves to fans following the conclusion of the NFL pre-season game between the Denver Broncos and the Atlanta Falcons on August 14th, 2026 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome back to the second installment of Hart’s Picks for the 2026 NFL regular season. For Week 1, I was 11-5 with my predictions . Not too shabby, but a few of the outcomes were a bit of a surprise—but that is what makes football fun. Let’s see how I do with my Week 2 slate of picks. Detroit Lions at Buffalo Bills — Thursday Night Football Both the Lions and Bills were able to hold off their opponents and eek out close victories in Week 1. In my opinion, this has the fixings of a high-powered offensive matchup. I believe we will see a lot of points on the scoreboard. Can Jahmyr Gibbs be stopped? Can Josh Allen keep the connection to DJ Moore strong? Those are things I’ll be watching closely. This is tough to predict, but I’ll take Buffalo at home in this one. Winner: Bills Carolina Panthers at Atlanta Falcons — Sunday (Early Game) This NFC South matchup features two teams who started their seasons off with a loss. The Falcons fell short in a one score game to the Pittsburgh Steelers, while the Panthers had 59 points dropped on them by Caleb Williams and the Chicago Bears. I don’t feel very confident about this pick, but I’m taking Carolina on the road with the Falcons poised to start Cooper Rush again. Winner: Panthers Houston Texans at Cincinnati Bengals — Sunday (Early Game) Two potential playoff contenders go head-to-head in this one. The Texans fell short to the Bills in Week 1, while the Bengals were able to topple Tampa Bay in a thrilling game. Early word on this game is quarterback Joe Burrow is dealing with some back issues which may hinder his ability to be at his best against a Texans defense known for bringing pressure. If so, that could be an issue. I’m thinking the Texans bounce back this weekend and come up with a big victory on the road. Winner: Texans Philadelphia Eagles at Tennessee Titans — Sunday (Early Game) Every week there are games on the docket that don’t require much analysis. Long story short, Cam Ward and the Titans offense will likely struggle immensely against Philadelphia and Vic Fangio’s defense. They didn’t look good at all against the New York Jets last weekend. Winner: Eagles Green Bay Packers at New York Jets — Sunday (Early Game) The Jets are coming off a win over the Titans, whilst the Packers had a hard time protecting Jordan Love who took a beating in their loss to the Minnesota Vikings. I’m concerned about their ability to run the football which was an issue going up against Brian Flores’ defense. Can their offense be more cohesive this weekend against the Jets and will their offensive line step up and give Love the time he needs to succeed through the air? They’ll have to or they’ll wind up being 0-2 to start the year. I think Green Bay finds a way to win on the road. Winner: Packers New Orleans Saints at Baltimore Ravens — Sunday (Early Game) Close only counts in horseshoes and hand grenades, but the Saints gave it all they had in their Week 1 overtime loss to the Lions. Unfortunately for them, they have a tough opponent on the road in the Ravens, who manhandled the Indianapolis Colts in Week 1. I’ll diverge here for a change and go with a home team for only the second time thus far. Winner: Ravens Minnesota Vikings at Chicago Bears — Sunday (Early Game) I love a good NFC North rivalry matchup and this one centers around two teams whose offenses really impressed in Week 1. It sounds like Carson Wentz is likely to start for the Vikings after Kyler Murray exited the game against Green Bay early on with a concussion. Though I’m not sure Wentz and Minnesota’s offense can keep up with Caleb Williams and the Bears who were on fire last week scoring 59 points. I think the Bears win this matchup. Winner: Bears Cleveland Browns at Tampa Bay Buccaneers — Sunday (Early Game) You can count on less than one hand the number of times you will see me pick the Browns to win a game this season. This Sunday against Tampa Bay isn’t going to be one of them. Winner: Buccaneers Pittsburgh Steelers at New England Patriots — Sunday (Early Game) The Steelers barely beat a bad Falcons team while Drake Maye struggled immensely against the Seattle Seahawks in the regular season opener. I’m still high on Maye’s ability as a quarterback and think he will have a much stronger performance against the Steelers in Week 2. I’ll take New England at home to get back to .500 on the season. Winner: Patriots Las Vegas Raiders at Los Angeles Chargers — Sunday (Afternoon Game) The Chargers losing in epic fashion to the Arizona Cardinals was one of my Ls in my Week 1 picks. I didn’t see that one coming. Meanwhile, the Raiders were able to handle the Miami Dolphins thanks to a strong rushing attack. Can Ashton Jeanty have similar success going up against the Chargers? That will be a must if they want to win. However, I think Justin Herbert will have a rebound game and avoid going 0-2—putting both these AFC West teams at 1-1 to start the ‘26 season. Winner: Chargers Jacksonville Jaguars at Denver Broncos — Sunday (Afternoon Game) Jacksonville impressed with a Week 1 victory while Denver was dominated by the Chiefs on Monday Night Football . Broncos Country isn’t going to be happy with me picking against our team, but the Jaguars were one of just three teams to deliver Denver a loss in 2025 and have a very good team. I’m not very optimistic Denver can right all their wrongs quickly on a short week. I’m taking Jacksonville here. Sorry friends. Winners: Jaguars Washington Commanders at Dallas Cowboys — Sunday (Afternoon Game) The loser of this NFC East matchup will be the bottom dwellers of the division to start the season. The Commanders played the Eagles tough and the Cowboys struggled to establish the run against the New York Giants. In order to win this weekend, Javonte Williams needs to have a much better game. They can’t put it all on the arm of Dak Prescott to lead them to victory. I’ll go with my gut and choose Dallas. Winner: Cowboys Miami Dolphins at San Francisco 49ers — Sunday (Afternoon Game) The 49ers toppled the Los Angeles Rams down under in Australia and the Dolphins lost to the Raiders. I think it’s a relatively safe bet to take Kyle Shanahan’s squad to go to 2-0 on the year hosting Miami. San Francisco all the way. Winner: 49ers Seattle Seahawks at Arizona Cardinals — Sunday (Afternoon Game) Okay, so the Cardinals surprised most all of us and beat the Chargers. That being said, there really isn’t a good reason to believe lightning will strike twice. The odds of them being the victors against the defending Super Bowl Champions? Not good. I’ll be taking the Seahawks. Winner: Seahawks Indianapolis Colts at Kansas City Chiefs — Sunday Night Football These teams both had strong performances from their running backs in Week 1, but Kenneth Walker II was on a different planet with the way he ran roughshod over the Broncos’ defense. I expect Andy Reid and the Chiefs to keep their ground game strong against a Colts defense who gave up nearly 200 yards on the ground to the Ravens in Week 1. Winner: Chiefs New York Giants at Los Angeles Rams — Monday Night Football The John Harbaugh era started off with a bang with the Giants toppling the Cowboys in Week 1. The Rams’ season started off on a low note being walloped by the 49ers in Australia. Even worse? Myles Garrett will be out for the foreseeable future after having knee surgery a few days ago. My heart wants me to pick the Giants for a feel-good story here, but my mind has settled on Sean McVay and the Rams rebounding and earning a dub in preimtime. Winner: Rams
author: Christopher Hart

title: Questions still linger for Broncos after Week 1 loss to Chiefs
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country. Monday’s loss to the Kansas City Chiefs was a gut punch for the Denver Broncos. Losses to division rivals always sting, but how badly they were defeated still sticks in my craw. That wasn’t something I—or most any of you—expected at all. How the Broncos respond this weekend against the Jacksonville […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY , MO - SEPTEMBER 14: Brandon Jones (22) of the Denver Broncos walks off the field after the Kansas City Chiefs' 31-10 win at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri on Monday, September 14, 2026. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country. Monday’s loss to the Kansas City Chiefs was a gut punch for the Denver Broncos. Losses to division rivals always sting, but how badly they were defeated still sticks in my craw. That wasn’t something I—or most any of you—expected at all. How the Broncos respond this weekend against the Jacksonville Jaguars remains to be seen. A sign of a great team is being able to bounce back after adversity. On Sunday, we will have a better idea of what kind of team this year’s Broncos are. Later today, I’ll have a few articles discussing the upcoming matchup against the Jaguars. For this morning, I thought I’d offer up some reflection and random thoughts I had after trying to digest the manner in which the Broncos lost. Feel free to let me know what you think about these questions in the comments section. How much is Denver’s defense missing Jonathan Franklin-Myers and Jonathon Cooper? Denver’s defensive performance against the Chiefs on Monday Night Football was concerning to say the least. They were outclassed and outmatched by Andy Reid and his staff who were able to concoct a great offensive gameplan. It’s hard to single out any particular player or reason for their rough evening. Most everyone on that side of the ball had some issues. I still can’t comprehend how the tackling that bad. But that got me thinking even more—would things have been different if Franklin-Myers and Jonathon Cooper had been starting? The lack of execution was across the board, but I honestly felt like their presence was missing a great deal. Sure, it’s only one game. Though without those two, the run defense seemed to struggle immensely and the pressure on Mahomes—even with short throws—just wasn’t consistent. I think it’s safe to say there is a pretty big dropoff from the aforementioned to the players Denver has trying to replace them. I’ll be keeping my eye on this as the next few games transpire to see if it was just an aberration, or something that could be an ongoing issue for the team moving forward. How long will it take for the Broncos’ offense to get better? There is no doubt Denver is a much-improved franchise now before Head Coach Sean Payton and his staff took over. It’s been a terrific turnaround even with the stench of the loss to the Chiefs still lingering. However, slow starts have been a common theme for the Broncos in that timeframe. This past Monday was emblematic of the early season offensive struggles over the past few seasons. There wasn’t enough emphasis on the run and too much of a burden put on Bo Nix’s shoulders. I’m still bullish on Nix’s potential and think he has a great shot at taking a leap in Year 3. Nevertheless, his outing versus Kansas City was one of the worst games of his career. Though I’ll say the offensive line didn’t look that impressive and contributed to some of his lackluster play. I felt that the interior combination of Ben Powers and Luke Wattenberg struggled when confronting Steve Spagnuolo’s interior and blitz pressure packages. At right tackle, I was underwhelmed with Mike McGlinchey who seemed to have issues holding his own one-on-one in pass protection against the Chiefs’ edge rushers. The Broncos’ offensive line has performed well the past two years. Even so, a part of me wonders if defensive coordinators across the league now have a bit of a blueprint to attack some of their weaknesses. There’s no doubt Denver’s linemen have to perform better on Sunday versus the Jaguars to give Denver an honest chance at winning. As always, thank you for reading. Here is today’s slate of articles for Horse Tracks .

title: Stock Up, Stock Down After the Broncos’ Loss to the Chiefs in Week 1
summary: We’re a few days out from the Broncos’ Monday Night loss to the Chiefs, and it still stings. The Broncos opened up the season with a disappointing and downright embarrassing 31-10 loss to the Chiefs. The debut of offensive coordinator Davis Webb was a failure, and the Denver Broncos defense had a historically high missed […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs attempts to evade Que Robinson #51 of the Denver Broncos as he looks to pass during an NFL football game on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re a few days out from the Broncos’ Monday Night loss to the Chiefs, and it still stings. The Broncos opened up the season with a disappointing and downright embarrassing 31-10 loss to the Chiefs. The debut of offensive coordinator Davis Webb was a failure , and the Denver Broncos defense had a historically high missed tackle rate It was all bad. Stock up and stock down is a weekly series where I go through the Denver Broncos roster and give you stock-ups and stock-downs on every player currently on the 53-man roster. After a game like that on Monday Night, we are looking at a lot of stock downs. So, with all that said, here are your stock-ups and stock-downs for the Denver Broncos after their blowout loss to the Kansas City Chiefs. Quarterback Bo Nix – Stock down: Monday Night was one of the worst games of Bo Nix’s career thus far. He had an opening-drive interception, later fumbled the ball, was lucky not to fumble the ball again, and was sacked a total of 4 times. Not all the blame falls on Nix; he was put in a bad situation by his coaching staff (no run game), his protection sucked, and there were drive-killing drops and penalties throughout. Still, it was not a great game for Nix, and he and the Broncos need to bounce back next week. Jarrett Stidham – Unchanged: He was the backup to Bo Nix, as expected Sam Ehlinger – Unchanged: He was the emergency third-string QB, as expected Running Back JK Dobbins – Unchanged: I thought about stock down here, but he played well when given the ball. He had 8 carries for 36 yards and averaged 4.5 yards per carry. That’s what you want to see from Dobbins, just more of it. The Broncos ran the ball 6 times at halftime, and then the game got away from them in the second half. RJ Harvey – Stock up: I thought Jonah Coleman was going to be the Broncos’ RB3, but RJ Harvey seems to be firmly their RB2 or even their 1B with JK Dobbins. He out-snapped Dobbins (likely due to game script and all the passing) and played well when given the ball. His pass blocking looked questionable at best, but overall, he seems like someone who’s going to be featured in their offense moving forward. Jonah Coleman – Stock down: Coleman saw 3 offensive snaps and returned a kick. I expected to see the rookie used a little bit more, but he’s clearly behind Dobbins and Harvey right now. Tyler Badie – Unchanged: He was inactive and is their RB4. Adam Prentice – Unchanged: Only saw 6 offensive snaps and did most of his work on special teams. There was a key 3rd-and-1 where his lead blocking or short-yardage ability would have come in handy. Wide Receiver Jaylen Waddle – Stock down: All that hype, and we get 3 targets and 1 catch for 2 yards. Waddle himself was not bad, though he did have a drop on 3rd down, but his lack of targets and usage was odd to me. I would have expected the Broncos to feature the new weapon they traded for and hyped up all offseason. Yet, just 3 targets and 1 catch for 2 yards. Courtland Sutton – Unchanged: Sutton wasn’t featured much either, but we know what he and Nix can do, so I am not going to overreact here. Still, he didn’t get his first target until the 3rd quarter, I believe, which is a very odd game plan. Pat Bryant – Stock up: He played 59% of the offensive snaps and led the way for the Broncos receivers with 6 targets and 4 catches for 42 yards. He came up big for them on their lone touchdown drive and showcased why he will be a key part of this offense moving forward. He did have a couple of holding calls, which I thought were mostly BS, so I am not holding them against him. His drop on a screen play that would have led to a 1st down did suck, though. Marvin Mims – Unchanged: Mims had another injury scare, but thankfully seemed to be okay. He didn’t do much on offense but did have a few nice kick returns. We did see Troy Franklin play more offensive snaps than him, so that will be something to watch moving forward. Troy Franklin – Stock up slightly: I thought Franklin was in danger of being inactive due to the Broncos going with Lil’Jordan Humphrey, but that did not happen. LJH played the procedural off and on the roster game this week, and Franklin was active and played 33% of the offensive snaps. However, he did see just 1 target, and it was a rather bad OPI call, which set the offense back. His usage gives him stock up, but that OPI was not great. Lil’Jordan Humphrey – Unchanged: It was reported prior to the game that the Broncos released Lil’Jordan, but it was simply a procedural move and that he would rejoin the team soon. On Tuesday, it was reported that LJH re-signed with the team. I would anticipate him being active and utilized a little more moving forward, but we shall see. Tight End Adam Trautman – Unchanged: He did catch 2 passes for 10 yards, but that’s not why he’s on the roster. He’s a run-blocking tight end, one that is being paid decently by a team that refuses to run the ball. Make that make sense. Evan Engram – Stock up: Engram led the Broncos in receiving yards and caught their lone touchdown on a well-drawn-up play that left him wide open in the end zone. This was the lone bright spot for the Broncos on Monday Night, but I think we’ll see Engram used a bit more moving forward. Nate Adkins – Unchanged: Played 13 snaps and is a blocking specialist for a team that does not run the ball. He did have 8 special teams snaps as well. Dallen Bentley – Unchanged: The rookie was inactive. Offensive Line Garett Bolles – Unchanged: I am no OL expert, but it was a rough night for the Broncos blockers. Bolles has earned the benefit of the doubt. Ben Powers – Stock down slightly: From the clips I did see, Powers had a rough night and gave up some pressure up the middle of the Broncos’ offensive line. Luke Wattenberg – Stock down slightly: In the same boat as Powers but also had a few iffy snaps. It was humid, and the ball was likely slippery, so hopefully that was the reason for that. Quinn Meinerz – Unchanged: Like Bolles, Meinerz has earned the benefit of the doubt from me. Mike McGlinchey – Stock down: I did notice a lot of pressure coming off that edge, and in the clips I did see, McGlinchey was having a rough time. Again, I am not an OL expert, but he’s the one loser I am going with from this group. Matt Peart – Unchanged: Reserve OT/Swing tackle and played 2 special teams snaps Alex Palczewski – Unchanged: Reserve OL and likely 6th offensive lineman, but saw just 2 special teams snaps. Alex Forsyth – Unchanged: backup center and saw 2 special teams snaps Kage Casey – Unchanged: The rookie OL was inactive Defensive Line Zach Allen – Unchanged: It was a rough night for the defense, but Allen gets the benefit of the doubt from me. I am sure he missed some, but I don’t recall him missing any notable tackles. DJ Jones – Stock down: When you’re a run-stuffing nose tackle and a team runs for over 200 yards on you, your stock is going down. The Broncos’ run defense has been leaky dating back to the playoffs, and Jones is the man in the middle of their defensive line. They need better play from him. Malcolm Roach – Unchanged: I went back and forth here, but settled on unchanged. He’s a run-stuffing DL on a team that sucked vs. the run, but he made some plays, including a nice PBU on 3rd down. Run defense needs to be better/ Eyioma Uwazurike – Stock down slightly: Need more from the Broncos’ big man. He was supposedly unblockable in camp, but that didn’t seem to be the case vs. the Chiefs. I am not sure if he played badly or not, but again, 200+ yards rushing. Everyone has a bit of stink on them. Sai’vion Jones – Stock up slightly: This is just based on usage. He played 15 defensive snaps and 7 special teams snaps…
author: Scotty Payne

title: Broncos vs Jaguars Week 2 preview: Denver looks to drastically improve
summary: The Denver Broncos were unmercifully flogged in their opener. What makes it even tougher is that it came against a hated rival. Now the Broncos have to learn from this, improve, and get ready for another tough matchup this Sunday. Teams face adversity, and Denver has that in spades early in the season. How do […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - DECEMBER 21: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos walks off the field after a 34-20 loss against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Empower Field at Mile High on December 21, 2025 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos were unmercifully flogged in their opener. What makes it even tougher is that it came against a hated rival. Now the Broncos have to learn from this, improve, and get ready for another tough matchup this Sunday. Teams face adversity, and Denver has that in spades early in the season. How do the Broncos respond? What improvements do they make against the Jacksonville Jaguars? To add a little flavor to the mix, you have the result from last season’s game between these two teams when Denver got whopped by the Jaguars in Week 16, 34-20. FanDuel Sportsbook currently has the Broncos as the -2.5-point home favorites on Sunday. The total sits at 45.5, with a lean towards the under at -115. Offensive Rankings Jacksonville : Fourteenth in total offense (360 yards per game), 11th in rushing offense (126 YPG), 10th in passing offense (234 YPG), sixth in scoring offense (34 points per game). Denver : Thirty-second in total offense (176 yards per game), 31st in rushing offense (61 YPG), 32nd in passing offense (115 YPG), tied for 28th in scoring offense (10 points per game). Defensive Rankings Jacksonville : Tenth in total defense (272 yards per game), ninth in rushing defense (87 YPG), tied for 13th in passing defense (185 YPG), tied for second in scoring defense (10 points per game). Denver : Twenty-fourth in total defense (392 yards per game), 31st in rushing defense (220 YPG), 10th in passing defense (172 YPG), tied for 23rd in scoring defense (31 points per game). Here are the MHR staff’s keys to Sunday’s game. Do the opposite of whatever Denver just did Whatever the hell we witnessed in Kansas City, the Broncos must do the complete opposite against Jacksonville. That starts by looking and playing like an NFL team. For Denver to do that, it needs to really hammer down the preparation this week. Bo Nix called the loss to the Chiefs “an ugly wake-up call.” Here’s hoping the Broncos got the message and don’t hit the snooze button. Come together as a team, do the little things, limit the costly mistakes, and execute. — Ian St. Clair Tackle! Watching Kenneth Walker embarrass the Broncos defense was eye-opening. Patrick Mahomes constantly escaping on that reconstructed knee was baffling. It wasn’t that the defense played horribly; it just found ways to miss tackles, making it impossible to win. If Denver can’t wrap up the Jaguars, mark down 0-2 and a major uphill climb to the playoffs. — Adam Malnati Better play on third down The Broncos struggled to stop the Chiefs on third down on Monday Night Football. Moreover, they kept shooting themselves in the foot on offense and were dreadful in that aspect. This was also an issue for them last December, when they lost to the Jacksonville Jaguars. If they can’t do better at extending drives or getting off the field in key situations, they’ll continue to be their own worst enemies. Their performance in these situations has to get better to be successful. — Christopher Hart Better offensive game plan We need to make sure the Jaguars don’t coat themselves in oil, making it impossible for our defenders to tackle them as the Chiefs did. Seriously, though, we need a better offensive game plan to counter what the Jags will do on defense. The Bronco offense looked completely unprepared for the funky blitz packages that Spags always uses. Also, the Broncos need to do a better job of convincing the refs not to call holding on them when they are blatantly holding. The Broncos should ask the Chiefs what their secret is. — Joe Mahoney Score more points than the other team Data and analytics tell you that the Broncos are winless when they score less than their opponent and are undefeated when they score more. So, the game plan is simple! Score more points than the Jaguars. You didn’t do that against the Chiefs, and we’re all angry and disappointed. Do that vs. the small-market Jags, and we’ll be happy again. — Scotty Payne What are your keys to Sunday’s game?
author: Ian St. Clair

title: Broncos at Chiefs: The No Bull Review
summary: The Denver Broncos decided to run it back with the best continuity in the NFL, brought in a top-tier wide receiver free agent, and had a healthy Bo Nix for week 1 of the NFL season. What did we get for all the chatter about being a Super Bowl ready team?  An absolute butt stain […]
full_text: The Denver Broncos decided to run it back with the best continuity in the NFL, brought in a top-tier wide receiver free agent, and had a healthy Bo Nix for week 1 of the NFL season. What did we get for all the chatter about being a Super Bowl ready team? An absolute butt stain of a performance from the Broncos on offense and defense. 31 – 10 is an embarrassment. Some may take great joy at digging into the failures and faults at every orifice of an abomination of a game, but I honestly find less and less joy doing that the more years I add to my belt. I’ve got some points to make worth talking about, but largely we’ll use the review to talk big picture (kinda my normal routine in recent years when the Broncos lay an absolute egg). Head Coach Sean Payton, for some strange reason, doesn’t understand how to get his teams ready to hit the gates running. He runs a complex offense that is scheme-dependent (which I honestly love because it works well when executed properly). He doesn’t seem to value playing starters much in the preseason, with many vets getting a couple of series in the warm-up games. It is hard to analyze this performance and not cast some doubt on the process being used when his teams year after year have problems executing early in the season. This team on both sides of the ball looked very unprepared for this game. The offense had no clue how to find a groove and keep it or how to execute any 3rd down play effectively. The “best offensive line in the NFL” pass blocked like a car full of clowns at a diarrhea fiesta. The defense looked like a unit full of undrafted rookies trying to make a big turnover on every play and forgetting that this is the kind of football where they have to tackle. Payton often takes the fault immediately in his pressers when the team plays this poorly, and I’m sure he did this week as well. Yes, Payton. It indeed is your fault. You did not prepare your team properly to play this game. You were outcoached in the most predictable ways. I’m a friggin nobody fan chugging Mountain Dews and eating Cheetos, and I knew the Kansas City Chiefs were going to run multiple tight ends / extra offensive linemen like the Bills did last year and run the ball with Kenneth Walker on repeat as their one and only way to create offensive production. Your team had no plan for that. Bo Nix’s one biggest weakness is his reluctance to throw the ball over the middle, and yet another offseason went by without any evidence of work being done to address that weakness. It kinda makes it easy to defend the pass when your QB only uses ⅔ of the field the majority of the time. Offense So let’s just say that all the talk about how awesome Davis Webb is and how ready he is for the play-calling duties is looking quite sus at this point in time. That looked like a weaker version of the offense we saw last year, with a play caller abandoning the run when it didn’t need to be, getting fancy on 3rd and short when you could have just run the friggin ball for an easy first down, and leaning on underneath throws when you just traded for one of the most potent downfield threats in the NFL. I do know that not all the calls were terrible. I liked a lot of the plays that they threw to Pat Bryant. I thought Waddle and Sutton both dropped catchable balls. I thought Nix lost plays quite often by trying to go outside instead of simply stepping up and throwing the ball. The execution on offense was lacking from the player side of things. Also, why are we still having to use timeouts and getting delays of game when we have this nifty young play caller? I thought this move was put in place to address that? One small pass I give the offense and Bo Nix that is worth mentioning is the wind. In the 2nd and 4th quarters, when the offense played its worst was when the wind was in their face, which is going to make most QBs more timid about throwing over the middle or deeper down the field. Those would have been great quarters to lean on the run game in my mind, but hey…the game plan called for check downs and screens…right? Quarterbacks Bo Nix looked like a rookie, plain and simple. The moment of this game was far too big for him. His early interception was horrendous, unforgivable, and pathetic. He stared down the only option on that side of the field, watched a guy with perfect technique defend it. Then Bo decided to throw him the ball (because there was a 0% chance of our guy ever catching that ball). The happy feet are back big time. The line did him no favors (regardless of how much Payton wants to crow about sacks being a quarterback stat). If Bo was audibling out of runs or choosing the pass option in RPOs, he needs coaching because we have backs who can run effectively now. Line Mike McGlinchey had an awful night and owes the offense a dinner or two. He got worked multiple times and was a core piece of many pressures on the night. Running Backs I’d love to crow about our running backs. JK Dobbins averaged 4.5 ypc, and RJ Harvey averaged 6 (small sample size). It seems like we maybe could have done better than 30% of the plays on the night being runs if we wanted to. Before anyone says a word about the game going sideways, please note that the team had 17 passing attempts vs. 6 runs in the first half, with the game being within one score. Don’t take that excuse from Sean Payton, other fans, or silly announcers. Receivers The good news is that the team seems to have figured out how to make Evan Engram a part of the offense. Also, Pat Bryant is currently the best wide receiver on the team, and it isn’t close. Cortland Sutton and Jaylen Waddle seemed to be largely placeholders on the field that Nix wasn’t interested in throwing to when coming open (which they were through the night constantly). Oh yeah, and Troy Franklin still sucks. Let’s rotate Lil’Jordan Humphrey back in and let the potato get picked off the waiver wire. Defense We need to stop all talk about Vance Joseph being one of the best defensive coordinators in the NFL right this second. He can’t even get his team ready to stop a team that can only run their bell-cow back on repeat to gain yards. Heck, the team outside of Zach Allen and Patrick Surtain doesn’t even understand the fundamental process of how to tackle in the NFL at any level. The effort of this defense was absolutely pathetic. The execution of this defense was what I would expect from a team of Pop Warner youths doped out on barbiturates. Positive notes for the defense: Kansas City was holding on damn near every pass play, and it was insulting to the game of NFL football that they were allowed to get away with it…I had not seen this level of holding abuse since 2015. If you are worried about our pass rush, don’t be. They still have it, but the refs decided Kermit gets different rules than other more common quarterbacks in the NFL. Front 7 The continued story of Alex Singleton being a liability at inside linebacker is alive and well. He was an embarrassment at linebacker with 2 good tackles out of his 15 in the game (let me point out again that getting a lot of tackles does not equate to a linebacker being good…where they make the tackle is rather important). We extended the worst starter on the team. I’m glad he’s a team captain and a feel-good story. I have never felt good about his play over any three-game stretch of his time here and have quite regularly thought he was a liability and a minus player for this defense. Secondary I had notes on many defensive backs in this game with good plays, but sadly had just as many of the same players missing a tackle. I’m not giving your name time when you can’t even square a player and wrap up properly on an NFL field. Hit the tackle dummies, boys…you need the work. Special Teams Jeremy Crawshaw has a phenomenal leg. He was the most effective player on the whole roster on Monday Night. Now pardon me while I go puke after typing that. Final Thoughts Now that we’ve exercised the demons of this game,…

title: Stat was a bad way to start the season
summary: The Denver Broncos lost the game in two of three phases on Monday – offensively and defensively. I would say that special teams was the only phase that the Broncos won. Jeremy Crawshaw forced the Kansas City Chiefs to start three drives inside their 10 (9, 6 and 3 yard lines). The Broncos only started […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Nick Bolton #32 of the Kansas City Chiefs knocks down a pass against Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos during the fourth quarter in the game at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos lost the game in two of three phases on Monday – offensively and defensively. I would say that special teams was the only phase that the Broncos won. Jeremy Crawshaw forced the Kansas City Chiefs to start three drives inside their 10 (9, 6 and 3 yard lines). The Broncos only started one drive inside the ten (on the 8). Marvin Mims averaged 18 yards on his two punt returns. That was about the end of the good for the Broncos. The offense finished the game 2 of 12 on 3rd downs and 0 for 1 on 4th downs. The offense got only 9 first downs in the game and fumbled three times (only losing one). As crazy it seems, the Broncos are not the worst in the NFL after week 1 in terms of 3rd down conversion. The Browns are worst going 1 of 8 on first team in their game. When only the Browns are worse, you know it’s bad. On the other side, the Chiefs had 19 first downs, and were 9 of 17 on third down. Defensively the Broncos are only seventh worst in 3rd down conversion rate allowed. The Cowboys allowed the Giants to convert on 9 of 11 which is crazy. The Broncos had 58 actual defensive plays (KC had 3 kneel-downs) and somehow managed to miss a tackle on 29.8% of those plays. There were 34 solo tackles for the Broncos and 40 assisted tackles. Since missed tackle percentage does not delineate what play the missed tackle happened on (two can and did happen on multiple plays on Monday) we don’t know how many of those plays involved a missed tackle, but the Broncos had 24 missed tackles last night. Their were at least two on the TD pass to Rashee Rice. However bad you thought the Broncos' tackling was against the Chiefs, it was even worse Denver's 248 missed tackle yards allowed were the most in a single game in @NextGenStats ' database. Their 29.8% missed tackle percentage is the third worst single-game score since 2018 https://t.co/Kd0zQjfUFl — Trevor Sikkema (@TampaBayTre) September 15, 2026 According pro-football-reference.com the Broncos only had 85 missed tackle s in the regular season in 2025. The defense did end up getting two sacks (both by Zach Allen) who also had three QBhits to go with those sacks, meaning that he had at least five pressures in the game. The rest of the defense combined for two QBhits, one by Que Robinson and one by Jonah Elliss. Nik Bonitto did not show up in either stat, though he might have had a pressure. Admittedly he should have had plenty of them given that he was going up a player in Kahlil Benson who had never played a snap at LT above the high school level. Admittedly, the Chiefs were getting rid of the ball quickly on Monday, but he still should have had something to show. It’s possible that he had a pressure since those have not been tabulated yet. According to NFL Next Gen stats, the Chief runners last night we getting -0.1 yards before contact, meaning that they were getting hit at or behind the LOS on most plays. They still managed to gain 223 yards on 35 actual runs on Monday (taking out the kneel-downs). That’s 6.37 yards per carry. That’s the second worst run defense in the league right now. Only the Panthers defense, which allowed 291 yards on 39 carries (7.46 ypc), was worse in week one.

full_text: CANTON, OHIO - AUGUST 08: A New Orleans Saints fan holds a cutout of Drew Brees during the 2026 Pro Football Hall of Fame Enshrinement Ceremony at Tom Benson Hall Of Fame Stadium on August 08, 2026 in Canton, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images Supposedly, Adam Schefter reported that Drew Brees flirted with the idea of helping save the Broncos’ playoff run last year when Bo Nix broke his ankle. This is a great talking point. We get to wistfully wonder, “What if?” But let’s be real, Broncos Country. There’s no way that would have ever worked. First of all, Brees left the game well cooked at quarterback. He got every possible iota of play out of his body before retiring. He was also still technically a Saint. Finally, would you really trust a guy who has sat out of football for the better part of 5 years over your backup who’s been drilling and prepping with the team all year long? Sure, the Sean Payton system is still very similar to what they ran in New Orleans. You can not tell me that there’s not a lot of nuance that has been moved about in the years since Brees was last playing the game. While it may be a fun talking point, it seems rather far-fetched…especially when we hear after the fact that Brees tested his arm and had problems with his wrist. title: 5 Lions vs. Bills thoughts after watching Buffalo’s Week 1 game
summary: To prepare for my “On Paper” preview between the Detroit Lions and Buffalo Bills, I watched Week 1’s game between the Bills and the Houston Texans. Taking notes along the way, I came up with five observations about Buffalo’s performance, and how it may impact Thursday night’s showdown. 1. Their run defense may be significantly […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills passes the ball against the Houston Texans during the third quarter of the game at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images To prepare for my “On Paper” preview between the Detroit Lions and Buffalo Bills, I watched Week 1’s game between the Bills and the Houston Texans. Taking notes along the way, I came up with five observations about Buffalo’s performance, and how it may impact Thursday night’s showdown. 1. Their run defense may be significantly improved I’m feeling pretty darn good about the Detroit Lions’ rushing attack after a strong Week 1 outing against a Saints run defense that was excellent last season. Heading into Week 2 against a Bills’ run defense that ranked 31st in both DVOA and EPA/rush, I figured this could be a huge advantage for the Lions to exploit. However, there were signs the Bills defense could be significantly improved this year under new coordinator Jim Leonhard. Yes, the Texans ran for 124 yards and two touchdowns, but it came on 32 carries, averaging just 3.9 yards per carry. What was particularly impressive was the Bills’ ability to generate negative plays in run defense. The Texans had the seventh-highest “stuffed” rate per FTN Fantasy—with 24% of their rushes being stopped at or behind the line of scrimmage. Now, the Texans rushing attack was terrible last year (27th in stuffed rate, 29th in DVOA), so this wasn’t the biggest test for the Bills run defense, but it was a promising start. 2. Jared Goff could have some time in the pocket On the other side of the Bills’ defensive front, they surprisingly did not produce much pressure against a questionable Texans offensive line. Per NFL Pro, C.J. Stroud faced the lowest pressure rate (21.4%) of any quarterback in Week 1, despite taking three sacks (and two forced fumbles). Now, when the game was on the line and the Texans were in the red zone to win it, the Bills pinned their ears back and picked up two of those sacks and the game-winning fumble recovery. But for most of the game, the Bills’ pass rush was largely invisible. 3. Josh Allen, Joe Brady are psychopaths Okay, this is nothing new, but Josh Allen was an absolute menace on Sunday vs. the Texans—throwing caution to the wind. It’s beautiful… pic.twitter.com/JckrAPPT5i — Nate Geary (@NateGearySports) September 14, 2026 It’s only been one game, but #Bills Josh Allen is: – 1st in air yards per attempt (12.6) – 1st in deep pass percentage (24.1%) – 3rd in EPA/drop-back (+0.49) – 11-of-16 throwing further than 10 yards Vertical passing game so far 📈📈 #BillsMafia @BuffTrenchTalk pic.twitter.com/2nyZPZ5Z0A — Carson Hayek (@CarsonHayek) September 15, 2026 Allen is every bit of the gunslinger he has been for the entirety of his career, but I also think Joe Brady’s promotion from offensive coordinator to head coach is enabling him even further. Take, for example, when the Bills got the ball up 24-21 at the end of the first half. They were on their own 17-yard line with 18 seconds left and the Texans had only two timeouts. Any sane coach would take a knee and go to halftime with a lead, but apparently not Brady and Allen. They dialed up a bomb to D.J. Moore, and while it fell incomplete, it just goes to show you they are going to be aggressive in any and all situations. They also lined up to go for it twice in field goal range on fourth-and-short. They failed to convert one and committed a penalty on the other, but expect them to be a little more aggressive than they were last year—although they’ve always been pretty aggressive on fourth down. Oh, and there was a hook-and-ladder thrown in there during the first half. The good news is that aggressiveness can can also get the Bills in trouble. Allen made an absolutely bone-headed throw during their game-winning drive that would’ve—and should’ve—been the game-losing pass. Kamari Lassiter Just Sold So Hard Bruhhh. Josh Allen Just Threw Up A Shot, And It Should Have Been Picked. pic.twitter.com/HMc5uXF1Yx — SM Highlights (@SMHighlights1) September 13, 2026 4. Tight ends could be a problem By now, you may have seen the graphic that shows the Bills were in 13 personnel (one running back, three tight end) 50 percent of the time . And while that puts a ton of pressure on the defense, I’m more concerned about what Dalton Kincaid can do to a defense on his own. He hauled in five catches for 130 yards against the Texans, displaying his elusiveness and athleticism. “He’s a mismatch in the pass game, man,” Dan Campbell said Tueday. “He’s one of these big skill, get through the defense, one-on-one matchups.” Last week, the Lions did an okay job against the Saints tight ends. Noah Fant caught four catches for 33 yards and a touchdown, while Juwan Johnson had three for 54 and a score. Perhaps the assumed debut of Lions nickelback Christian Izien will help, but with the threat of Allen running, a decent run game, and a lethal play-action pass, Kincaid feels like a nightmare matchup. 5. Penalty prone? It’s a one-game sample size, but the Bills committed 10 penalties for 85 yards—five of which gave the Texans a first down. They were particularly handsy in the secondary, committing four defensive holding penalties and a defensive pass interference. Five different defensive backs were called for a penalty, but that may just be something the Bills will live with, because they were sticky in coverage, allowing the seventh-lowest separation rate of all Week 1 teams.

full_text: After a Week 1 win over the New Orleans Saints came down to the wire, the Detroit Lions travel to Western New York to take on the Buffalo Bills in Week 2 of the 2026 NFL season. Coming off of a close win against the Houston Texans in Week 1, Buffalo will be looking to get their second win of the year in what will be the first regular season game played in their brand new stadium. To preview the matchup, my good friend Meko Scott and I are back with another episode of, “Before the Roar.” From the beginning, we dive into the player that really makes everything happen in Buffalo, quarterback Josh Allen. As you probably know if you are reading this, Allen is one of the best players in the league, and has been for some time now. Simply put, he can do it all. Extend plays with his size and speed, make tight-window throws with the howitzer that is attached to his right shoulder. Anything you want from a modern-day NFL quarterback, Allen delivers in spades. Combine that with the fact that Buffalo’s skill-players are among some of the best in the league, and it’s easy to see why Buffalo’s offense has been so dynamic over the course of the last several years. On the defensive side of the ball, we discuss the Bills’ talented defensive line, and how their transition to a 3-4 defense under new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard could impact how the Lions approach Thursday night’s game. You can watch the entire episode right here , and listen wherever you get your podcasts. If you haven’t already, please be sure to like and subscribe to the Pride of Detroit YouTube Channel. Your support allows us to continue to grow, and reach other Lions fans around the world.

title: Lions Week 2 preview: Breaking down Bills’ offensive, defensive schemes
summary: The Detroit Lions and Buffalo Bills will square off in a “Thursday Night Football” battle to kick off Week 2.
