full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Head Coach Joe Brady of the Buffalo Bills arrives at the stadium prior to the game at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions and Buffalo Bills will square off in a “Thursday Night Football” battle to kick off Week 2. The Bills went through a coaching change this offseason, and while an internal promotion of Joe Brady to head coach kept their offense intact, hiring Jim Leonhard as defensive coordinator has the Bills’ defense shifting from a 4-2 to a 3-4 front. Let’s take a closer look at the Bills’ coaching staff, the scheme they run, and some scouting notes from last week’s game along with some previously viewed games in 2025. Bill s head coach: Joe Brady NFL coaching seasons: Entering ninth season in the NFL Offensive coordinator : Four; Bills 2024-25 and Panthers 2020-21 Passing game coordinator : LSU 2019 (National Championship – QB Joe Burrow) Influences: Sean Payton Coached under: Payton (Saints), McDermott (Bills), Matt Rhule (Panthers), Ed Orgeron (LSU) Playcaller : Yes Dan Campbell coached alongside Brady during the 2017-18 seasons in New Orleans, and has this to say about the start to Brady’s head coaching career: “I know Joe Brady very well. That’s a heck of a start there.” Offensive coordinato r: Pete Carmichael NFL coaching seasons : Entering 27th season in the NFL Offensive coordinator seasons : Entering 16th season Previous coaching positions : Senior offensive assistant, passing game coordinator, QB coach, WR coach, TE coach Influences: Sean Payton (20 seasons), Marty Schottenheimer, Pete Carmichael Sr. (Father) Coached under: Payton (Saints, Broncos), Schottenheimer (Chargers, Washington), Chris Palmer (Browns) Detroit staff connection: John Fox, Senior Assistant (with Lions in 2023) Offensive scheme Passing game : Pro-Spread Running scheme : Man, Inside-Zone Scouting notes : Efficient offense due to success in the run game and quick pass completions Spread philosophies at their core Heavy influences from Payton (Saints) and Bengals-style (how they use Joe Burrow) Week 1: 11 personnel 33% of snaps, 12 for 12%, 13 for 40% Note: Bills spent so much time in 13 in Week 1 because Texans stayed in nickel sets 60/40 pass-run split in Week 1 QB Josh Allen can throw to all levels of the field Tested Texans deep in Week 1 more than he’s done in the past Under center 65% of the time in Week 1 Play-action 41% of dropbacks in Week 1 Allen has 81 career rushing TDs (most among QBs in NFL history) North-South rushing attack runs right at the teeth of the defense Week 1 blocking percentages: Man roughly 40%, Inside-Zone 30% Dan Campbell on Bills’ offense: “Can’t say enough about this quarterback. He’s a catalyst for them. And it’s a good O-line. They’ve got weapons, and a good back.” “They have three tight ends. They have three real guys that have three different roles that they’re all three pretty good at. And (Jackson Hawes) 85 can block a little bit. We liked him coming out and he proved to be a pretty good blocker last year. So, he’s kind of their heavy-Y. And then Dalton (Kincaid), 86, he’s a mismatch in the pass game, man. He’s one of these big skill, get through the defense, one-on-one matchups. And then (Dawson) Knox does it all. He does everything. He’s the guy, he’s the jack of all trades and he makes it right. He’s kind of the glue that, ‘What do you need? I’m the release guy, I’m the blocker, I’m the hybrid H-back, I’m the split me out one-on-one.’ He does it all.” Defensive coordinator: Jim Leonhard NFL seasons as a player : 10 years at safety (Bills, Ravens, Jets, Broncos, Saints, Browns) NFL coaching seasons : 3 years in the NFL (8 in college) Defensive coordinator seasons : First-year Previous roles : DBs coach, passing game coordinator, assistant head coach (Broncos) Influences: Rex Ryan, Mike Pettine, and Vance Joseph for scheme; Sean Payton for coaching style Coached under: Payton (Broncos), Joseph (Broncos), Bret Bielema (Illinois), Paul Chryst (Wisconsin) Played for : Pettine (Browns, Bills, Jets), Ryan (Jets, Ravens), Payton (Saints), John Fox (Broncos), Jack Del Rio (Broncos), John Harbaugh (Ravens), Dick Jauron (Bills) Defensive scheme Base : 3-4 Base, attacking front Coverage : Zone-heavy Scouting notes (from Week 1): Defense modeled after the Broncos 3-4 attacking scheme Big defensive shift after previously playing in a 4-2 front; required new personnel Defensive philosophy switch will take time to adapt 5-man front in base (3 down DL, 2 pass-rushing LB) – roughly 40% of defensive snaps in Week 1 4-man front in subpackages (2 DL and 2 PR-LB) – roughly 60% Vs. 11 personnel: faced 42 snaps, 25 in nickel (36% of snaps) and 17 in dime (24%) Vs. 12, 13, and Jumbo: 30 snaps, 28 in Base defense (39%) Picks and Stunts are foundations of pass rush Pressure on 36% of passing snaps Blitz 26% of snaps Zone coverage around 80% — Cover-3 was highest at 31%, then Cover-6 (22%), Cover-4 (19%), Cover-2 (7%) Man 18% —mainly Cover-2 (10%) and Cover-1 (8%) Dan Campbell on Saints’ defense: “This defensive line is their catalyst over there. (DT) Ed Oliver and (EDGE Greg) Rousseau, man, really good player. Length, explosive. They’ve got (EDGE Bradley) Chubb on the other end. Big boy in the middle, man. That’s an active defense and it was a big win for them (in Week 1).”

title: Packers vs. Jets preview: A crash course on New York’s personnel
summary: It’s time to stop licking our wounds, and time to focus on the Green Bay Packers’ next opponent. To set the table for some of the analysis that will come out later this week, let’s talk about the New York Jets’ roster and their starting players — as the Packers hope to best them to […]
full_text: (Photo by Chris Carter/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s time to stop licking our wounds, and time to focus on the Green Bay Packers’ next opponent. To set the table for some of the analysis that will come out later this week, let’s talk about the New York Jets’ roster and their starting players — as the Packers hope to best them to avoid an 0-2 start. Last week, the Jets ran for 152 yards in a fairly low-scoring 23-10 game against what looks to be a very poor Tennessee Titans. For what it’s worth, they held quarterback Cam Ward to just a 34.4 QBR in Sunday’s win. Skill Players QB Geno Smith RB Breece Hall WR Garrett Wilson WR Adonai Mitchell WR Isaiah Williams TE Mason Taylor TE Jeremy Ruckert On film, quarterback Geno Smith looked spry — more like the Seattle Seahawks version of himself than what we saw with the Las Vegas Raiders last year. Obviously, New York’s number one running back is Breece Hall, but expect former Badger Braelon Allen to get some touches throughout the game, too. Running back Kene Nwangwu, best known for his contributions as a returner, missed Week 1 (he was listed on the injury report as doubtful), and he was listed as a non-participant in practice on Wednesday . Rookie receiver Omar Cooper Jr. is expected to miss several weeks with an ankle sprain, a pretty big blow for the Jets, who are already down a projected starting receiver in Tim Patrick — who is on the injured reserve with a groin injury. At the moment, New York’s third receiver appears to be Isaiah Williams, a third-year undrafted free agent who is already on his third NFL team. Frank Reich is a demon pic.twitter.com/9FnVGNHO2H — Jalen Brunson enthusiast (NBA CHAMPIONS) (@GothamCityM) September 14, 2026 Because of the issues at receiver, don’t be surprised if the Jets lean into their tight ends in this game, which would put the Packers’ base 3-4 defense on the field more frequently. New York’s most-used tight ends were Mason Taylor and Jeremy Ruckert in Week 1, but first-round pick Kenyon Sadiq, Jelani Woods and fullback Andrew Beck (a former Packer) also got playing time. In fact, the Jets had the bright idea to play all five of them on the field at once in the red zone in Week 1, featuring Sadiq (who got a rushing touchdown on another play) in the backfield. Offensive Line LT: Olu Fashanu LG: Dylan Parham C: Josh Myers RG: Joe Tippman RT: Armand Membou The Jets’ tackles are young, but you’ll recognize an old name in the middle of the offensive line: former Packer Josh Myers. I’m sure that if the Packers struggle at any point with their own offensive line, we’ll be hearing a lot of would-have, could-have, should-haves about Myers on Sunday. Defensive Line David Onyemata Harrison Phillips T’Vondre Sweat The Jets talked a lot about running a 4-3, 3-4 hybrid this offseason, but they almost exclusively played a 3-4 defense in base in Week 1. Their new-look defensive line mostly featured David Onyemata (a free agent signing) and T’Vondre Sweat (a trade) on the line of scrimmage. For what it’s worth, rookie Darrell Jackson Jr., who was a draft crush of many, was New York’s fifth-most-used defensive lineman last week. Edge Defender David Bailey Kingsley Enagbare This was supposed to be a four-man rotation, but edge defender Joseph Ossai missed last week’s game with a plantar fascia injury and started this week as a non-participant in practice. Without Ossai, it’s really a three-man unit with first-round rookie David Bailey, former Packer Kingsley Enagbare and Will McDonald IV spearheading the unit. Yes, McDonald, who was taken two picks after Lukas Van Ness, has been relegated to a backup role going into Year 4 of his NFL career. Off-Ball Linebacker Demario Davis Jamien Sherwood This one is pretty straightforward, as these players are every-down players for the Jets. Demario Davis is the team’s veteran presence at 37 (!) years old, while Jamien Sherwood is New York’s run-and-chase linebacker. There’s been mixed results on the Sherwood front after the team signed him to a three-year, $45 million contract that helped reset the off-ball linebacker market for non-Pro Bowlers in the 2025 offseason. Cornerback Brandon Stephens Azareye’h Thomas Jarvis Brownlee Jr. (slot) Rookie second-round pick D’Angelo Ponds missed last week’s action with a calf injury after being listed as doubtful going into the weekend. For what it’s worth, Ponds was also a limited participant in practice on Wednesday, as it’s unclear whether or not he will play this week. With Ponds out (and a major injury at safety), the outside cornerbacks right now are Brandon Stephens and Azareye’h Thomas, with Jarvis Brown Jr. playing in the slot. Safety Dane Belton Andre Cisco Starting safety Minkah Fitzpatrick left Week 1 early with a groin injury and is expected to miss several weeks, meaning he obviously won’t play against the Packers. Without Fitzpatrick, the safeties were Dane Belton and Andre Cisco, two journeyman players. — In kicker news, the Jets had to call up veteran Jason Sanders from the practice squad for Blake Grupe last week. The two are in a kicking competition right now, and it’s not clear who will be on the field against the Packers on Sunday.

title: The Packers sparked an NFL memo on ineligible players
summary: On Wednesday, the NFL sent a memo to club decision-makers stating that players who left the league to try to return to college football in 2026 were ineligible to be signed or to visit NFL teams. This is specifically relevant to the Green Bay Packers, who made the choice to bring in defensive lineman Zxavian […]
full_text: (Photo by Joe Robbins/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images On Wednesday, the NFL sent a memo to club decision-makers stating that players who left the league to try to return to college football in 2026 were ineligible to be signed or to visit NFL teams. This is specifically relevant to the Green Bay Packers, who made the choice to bring in defensive lineman Zxavian Harris on Tuesday. Today’s full NFL memo, clarifying that Zxavian Harris and Dae’Quan Wright are barred from visiting, trying out with or being signed by NFL clubs during the 2026 NFL season. https://t.co/mhYoCGBd9T pic.twitter.com/TikNSW1nus — Tom Pelissero (@TomPelissero) September 16, 2026 Harris was one of the highest-rated undrafted free agents from the 2026 draft cycle, as the 6’8”, 330-pounder fell out of the draft due to character concerns. Notably, he was arrested for domestic violence, obstructing arrest, DUI, reckless driving, being a minor in possession, not using headlights and running a stop sign over two occasions during his time at Mississippi. Harris signed as a UDFA with the New Orleans Saints but was waived by the team in early August. From there, Harris tried to join LSU’s football program, following former Mississippi head coach Lane Kiffin. Harris never practiced with the team, unlike tight end Dae’Quan Wright, a former Cleveland Brown, but both players did enroll at LSU. Ultimately, under pressure from the conference and other SEC programs, the Tigers didn’t add either Harris or Wright to their 2026 roster, which was only finalized 24 hours before their opening kickoff of the season. For weeks, the NFL has stated that clubs cannot sign players who elected to join non-NFL teams, treating Harris and Wright similarly to athletes who signed with the CFL, for example. CFL players are not eligible to be signed until the completion of both seasons. On paper, Harris and Wright should be eligible to sign as free agents once reserve-futures deals get handed out when teams’ seasons end, but not until then. Despite that, the Packers brought in Harris for a visit on Tuesday, and the NFL wanted to let clubs know that was against the league’s rules. Maybe there was no clarity on whether Green Bay could have brought in a player for a tryout, even if they knew they couldn’t actually sign Harris at the moment. Maybe they were just trying to pull a fast one. Either way, the NFL made its stance clear, stating that it’s each club’s responsibility to verify player eligibility and that violations are subject to club discipline. So far, the league has not announced any punishment for the Packers. Update: Apparently, the NFLPA will be fighting for Harris and Wright to get NFL employment this season. Front Office Sports’ Amanda Christovich received a statement from the NFLPA , saying, “We are aware of the memo and are in touch with each of the players’ representatives. We will explore all options to ensure each players’ rights are protected within the Collective Bargaining Agreement.” The Packers have not made a statement on bringing in Harris for a tryout.

full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers announced on Wednesday that they have signed defensive lineman Eric Johnson II and receiver Quincy Skinner Jr. to their practice squad. Both players worked out with the team earlier this week, and the Johnson signing was reported on by Sports Illustrated ’s Bill Huber on Tuesday . Skinner replaces Chris Hilton Jr., who was released from the Packers’ practice squad this week, while Johnson slides into the spot that was previously held by Jaden Crumedy, who was poached off Green Bay’s practice squad to the Houston Texans’ 53-man roster last week. The Packers’ defensive line room has been raided, as Nazir Stackhouse was signed off waivers at the cutdown deadline, too, leaving the team with no option on the practice squad other than Crumedy. On top of that, three of Green Bay’s defensive linemen are currently on the injury report , leaving them short on bodies for practice. At the moment, here is where the Packers’ practice squad stands: QB: Kedon Slovis RB: Pierre Strong Jr. and Damon Bankston WR: Isaiah Neyor and Quincy Skinner Jr. TE: Drake Dabney OL: Dalton Cooper, Josh Gesky and Dillon Wade DL: Eric Johnson II ED: Nyjalik Kelly and Arron Mosby LB: Kristian Welch CB: Domani Jackson S: Kahlef Hailassie K: Lenny Krieg (international exemption) Green Bay currently still has one open spot on the practice squad. The Packers might be eyeing offensive lineman Cordell Volson for that spot, as they worked him, and only him, out on Wednesday per the NFL transaction wire. Cordell Volson was drafted with pick 136 of round 4 in the 2022 draft class. He scored a 6.06 #RAS out of a possible 10.00. This ranked 511 out of 1293 OG from 1987 to 2022. https://t.co/ygrnAfR7li pic.twitter.com/rs9PGI4th0 — RAS.football (@MathBomb) March 23, 2024 Volson was picked in the fourth round out of North Dakota State back in 2022. Over his rookie contract, he played 50 games (48 starts) with the Cincinnati Bengals at guard. He didn’t play at all during the 2025 regular season, though, because he had a season-ending surgery on his right shoulder. #Titans Cordell Volson is working his way back after missing last year due to injury. Volson said his reaction time is a little slower but will get better with more reps. pic.twitter.com/jop7ntZsMW — TURRON DAVENPORT (@TDavenport_NFL) August 4, 2026 After the completion of his rookie contract, he signed a one-year, $3.2 million contract with the Tennessee Titans this offseason, which included $2 million in guaranteed money. He did not make it through final cuts with the Titans, so he’s now a free agent. For what it’s worth, Volson worked out with the Dallas Cowboys last week, who ultimately ended up signing former Pro Bowler Laken Tomlinson to their practice squad. Going into camp, it was projected that Volson was going to be the Titans’ starting right guard, but rookie fifth-round pick Fernando Carmona Jr. ended up winning the job. For what it’s worth, Volson had a 29.1 grade in true pass protection sets in the 2024 season per Pro Football Focus, the last year in which he was active for a regular-season game.

title: Packers Injury Report: Lukas Van Ness and Javon Hargrave have concussions
summary: A couple of new injuries popped up on the Green Bay Packers’ first injury report of the week, despite head coach Matt LaFleur stating that there were no long-term injuries sustained in the Packers’ loss to the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday. Beyond what was reported during the game, like cornerback Brandon Cisse’s cramps, both defensive […]
full_text: (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images A couple of new injuries popped up on the Green Bay Packers’ first injury report of the week, despite head coach Matt LaFleur stating that there were no long-term injuries sustained in the Packers’ loss to the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday. Beyond what was reported during the game, like cornerback Brandon Cisse’s cramps, both defensive lineman Javon Hargrave (who was already on the injury report with a knee injury) and edge defender Lukas Van Ness were given concussion designations by the team. Both Hargrave and Van Ness played into the fourth quarter, with Hargrave even being on the field for the last play of the game (a kneel-down). Neither was reported to have concussions during or coming out of the game. Overall, the only player who was a non-participant in practice today was defensive lineman Warren Brinson (calf), who missed Week 1’s action with his injury. The following players were also limited on Wednesday, along with the players who have concussions: LG Aaron Banks (knee), RT Zach Bako-Bewele (knee), DL Devonte Wyatt (ankle), ED Barryn Sorrell (foot) and LB Ty’Ron Hopper (Achilles). Banks and Hopper did not play against the Vikings, so their situations will be interesting to monitor, as the Packers are staring down two games in five days over the next two weeks. Green Bay’s next opponent, the New York Jets, are pretty banged up already. Receiver Omar Cooper Jr. (ankle) and safety Minkah Fitzpatrick (groin) are expected to miss Sunday’s game and were non-participants today. Other non-participants due to injury are running back/returner Kene Nwangwu (back) and edge defender Joseph Ossai (foot), who both did not play in Week 1. Limited participants in practice for New York were cornerback D’Angelo Ponds (calf) and linebacker Jamien Sherwood (knee). Ponds, like Nwangwu and Ossai, was inactive in the Jets’ win over the Tennessee Titans. title: Packers Film Room: Week 1 blitz of the week
summary: Even though the Green Bay Packers ultimately lost their opening game 39-22 in week one, no one has a leg to stand on if they want to blame the Packers defense for this one. Until the last six minutes of the game, the defense stood firm and kept giving the offense chances with the ball. […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: Keisean Nixon #25 of the Green Bay Packers celebrates with teammates after pulling in a first quarter interception against the Minnesota Vikings of the game at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Even though the Green Bay Packers ultimately lost their opening game 39-22 in week one, no one has a leg to stand on if they want to blame the Packers defense for this one. Until the last six minutes of the game, the defense stood firm and kept giving the offense chances with the ball. They only surrendered two late touchdowns to the Minnesota Vikings because of field position surrendered by the offense with turnovers. On the second play of the young season for the defense, they intercepted Vikings quarterback Kyler Murray on an all-out blitz, giving the Packers the ball at their 47-yard line. The pressure forced Murray to hurry his throw, resulting in an errant pass. The play call was a quarters coverage hot blitz where the defense shows cover-0 from a zone alignment, the standard way to present cover-0 these days. Instead of playing straight man-to-man, the corners are reading the route distribution of the receivers and a low hole vision dropper will rob anything short over the middle. The safeties are keying on the inside routes of the slot receivers. The Vikings are in 11 personnel (one running back, one tight end) shotgun empty running a mirrored curl/seam route concept called “HOSS Y-JUKE”. The Packers defensive shell shows man across the board with a zone alignment but they’re actually playing quarters coverage principles in the secondary. The corners are going to play “man on deep” and let anything shallow go underneath. Once they see the receiver sit, they’ll bail to the deep quarter to help the safety. The safeties are going to take anything vertical from the inside receivers. Up front, the pressure brings six and the Vikings have five in to pass block. That leaves one extra free rusher unaccounted for and means Murray has a hot throw. On this throw in the Shanahan/McVay offense, of which Kevin O’Connell is part of, the hot throws are the seam routes and the trips side 6-yard stop route. Zaire Franklin (No. 44) is mugged up in the A-gap and blitzes as the interior rusher in that gap. The offensive right guard should pick up the blitzing linebacker, making the furthest edge defender the widest rusher, but he lets Franklin go unopposed up the middle. This shorter time to pressure causes Murray to heave an errant pass up the seam where it hangs on him and is intercepted by Keisean Nixon, who fell off the shallow curl route to sink under the pass. This was Jonathan Gannon’s most effective pressure call of the game and it gave the Packers the ball at midfield, where they were able to drive into scoring range but only for what ended up being a 59-yard field goal.

title: Packers vs. Jets Week 2 TV Broadcast Map
summary: For the first time in the 2026 season — and one of the few times that this is scheduled to be the case — the Green Bay Packers will be buried in the midst of the early Sunday kickoff window in Week 2. Green Bay’s matchup with the New York Jets, to be aired on […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - AUGUST 28: New York Jets fans react during the first half of a preseason game against the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on August 28, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Elsa/Getty Images) | Getty Images For the first time in the 2026 season — and one of the few times that this is scheduled to be the case — the Green Bay Packers will be buried in the midst of the early Sunday kickoff window in Week 2. Green Bay’s matchup with the New York Jets, to be aired on FOX, is far from a prime game for the network. This week, FOX has the nationwide doubleheader, with Commanders-Cowboys set to be their primary game in the late window. They still have four games on in the 12:00 Noon Central kickoff time slot, however, with Packers-Jets being among them. That means that Packers fans outside the Wisconsin and New York media markets will have a lesser chance of seeing the game, something made worse by an NFC North divisional matchup in the same window. Yes, Packers-Jets goes up against Vikings-Bears, which will be shown to most of the country this week. The other two competing games — Eagles-Titans and Panthers-Falcons — will be limited in their broadcast areas as well. Here’s the country’s TV map for the early window on FOX, from 506sports.com, showing Packers-Jets in green: That’s Minnesota-Chicago in blue, getting most of the airplay, with Eagles-Titans in red and Carolina-Atlanta in yellow. Adding insult to injury for Packers fans this week is FOX’s choice of commentators for their game. Kenny Albert and Jonathan Vilma will be on the call for Packers-Jets, and the pairing ranked 14th out of 18 NFL announcer tandems in Awful Announcing’s NFL fan survey ranking for the 2025 season .

full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: Brandon Cisse #2 and Kaleb Johnson #26 of the Green Bay Packers run onto the field prior to the game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. Yes, Justin Jefferson got the better of him on one noteworthy play, but Justin Jefferson has a way of doing that. He’s victimized better corners than Cisse well past the first game of their career. But outside of Jefferson’s score, Cisse was on target and on task, playing 49 snaps in his first game in the NFL, the most of any Packers defender that didn’t hit 100% in Week 1. The Packers’ defensive backfield has been the target of no small number of questions this offseason, but if this is what we can expect from Cisse, those questions should largely go away. title: Carrington Valentine got picked on in the red zone vs. the Vikings
summary: While the Green Bay Packers’ defense did well on Sunday — if you can believe it — as the unit ranks among the NFL’s highest in fewest yards per play allowed through Week 1’s action, one glaring issue on the defense did pop up at the end of the Packers’ loss to the Minnesota Vikings: […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images While the Green Bay Packers’ defense did well on Sunday — if you can believe it — as the unit ranks among the NFL’s highest in fewest yards per play allowed through Week 1’s action, one glaring issue on the defense did pop up at the end of the Packers’ loss to the Minnesota Vikings: cornerback Carrington Valentine’s play when the Vikings were on the warning stripe of scoring a touchdown. Valentine played for just 13 snaps as Brandon Cisse’s replacement at left cornerback, as the second-round rookie dropped out of the game due to a cramp. You’ll see it out there that Benjamin St-Juste played one snap of defense on Sunday, but he was only on the field for a kneel-down, not a real play against a live offense. It was Keisean Nixon and Cisse at outside cornerback, and when Cisse left, it was Valentine who subbed in for him. Unfortunately, Valentine had five pretty bad plays in those 13 reps, and they all came when Minnesota was over the 50-yard line. CV pic.twitter.com/ME47WYs76N — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) September 16, 2026 The first play was an explosive run; Valentine did little at the point of attack. This has been an issue for Valentine since he came into the NFL, and it was why the Packers actually rotated in Kamal Hadden and Nate Hobbs for Valentine on run looks before those two players were ultimately injured last season. If you need a reminder of Valentine’s ability to play strong on the perimeter, here’s another example: a screen-turned-touchdown from the Philadelphia Eagles’ Dallas Goedert in the Packers’ playoff loss from the 2024 season. The second play was a bootleg where Valentine had to follow Justin Jefferson across the field, and Jefferson was able to cut the distance to the goal in half without Valentine ever being a factor on the play. The third play is a pin-and-pull play where Valentine doesn’t set a hard edge until he’s basically out of bounds, making it more difficult for his teammates to be involved. Valentine doesn’t initiate contact with the running back until they hit the goal line, at which point it doesn’t even matter. The fourth play? Another run directly at Valentine. This one starts on the right hash, and Valentine doesn’t set an edge until he’s outside of the numbers, letting the Vikings cut the distance to the sticks in half. And the final play is that same boot action look again, as Minnesota found a call they liked, but this time Jefferson scores a touchdown because Valentine missed a tackle around the seven-yard line. All in all, it was a pretty poor showing for Valentine on Sunday. The worst place to play him is in the red zone, as the Vikings showed, but it’s where the defense spent a lot of time because of the failures of the offensive line . Personally, I don’t think it’s a bad idea to start spelling Valentine with St-Juste, if Valentine does get playing time, in obvious run looks or the red zone. St-Juste was clearly brought in as a CB4 and a special teams contributor, but with a 6’3”, 200-pound frame, I feel like he gives you a better chance on the perimeter than the 5’11”-and-change, 189-pound Valentine in those situations. Valentine is fine as a middle-of-the-field coverage player, but a goal-line threat he is not.

summary: Welcome back to Battle Red Blog’s NFL Power Rankings roundup! Houston is fortunate not only to have one of the more successful programs in the NFL, but also some of the best coverage in the league, highlighted by ESPN’s DJ Bien-Aime, Sports Illustrated’s Conor Orr, and Yahoo! Sports’ Frank Schwab. All three have frequently appeared on the list below, and I’ll be looking forward to seeing their hot takes this season. Orr was one that I took note of being a bit more harsh on the Texans than other pundits, much to my chagrin. But, following his Sports Illustrated cover story of Will Anderson Jr., it appears Orr has now joined the Texans bandwagon! Hopefully, his seal approval is more of a blessing than a curse this season. Last year, I teed off the 2025 power rankings by attempting to set the table on what I thought to be the expectations on the Texans entering the 2025 season: While the Texans still had a very successful 2024 season by most standards, they ultimately still did not break through the glass ceiling of the divisional round, where every Texans team of the past has met their high watermark. Now, with the element of surprise in the rearview mirror, the Texans need to prove that they have learned from last year’s faults. They have to prove it to the fans and critics alike that they truly have Super Bowl talent. They have to prove to everyone that, finally, this year will be different – NFL Power Rankings Week 1: Where are the Texans? (2025) …well, last year ended up not being very different! A third divisional round loss in a row for this new era of Texans football has fans feeling some Deja vu, if not a sense of impending doom for the end of this season. Led by coach DeMeco Ryans and quarterback CJ Stroud, these Texans have enjoyed remarkable success since the 2023 season, carrying Houston to arguably its most dominant stretch in the franchise’s 25-year history. As for the 2025 season specifically, it may have gone down in flames, but if you put weight in analyst Aaron Schatz’s famous DVOA (Defense-Adjusted Value Over Average) metric, then you’d be pleased to hear that the 2025 Texans were the highest rated team in franchise history (Bryan Knowles, Aaron Schatz’s FTN Football Almanac 2026, p. 97). So, maybe the Texans did improve their playoff record in 2025, but they at least are making progress somewhere. That is a HELL of a throw from C.J. Stroud to Nico Collins. pic.twitter.com/azBOAHZCn6 — Jacob Barzilla (@JacobBarzilla) September 13, 2026 That leads us to this season, the big one. The one Texans fans the world over have been waiting for. 2025 was just an appetizer in comparison to the hype that this year’s Texans team has built. Not only did Houston firmly establish itself as a Super Bowl contender with their weekly destruction of opposing offenses all of last year, they also spent all of this offseason proving to the public that they are “all-in” on winning the championship this season. Texans general manager Nick Caserio spent heavily to keep their young core on defense happy, signed multiple starting-caliber offensive linemen in free agency, and then used two top-40 picks in the 2026 NFL Draft to further secure Houston’s biggest weak spots: defensive tackle (McDonald, 36th Overall) and interior o-line (Rutledge, 26th Overall.) This time last year, Houston was still proving itself to suspicious national analysts, but now, many of those same analysts are picking the Texans to be a Super Bowl team in 2026. The expectations quite literally couldn’t be higher, and, if they go another year fizzling out in the second round of the postseason, there could be mutiny. The same result three years in a row has created tension in the fanbase, and the controversy surrounding QB CJ Stroud only magnifies the tension. His and the Texans’ decision to “table” extension negotiations until after the season places a massive personal stressor onto Stroud to ball out this year, and will encourage fans to demand perfection from him in every game. title: Colts Week 1 Film Analysis: Beatdown vs. Baltimore
summary: The thing about the NFL is that you can NEVER get too high or too low, even if the Colts gave everyone a million reasons to be low on them. An uninspiring performance where they didn’t even look competitive, a rarity in the Shane Steichen era. The Colts haven’t been able to win big games […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - SEPTEMBER 13: Indianapolis Colts head coach Shane Steichen during a NFL game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Indianapolis Colts on September 13, 2026 at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The thing about the NFL is that you can NEVER get too high or too low, even if the Colts gave everyone a million reasons to be low on them. An uninspiring performance where they didn’t even look competitive, a rarity in the Shane Steichen era. The Colts haven’t been able to win big games in his tenure, but they almost always look prepared. The Colts didn’t look prepared whatsoever. I’m not going to try and view this game through rose colored glasses and tell you “it wasn’t so bad!” because that’d be very disingenuous. But I’m also not going to sit here and press the panic button either. OFFENSE Daniel Jones getting to a man beater on the opening drive after using a Jonathan Taylor motion to confirm coverage. But man that is a filthy route from Josh Downs pic.twitter.com/enCqc7raFd — Colts Film Room (@ColtsFilmRoom) September 15, 2026 The Colts seemingly picked up right where they left off on the opening drive of the game. This motion form Jonathan Taylor is strictly use to confirm coverage and see who follows him outside. Once they recognize man, Daniel Jones knows his best option is to hit Josh Downs on this choice route. It’s a nasty route, and I still am confused as to why Josh Downs didn’t see much action after this drive. Daniel Jones INT Obviously a great play from Roquan Smith, but timing of the play is a bit off here. Downs working back to the right hash brings Roquan back into the throwing window where they're trying to create a vertical stretch to get the ball to Allen. pic.twitter.com/2lhHNQMiL3 — Colts Film Room (@ColtsFilmRoom) September 15, 2026 This was a costly INT that gave the Ravens amazing field position to let the game get out of hand. It’s obviously easy to blame Daniel Jones for throwing this, but it’s also an incredible play from the linebacker. Often times in football the smallest of details matter, and I think this one is the case here. Josh Downs is running a sit or maybe a return route? Either way, when he recognizes the route is dead he tries to keep himself alive by working back toward the sideline. That movement brings Smith right back into the throwing window where he can make the play on the ball. Daniel Jones sack in a backed-up scenario Nightmare all around! Minter knows Steichen loves to move the pocket to simplify the picture for Jones/get him into a rhythm and were keyed in all game. Either way can't have two WRs run into each other on crossing routes. pic.twitter.com/cvQm6FNOyj — Colts Film Room (@ColtsFilmRoom) September 15, 2026 This sack to me is on Daniel Jones. The QB is always responsible for the unblocked player to the side your rolling out too. If he isn’t biting on the run fake and in your face when you turn your head back toward the defense, you better have a plan. But I also think the Colts need to evolve in their movement passing game, teams have caught up to it since mid-November. It’s such a big staple of their offense that when it isn’t working, there’s way more drop back pass where Jones has to hang in the pocket and execute full field reads, susceptible to way more pressure, and limits someone like Tyler Warren who is the primary read more often than not. DEFENSE First play is really a microcosm of the entire day.. I know they wanted to give Bynum the green dot because he's a captain, in his second year as a starter, and one of the few guys who can do it.. But having a safety as your green dot seems more like a logistical issue to me pic.twitter.com/JiCecArvEd — Colts Film Room (@ColtsFilmRoom) September 15, 2026 Starting with the first play of the game, the Ravens come out in a Sugar Huddle. That means they’re bunched up close the line of scrimmage before they run to their spots and quickly snap the ball before the defense can adjust. It works perfectly, partially because the Colts couldn’t get lined up all day, and Zay Flowers gets a massive gain. Justin Walley, who was picked on most of the game, was the main culprit. A lot of times he’s just out of position to make a play on the ball. This is so frustrating because it's actually very sticky coverage…. Except for the one wide open receiver who gets open off of a miscommunication pre-snap. https://t.co/47a4NxNoIE pic.twitter.com/u4PJg75jLl — Colts Film Room (@ColtsFilmRoom) September 16, 2026 The Colts are playing Cover 1 here and “leveling the stack” that means that each player has the man in front of them, but once the TE motions over, Sauce is likely trying to get Walley to check to “Top Hat” coverage, to avoid being picked by Charvarious Ward who is running across the field. When teams motion into bunches, they are trying to create traffic for defenders and get guys to spring open. Sauce knows that if someone is motioning to create a bunch, the point man of that bunch is probably running inside because they want him to collide with the player who’s traveling with the motion man. Top Hat would mean Sauce would take the guy off the ball, while Walley who is aligned off the line of scrimmage would take the inside guy. Walley never sees the check from Sauce and gives up a free inside release and is out of position right from the jump. OVERALL THOUGHTS I didn’t breakdown every play here, just some of the key plays in the game that contributed to deciding the outcome. While this is a humbling and a tough pill to swallow for the Colts, it also sorta makes sense that a bad game turned ugly very quickly. If you let a Baltimore Ravens team get out in front early, it’s over. They will tire you out and then make you try and tackle Derrick Henry when you need a stop the most. Henry had 13 carries for 107 yards and 8.2 yards per attempt when the Ravens had at least a two score lead. If the Colts can figure out how to line up properly, I’m not sure this game is as ugly as it looks. They got dominated in the field position game and spent the 2nd and 3rd quarter in a lot of backed up scenarios. It was a bad game script for them to ever get back into that game. They were embarrassed but I don’t think this season is a lost cause. They have talent, even if that talent is rusty. Pierce looked good in his new role, even if on a limited snap count, and JT looked great. The DT duo up front were dominant and Sauce Gardner shut down his man the entirety of the game. I expect a bounce back performance from guys like Warren, Jones and Steichen. It’s a long season and I’m definitely not ready to press the panic button yet.

title: Colts’ Week 1 QB Analysis: Not a good start boys.
summary: Thanks to the nflFastR project, Pro Football Focus for the timely sources of data. For those of you new to this, I will publish key QB stats each week judging how well the Colts’ QB performed. Yes, O-Line, receivers, and play-calling impact these numbers but they are primarily QB measures. I will probably modify the charts throughout the season. […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts reacts against the Baltimore Ravens during the third quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images Thanks to the nflFastR project, Pro Football Focus for the timely sources of data. For those of you new to this, I will publish key QB stats each week judging how well the Colts’ QB performed. Yes, O-Line, receivers, and play-calling impact these numbers but they are primarily QB measures. I will probably modify the charts throughout the season. Commentary will be brief but feel free to let me know in the comments that stats aren’t everything. (click charts for larger view) After a very good 2025 season, Daniel Jones returned from injury looking to pick up where he left off. Week 1 didn’t exactly go according to plan. The Colts struggled to consistently move the ball through the air, and Jones finished near the bottom of the league in several key measures. So was it just a little rust after the layoff, or is there more going on? Let’s dig into the numbers and see what happened. HOW WELL? mouseover definitions: median EPA gain in similar game situation (down, distance, etc.)”> arsr , 3 yards to gain in game-neutral situations”> edp , sg% , oz% , pr% , tip , ttt , adot , ay/c , yac , yacoe , yd/c , ac% , cpoe , aypa , drp , scr% , ta% , sck% , aa% , ny/d , ny/p , 1st% , td% , to% , 0″> qbsr epa/p , adj/p The Colts had one of the best rushing attacks in Week 1, but for they still leaned heavily on the pass on early downs (3rd ARSR, 5th EDP). Jones faced a lot of pressure despite getting the ball out relatively quickly. He wasn’t spending much time in the pocket though and with the short target depth, this looks like an offensive line that wasn’t giving him enough time for much to develop downfield (10th PR%, 19th TIP, 16th TTT, 23rd ADOT). The short throws turned into short completions, and Jones didn’t get much help from his receivers after the catch either. With very little production through the air or after the catch, the Colts ended up near the bottom of Week 1 in yards per completion (22nd AY/C, 24th YAC, 23rd YACOE, 26th YD/C). Jones didn’t exactly help matters with his accuracy. Even with the relatively short throws, his adjusted completion rate was below average, completing fewer passes than expected, although the pressure and limited pocket time probably didn’t make his job any easier (23rd ADOT, 19th AC%, 25th CPOE). With short completions, little YAC, and poor accuracy—and it’s not surprising he finished near the bottom of Week 1 in yards per attempt (27th AYPA). When things broke down, Jones rarely tried to escape with his legs and instead threw the ball away against pressure. His overall abandoned-attempt rate ended up right around average (10th PR%, 24th SCR%, 6th TA%, 18th SCK%, 16th AA%). But that didn’t fix the bigger problem and once everything was accounted for, Jones still finished near the bottom of Week 1 in overall yards per play (29th NY/P). With such little production, it’s not surprising the Colts pass game struggled to get first downs and touchdowns. The turnover didn’t help eiether (29th NY/P, 22nd 1ST%, 22nd TD%, 13th TO%). The final numbers are about what you’d expect from everything above. Jones wasn’t consistently producing successful plays, and the plays that went badly were costly enough to push his EPA per play all the way down to 30th in Week 1 (21st QBSR, 30th EPA/P). mouseover definitions: ay< , dp% , ay/c , yac , yd/c , ac% , aypa , drp% , aypa , ta% , ypa , sck% , ny/a , scr% , ny/d , car% , ny/p , 1st% , any/p , td% , any/p , to% , any/p , epa/p , opd , adj/p adj/p Jones’ efficiency curve shows pretty clearly how the pieces came together. His lack of deep passing pulled down his completion depth, and the combination of limited yards after the catch and poor accuracy pushed him near the bottom of the league in adjusted yards per attempt. His poor first-down and touchdown production didn’t lift his efficiency and by the time everything is accounted for, his EPA per play finishes near the bottom of Week 1. The game was defined by a handful of costly negative plays that overwhelmed the few productive stretches. The biggest damage came from the first-quarter interception (-4.8 EPA) and two costly sacks (-1.9 and -3.4 EPA). Jones did have some strong positive plays, particularly in the fourth quarter, but he just could not get consistant positive plays. Compared to last year, Week 1 continued the downward trend of Indianpolis passing. Of course that is comprised of 3 different QBs, but still, not good. HOW FAR? Too many incompletions and no deep passing. The clearest rhythm came toward the end, when Jones put together a long stretch of first downs driving to a touchdown, but too little, too late. After attacking much farther downfield over the final three weeks of last season, the Colts went considerably shorter in Week 1. Jones’ 6.6-yard average depth of target and 5.0-yard average depth of completion were both well below those recent levels. Shot throws, short yac, lots of incompletions. TO WHO? Pierce led the way in yardage. Nobody else worth metioning. At least Pierce and Downs are in the good quadrant. HOW ACCURATE? When adjusting completion rate by removing drops and throw aways, Jones was about average, but according to CPOE he should have done better. Deep passing was almost non-existant. HOW FAST? Jones got rid of the ball with average quickness but when adjusted for depth of target it was a little slow relative to the league. TO WHERE? That’s a lot of red. No real story there other than passing was poor pretty much everywhere.

title: Colts move green dot from Cam Bynum to Akeem Davis-Gaither
summary: The Colts are already making a significant change after their ugly defensive performance in Week 1. After Cam Bynum wore the green dot in the season opener against the Ravens, Indianapolis will now shift that responsibility to linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither. The green dot allows one defensive player to hear the call from defensive coordinator Lou […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Cam Bynum #0 of the Indianapolis Colts celebrates after breaking up a pass against the Baltimore Ravens during the second quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Colts are already making a significant change after their ugly defensive performance in Week 1. After Cam Bynum wore the green dot in the season opener against the Ravens, Indianapolis will now shift that responsibility to linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither. The green dot allows one defensive player to hear the call from defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo and relay it to the rest of the defense. The move comes after the Colts gave up 41 points and 504 yards against Baltimore, with several issues showing up before and after the snap. Indianapolis struggled to get lined up, looked late reacting to motion and repeatedly appeared disorganized against one of the more difficult offenses in the league to defend. “The communication wasn’t where it needed to be Week 1,” Shane Steichen said, according to the Indianapolis Star. “It frees up Cam on the back end to communicate with A.J. and Sauce and Mooney and all those guys, and obviously Akeem’s right there in the middle.” This was something I mentioned after the Ravens game because the Bynum green dot plan always felt a little questionable. Bynum is a good player, and none of this should be viewed as a knock on him individually. The issue is more about the structure of the defense. Safeties can end up 10, 15 or even 25 yards away from the line of scrimmage depending on the play, the coverage and where the ball ends. That makes it harder to get the call, relay it, communicate checks and still get back into position before the snap. Linebackers are usually the green dot players for a reason. They are closer to the nucleus of the defense. They are near the defensive line, connected to the second level and still close enough to communicate with the safeties behind them. When the offense is moving quickly, that positioning is very important. The Colts apparently saw enough in Week 1 to go back to the more traditional setup. Davis-Gaither played 94 percent of the defensive snaps against Baltimore, so if he is going to be on the field that often, giving him the green dot makes sense. It should also allow Bynum to focus more on organizing the back end with A.J. Haulcy, Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward instead of carrying the full defensive communication burden himself. The move also says something about the Colts’ linebacker situation. CJ Allen was drafted in the second round with the belief that he could become an every-down player and eventually handle major communication responsibilities. Chris Ballard even called him a green dot type of player after the draft. Allen, however, did not play a single defensive snap in Week 1, and Steichen noted that the Colts are rotating linebackers. “We’re rotating linebackers in there,” Steichen said. “Only one guy can wear the green dot.” For now, that guy is Davis-Gaither. This does not fix everything by itself. The Colts need to be better at just about everything after Week 1. Changing the green dot is not some magic solution. However, it is a logical correction after the defense looked scattered against Baltimore. If the communication improves and Bynum looks more comfortable focusing on the secondary, this could be a simple but important adjustment. At the very least, the Colts recognized the Week 1 setup did not work. Now they are going back to a structure that makes more sense on paper, with the linebacker in the middle of the defense calling the plays.

title: The Chiefs dismantling the Broncos has some Colts fans sweating
summary: The Denver Broncos had one of the best defenses in 2025. It’s what carried them to a No. 1 seed in the AFC. Sure, it might have been a bit of a down year for the conference but there was no denying their defensive prowess. Teams change and personnel is different every year, but what […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - NOVEMBER 23: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts is tackled by Drue Tranquill #23 of the Kansas City Chiefs in the fourth quarter of the game at Arrowhead Stadium on November 23, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos had one of the best defenses in 2025. It’s what carried them to a No. 1 seed in the AFC. Sure, it might have been a bit of a down year for the conference but there was no denying their defensive prowess. Teams change and personnel is different every year, but what the Kansas City Chiefs did to the Broncos on Monday Night Football should keep some Indianapolis Colts fans up at night. A ton of that concern comes from the Chiefs hanging 31 points on that defense. More concern comes from the fact that the Chiefs’ defense shut down Bo Nix and the Broncos’ offense as well. The most concerning part has nothing to do with either the Chiefs or the Broncos, however. The main concern stems from what we witnessed on Sunday against the Ravens as the Colts were absolutely shredded. 31 points were surrendered by halftime with Lamar Jackson having 324 yards through the air, while he and Derrick Henry picked up another 184 on the ground. Let’s also not forget that Zay Flowers had 150 yards and barely played half a game. Overall, the defense couldn’t get off the field. Third and long was no problem as the Ravens converted with ease, especially in the first half. Justin Walley was targeted on repeat and left the game cooked. The line didn’t generate enough pressure and failed to tackle Jackson when they had the chance. Flowers, Henry, and even Mark Andrews ran free and wild. If the Chiefs took the Broncos to the woodshed, they must be licking their chops after witnessing that incredibly lackluster effort from the Colts. The season isn’t over by any stretch of the imagination, and no one in the organization should panic. One good game gets them right back into things. To be without nerves after watching each team play, however, would be foolish. One team looked primed for another go at a Super Bowl. The other looked like they will be watching the playoffs from home again. Something has to change if the Colts are going to win at Arrowhead.

title: The Jaguars’ Special Teams Problem Just Got More Complicated
summary: Following Wednesday’s injury report and roster moves, Sunday’s Jacksonville Jaguars matchup versus the Denver Broncos just became much more unpredictable. However, the reason has less to do with the offensive or defensive depth chart than it does with a unit Jacksonville has been quietly struggling to get right since the preseason. BJ Green Loss Hurts […]
full_text: Jacksonville Jaguars defensive end BJ Green II (95) walks off the field after the game of an NFL preseason matchup at EverBank Stadium, Saturday, Aug. 9, 2025 in Jacksonville, Fla. The Steelers defeated the Jaguars 31-25. [Corey Perrine/Florida Times-Union] | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Following Wednesday’s injury report and roster moves, Sunday’s Jacksonville Jaguars matchup versus the Denver Broncos just became much more unpredictable. However, the reason has less to do with the offensive or defensive depth chart than it does with a unit Jacksonville has been quietly struggling to get right since the preseason. BJ Green Loss Hurts More Than Pass Rush When the Jacksonville Jaguars officially placed B.J. Green II on Injured Reserve (IR) early Wednesday, the immediate conversation centered on the pass rush depth. That is understandable, as Green’s four-sack performance in the Teal and White scrimmage and his consistent growth as a rotational edge rusher throughout training camp made him one of the summer’s more noticeable candidates to take a second-year leap. But the loss that matters more, for the near future, goes beyond the defensive snap count, as Green was primarily a special teams player in 2025 (42 percent snap share), with a rotational edge presence. His defensive snap share sat at just 9.6 percent on the depth chart entering the 2026 season; what made him valuable to this roster on a week-to-week basis was his work on the special teams units, particularly kickoff coverage. And that is exactly where his injury happened. Liam Coen confirmed Wednesday that Green was hurt on the opening kickoff of the Browns game. He was injured while working to cure one of Jacksonville’s most publicly vulnerable areas across both the 2026 preseason and the regular season opener. “He’ll be out for a little bit here and we announced that we’re putting him on IR,” Coen said Wednesday. “Unfortunate for B.J., did it on the first play of the game and really played another, like, 15 snaps with an injury. And so, it kind of tells you about the guy, the type of dude that he is.” The grit to play through an elbow injury for fifteen additional snaps is notable. So is the fact that one of Jacksonville’s most dependable special teams contributors was hurt before the defense played a single snap. An area of opportunity potential took a step back. Numbers Behind The Coverage Problem Green’s absence adds urgency to a problem that was already visible. In Week 1 against the Browns, Jacksonville’s kickoff coverage unit allowed Cleveland returner Raheim Sanders to average 43.3 yards on three returns, including a 74-yard return in the third quarter that gave the Browns their best field position of the game. And while the Jaguars won 34-10, comfortably enough that the special teams lapses did not define the outcome, in a tighter game, they would have. Most fans likely know that this pattern didn’t just begin in Week 1. Coverage concerns on kickoffs were a recurring theme during the 2026 preseason, and the issue has carried directly into the regular season. Losing Green, who was a consistent contributor on that unit, does not simplify the problem. Notable 2026 Kickoff Returns Preseason Week 1 against the New Orleans Saints: Ty Chandler had an 86-yard return while Jalen Moreno-Cropper returned another for 34-yards. Preseason Week 2 against the Carolina Panthers: Anthony Tyus III had a 37-yard return, while Trevor Etienne added a 34-yarder. Preseason Week 3 against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers featured no Tampa Bay kick returns Regular Season Week 1 against the Cleveland Browns: Raheim Sanders, Dylan Sampson, and Malachi Corley had notable returns of 74, 37, and 34 yards Jack Kiser: The Plug-and-Play Solution? The activation of linebacker Jack Kiser from the practice squad to the 53-man roster is directly connected to Green’s absence, and the primary purpose is special teams. Kiser is not expected to push into the linebacker rotation behind Foye Oluokun, Ventrell Miller, and Branson Combs. All three performed well in Week 1 and their roles are clearly defined, following Kiser’s preseason placement on the practice squad. What Kiser offers is the special teams experience and versatility to step directly into Green’s coverage unit role. His familiarity with Jacksonville’s special teams system, instead of an outside addition, makes him the most natural fit to absorb those responsibilities over the next month. A Break for Heath Farwell’s Unit? Denver’s Wednesday injury report became genuinely significant with two of the Broncos’ primary contributors in the return game both listed as estimated did not participate following Monday Night Football. Their potential absence could directly benefit a Jacksonville coverage unit that has yet to find its footing in 2026. Wednesday's #JAXvsDEN injury report: Note: We did not practice today, so this report is an estimation. 📰 » https://t.co/jnhzJgVZu9 pic.twitter.com/fZqCgpkHbd — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) September 16, 2026 Running Back RJ Harvey Harvey suffered a hamstring injury during Monday Night Football against the Kansas City Chiefs and did not practice Wednesday. His 2026 value to Denver seems to extend across multiple dimensions, as on Monday he handled 55 percent of the offensive snaps, drew four targets in the passing game, and served as the team’s primary kick returner with four returns averaging 27.8 yards. His rushing contribution of three carries for 18 yards understates the overall role he plays. For example, JK Dobbins carried the ground game load with eight runs for 36 yards at 40 percent of the snaps, but drew zero targets in the passing game, a meaningful hit to the passing game if Harvey cannot go. Additionally, should Harvey remain a DNP on Thursday’s injury report, Jacksonville’s coverage unit could be eyeing the potential of a considerably less threatening kick return game on Sunday. Wide Receiver Marvin Mims Jr. Mims is Denver’s primary punt returner and was also listed as an estimated did not participate with a foot injury. On Monday, he brought back two punts for 36 yards against the Chiefs, an 18.0-yard average. His potential absence would remove another dangerous special teams weapon, this time in the punt return game. Both injuries are listed as estimates ahead of an official practice report to come later. Players not being listed as a DNP on the first day of a short week is a pretty normal occurrence around the NFL. Because of the specific injuries listed, however, the Thursday designations will be a clearer indicator of where each player stands heading into the weekend. Foot issues and hamstrings can often be trickier and/or potentially longer injury types. The lingering possibility of Denver taking the field Sunday without either of their primary returners, against a Jacksonville coverage unit that has been searching for answers since the preseason, is easily the most important special teams storyline of the entire Week 2 slate. BJ Ojulari Added to Practice Squad To address the pass rush depth created by Green’s absence, Jacksonville signed former Arizona Cardinals edge rusher BJ Ojulari to the practice squad. Ojulari, 24, was a second-round pick out of LSU in 2023, 41st overall, who posted 40 tackles and 4.0 sacks in a promising rookie campaign before tearing his ACL in 2024 training camp and missing the entire season. He returned for eight games in 2025, recording one sack, before being waived by Arizona in August. He carries legitimate developmental upside, while allowing Jacksonville an opportunity to confirm his progress towards bouncing back to his rookie ability. He also gives Jacksonville a potential elevation candidate if the pass rush depth were to require additional depth. Career NFL Statistics Games Played: 25 Total Tackles: 49 Sacks: 5.0 Pass Deflections: 1 What are your thoughts on the BJ Ojulari signing, the BJ Green placement on IR, and Jack Kiser re-joining the active roster? title: Chiefs Mailbag: How concerning was the passing game against Denver?
summary: Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag! Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions about the Kansas City Chiefs! Coming off a monster 31-10 victory over the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football,” let’s see what’s on our readers’ minds. TheSovereign1587 asks: What specifically stood out the most […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs looks to pass against the Denver Broncos during the second quarter in the game at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag ! Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions about the Kansas City Chiefs ! Coming off a monster 31-10 victory over the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football,” let’s see what’s on our readers’ minds. TheSovereign1587 asks: What specifically stood out the most about the passing game that made it look as rough as it did? Was it Patrick Mahomes being rusty? Did his knee affect his throwing ability/accuracy? Was it the WRs, not getting open, mistakes, etc? Were the pass plays and routes not effective? Tackle play will take the bulk of the blame for the Chiefs’ disappointing results through the air Monday. That certainly played a role as rookie Kahlil Benson’s inexperience at left tackle significantly dictated the game plan. The uncertainty on the left side masked legitimate concerns about Jaylon Moore’s ability to man the right tackle spot. However, I think other factors combined with Benson and Moore to make for a perfect storm against the Chiefs’ passing attack. Mahomes definitely appeared rusty, especially in the first half. He looked like a player who had not been on the field competitively since December. In addition, wide receivers Rashee Rice and Xavier Worthy played as they had been in and out of the lineup throughout training camp. Week 1 was essentially the preseason for the full starting offense. Also, the Denver secondary — arguably the league’s best and a group very familiar with the Chiefs — deserves credit. The Broncos’ defensive backs apparently were Denver’s only unit that was aware a game was scheduled for Monday night. I think Mahomes will get at least some of his timing back, the tackle play will improve, and most defensive backfields do not have the talent to match Denver’s game plan. However, I am taking real concerns from Monday night and am unsure how much it can be improved. I will probably wait until after Kansas City’s Week 5 bye to determine how panicked or confident to be. RoyalsFanBill asks: Will the Chiefs continue to feature the running game? Hope this isn’t the ole Marty Schottenheimer trick of starting a game with a deep pass only to not pass the rest of the game. I don’t think we will revert back to the old offense, but it would be my major question going forward. Kenneth Walker is effectively signed to a two-year contract worth $28.7 million with a team option for a third year in 2028. I think the Chiefs plan to make him their workhorse over that period. Outside of Mahomes and defensive tackle Chris Jones, Kansas City’s biggest investment has been on the interior of their line. With the money owed to Walker, center Creed Humphrey and guard Trey Smith, it would be incompetence not to rely on the run game early and often. I do think we will see a bit more balance in the coming weeks. It also won’t surprise me if rookie Emmett Johnson sees more work in the backfield on a short week after Walker’s heavy Monday night workload. But I think the days of the run game being an afterthought in the Andy Reid offense are officially over. ReadyForFBSeason asks: What will other teams see on film that they can exploit? Denver clearly didn’t adjust well during the game. What will the Indianapolis Colts be preparing to do differently in Week 2? The Broncos’ inability to answer Walker may be all that is keeping the Indianapolis Colts ’ struggles against Derrick Henry of the Baltimore Ravens from becoming a major Week 1 story. Indianapolis gave up 324 passing yards and 202 yards on the ground. We will see what adjustments they make, but Colts defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo — a longtime Mahomes nemesis — has a lot to fix in a week’s time. One mistake on Denver’s part was abandoning the run game early and only having 11 rushing attempts by running backs. Expect the Colts to try to work around Kansas City’s rejuvenated pass rush with a heavy dose of tailback Jonathan Taylor — who totaled 121 scrimmage yards and a pair of touchdowns on Sunday. wbenk307 asks: Can we continue to expect that level of domination from our D-line and third down defense? Denver had the best offensive line last season, so I am wondering if this was Week 1 wonkiness or the tone for the rest of the year. Broncos quarterback Bo Nix might still be having nightmares about Kansas City’s newfound pass rush when the teams meet again in Denver during Week 8. I think what the Chiefs did early on should be taken very seriously. The most encouraging sign of the Chiefs’ defensive dominance came via the snap counts. Chris Jones, Peter Woods, R Mason Thomas, and Felix Anudike-Uzomah all made their presence felt while playing less than 60% of the defensive snaps. The timeshare approach may not lend itself to individual players putting up huge sack numbers, but the Broncos’ offensive line quickly proved more tired than the Chiefs’ defensive front, with fresh players constantly switched in. George Karlaftis will assuredly lead the group in defensive snaps most weeks, but I expect his 86% snap count to trend down, likely inversely to Ashton Gillotte’s 27% trending up as his foot heals. The Chiefs have the players in place to imitate the constant rotation that helped the Seattle Seahawks and New England Patriots advance to last year’s Super Bowl. Health will ultimately determine Kansas City’s defensive dominance. The Chiefs’ secondary worked around the absence of rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane after the first defensive series. However, an effective pass rush needs top-notch defensive backs to be maximized. The Chiefs’ defensive line played inspired against Denver, but it remains a group with little depth. With the current roster, even one injury could prove catastrophic to what the Chiefs want to do. Second-year defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott will hopefully return from the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list soon after the bye. We will see if rookie edge rusher Jack Pyburn — recently claimed off waivers — can carve out a role this season. But Monday night’s group missing any round of rotational snaps could leave the defensive line very tired, very fast. Papajazz asks What are reasonable expectations going forward? Week 1 is generally a terrible sample to use for the sweeping predictions people inevitably fire off immediately after. I am not going to predict the Chiefs to win the Super Bowl based on one game. I remain high on the Chiefs as a playoff team that should challenge for the AFC West title. The next few weeks should dictate our expectations. In the short term, Kansas City came out on top of their seemingly toughest early-season matchup. It would be very disappointing if they enter the bye week (with the Colts, the Miami Dolphins , and the Las Vegas Raiders on tap) at anything less than 4-0. Thank you for reading this week’s Arrowhead Pride Mailbag ! We will be back after the Chiefs’ season continues with the Colts on “Sunday Night Football.” Keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to ask your questions.

You just run through them, and you know, they make our job a lot easier.” Tonga also played nearly 50% of the team’s snaps on defense, and played on special teams. That’s quite a Week 1 contribution from the 2026 free-agent signing. Chiefs receive a crucial update on rookie DB Mansoor Delane’s injury | Chiefs Wire The Kansas City Chiefs impressively began the 2026 season with their dominant victory over the defending AFC West champions. The victory was bittersweet as their 2026 first-round pick was injured and unable to return early in the game. According to NFL Insider Ian Rapoport, Chiefs rookie defensive back Mansoor Delane should miss minimal time with his shoulder injury. Delane suffered the injury early in the first quarter in the Week 1 victory over the Denver Broncos. Biggest Winners and Losers From Chiefs’ Week 1 Win Over the Denver Broncos | Sports Illustrated Special Teams The punting and kicking were about the only two things the Chiefs got right in the kicking game Thursday. Matt Araiza boomed four punts for an average of 54.5 yards, pinning two inside the 20, while Harrison Butker went 1-for-1 on field goals and 4-for-4 on extra points. The return and coverage units were another story, and they handed Denver a real edge in field position frequently. Kansas City was flagged seven times, but four of those penalties came on special teams. Kansas City Chiefs’ lopsided victory Monday capped a quirky first in NFL history | The Kansas City Star Andy Reid ties Bill Belichick Tight end Travis Kelce wasn’t the only one to move up on a career NFL list during the Chiefs’ lopsided win. Reid got the 18th win in a season-opening game, which tied former Patriots coach Bill Belichick for the second-most in NFL history. Only former Cowboys coach Tom Landry had more with 21 as X user NFL Researcher noted earlier this month. Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce named victim in $25 million fraud scheme | KY3 A 2021 Forbes article states Kelce was an investor in a fund created by Swiftarc, which the defendant, Sid Jawahar, co-founded. Jawahar pleaded guilty in January to federal wire fraud charges related to an investment scheme. Prosecutors said Jawahar used money made from new investors to repay older financiers “and to fuel an extravagant lifestyle that included flights on private planes, stays at luxury hotels and expensive outings at fancy restaurants.” Around the NFL Sean Payton ‘never heard’ about Drew Brees’ comeback attempt with Broncos in playoffs | The Athletic “I just know that I was the odd man out,” Payton said after the Broncos suffered a 31-10 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs on Monday. “I never heard anything about it. It never came to anything. I was only told about it later, so I was just like you guys.” No comeback ever materialized for Brees, who was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in July, with Payton presenting. Payton said Tuesday he heard the story during the Hall of Fame weekend about Lombardi and Carmichael approaching Brees, but Payton thought they meant it happened during the 2020 season, when Brees missed four games due to injury. Source: Chargers signing Valdes-Scantling to practice squad | ESPN A fifth-round choice in 2018 out of South Florida, Valdez-Scantling spent training camp with the Dallas Cowboys, but the team released him when it cut its roster to 53 players. Valdes-Scantling’s signing comes after Sunday’s loss to the Cardinals in which wide receivers Ladd McConkey (rib), KeAndre Lambert-Smith (hamstring) and Derius Davis (undisclosed) were injured. On Tuesday, the Chargers put Lambert-Smith on injured reserve, meaning he’ll sit out at least four games.​ Ben Johnson suggests he wanted Bears to score 60 points at Carolina | Pro Football Talk In a Monday interview of coach Ben Johnson on ESPN 1000, Jeff Joniak said this about the 59-37 win over the Bears: “At that point I was hoping for 60. I was thinking a two-point try at some point.” Johnson paused, smiled, and said, “I don’t think you were the only one.” It’s on brand for Johnson. He wants to score a lot of points. He wants to blow teams out. Whenever, wherever, however. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride 5 things we learned about the Chiefs from Week 1 win over Denver This team is going to be hard to pass against The severity of rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane’s injury hurts this defense. He is a special talent who looks like a cornerstone you can build around for years to come. But even without Delane for most of Monday night, the Chiefs secondary locked down Denver’s vaunted wide receivers, holding Jaylen Waddle and Courtland Sutton to three receptions for 13 yards. Do I think this performance was an outlier? Nope. title: Chargers Power Rankings Roundup: Bolts see drastic fall after loss to Cardinals
summary: The Chargers and their entire fan base were shocked by the double-digit loss to the Cardinals in Week One. For the most part, the Bolts were seen as a potential top-10 team to begin the season and mostly were seen ranked inside the top 16 across the board. However, a sloppy loss to the Cardinals […]
full_text: Inglewood, - September 13: Running back Omarion Hampton #8 of the Los Angeles Chargers runs for the touchdown against the Arizona Cardinals in the first half of a NFL football game at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood on Sunday, September 13, 2026. (Photo by Keith Birmingham/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images The Chargers and their entire fan base were shocked by the double-digit loss to the Cardinals in Week One. For the most part, the Bolts were seen as a potential top-10 team to begin the season and mostly were seen ranked inside the top 16 across the board. However, a sloppy loss to the Cardinals has seen them take a big hit in this week”s updated rankings. There’s only so much to recap as to what led to the drop and most of you likely don’t want to read about it again, so let’s just dive right in to this week’s roundup. Sports Illustrated – #17 I agree with MMQB Podcast co-host Albert Breer who said this on our Monday morning recap show: It’s most concerning to me that L.A. did not dazzle in the run game despite having most conceivable advantages over the Cardinals. Alas, this is the opening week loss no one saw coming (especially the boobs who used ChatGPT for help in their knockout pools. All of you get what you deserve).‘” – Conor Orr Bleacher Report – #19 Are we sure that Mike McDaniel is an offensive guru? Justin Herbert never seemed to find a rhythm, and the Los Angeles Chargers offense looked every bit as disjointed as it did under Greg Roman last season. Unfortunately, the top-tier defense we saw from L.A. in 2025 was nowhere to be found. Maybe the Arizona Cardinals are simply far better than anyone expected. However, the version of the Chargers we saw on Sunday looked like a team that could be headed to the AFC West basement. – Kristopher Knox Yahoo Sports – #19 “There’s nothing good to say about the Chargers’ Week 1 loss. It was so dispiriting that head coach Jim Harbaugh lamented sitting his starters for most of the preseason. The offense, with new coordinator Mike McDaniel, had two plays longer than 15 yards against an Arizona defense that isn’t expected to be good. (Don’t tell Andrew Wingard I said that.) The defense, without last year’s star coordinator Jesse Minter, allowed points or a missed field goal on seven of 10 possessions before a kneel-down at the end. The Chargers’ early-season schedule is brutal, and the Cardinals game was supposed to be a rare easy win.” – Frank Schwab ESPN – #19 The second-round pick out of Florida was put in a tough position. Slaughter spent most of his college snaps at center, but he competed for the left guard spot throughout most of training camp. When starting center Tyler Biadasz suffered a preseason ACL injury, Slaughter was thrust into the starting role. On Sunday, he had as good a performance as you’d hope a rookie center to have, with no major blunders. He allowed just one quarterback pressure, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. – Kris Rhim The Athletic – #19 Maybe that’s an overreaction, but the Chargers lost to the Cardinals, a team that had a preseason win total over/under of 3.5. Justin Herbert wasn’t good, the running game struggled and the defense allowed 393 yards of offense to a team with Jacoby Brissett at quarterback and Kendrick Bourne as its top-producing wide receiver in the game. – Chad Graff and Josh Kendall SB Nation – #19 NFL.com – #20 Did the Chargers take the Cardinals lightly? Perhaps. Their performance suggested they may have, but what I saw from Jim Harbaugh’s crew was evidence of rust. It’s not uncommon in Week 1 — however, it is alarming for a club aiming to improve on its recent postseason one-and-dones. If anything, the uneven showing reminded the Bolts that they cannot underestimate any opponent in the NFL. They better take the field with more fire in the next few weeks. – Nick Shook USA Today – #25 Jim Harbaugh had never lost an opener as an NFL head coach … until Sunday, a defeat that dropped him to 6-1 in Week 1. The Bolts’ putrid performance also makes it worth wondering if Harbs is headed to his first sub-.500 campaign under an NFL headset. – Nate Davis
