summary: After one week of NFL football being back, the New Orleans Saints currently sit with a record of 0-1 following their 31-30 loss to the Detroit Lions. Attention will now shift to another road matchup, this time versus the Baltimore Ravens, who are coming off of a 41-23 win over the Indianapolis Colts. The Saints […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Devaughn Vele #14 of the New Orleans Saints scores a touchdown against the Detroit Lions during the third quarter of the game at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images After one week of NFL football being back, the New Orleans Saints currently sit with a record of 0-1 following their 31-30 loss to the Detroit Lions. Attention will now shift to another road matchup, this time versus the Baltimore Ravens, who are coming off of a 41-23 win over the Indianapolis Colts. The Saints will enter week two as the fourth-ranked offense in the league after gaining 469 total yards. They accumulated 378 passing yards (1st in the league) and 91 rushing yards (22nd in the league) during last Sunday’s slate. QB Tyler Shough leads both New Orleans and the NFL with 410 yards through the air even after throwing two interceptions and being sacked five times. Former Jacksonville Jaguar RB Travis Etienne Jr. led the Saints with 46 rushing yards, averaging just over five per carry. WR Chris Olave is also league-leading after his career-high 182 receiving yards on ten receptions even though he was kept out of the endzone by Detroit. Size in the passing game led to majority of the Saints’ scoring after WR Devaughn Vele and TEs Juwan Johnson and Noah Fant hauled in touchdowns. RB Kendre Miller punched in the other New Orleans TD on the ground. Meanwhile, the Baltimore defense is currently ranked sixth overall in the league after giving up just 251 yards of offense in week one. The Ravens allowed 149 yards through the air (5th in the league) and 102 yards rushing (13th in the league) in their first outing. Ravens LB Roquan Smith had a team-leading 11 tackles versus the Colts and secured an interception. CB Marlon Humphrey came up with the only other turnover for Baltimore after forcing and recovering a fumble. Safety Malaki Starks and LB Tavius Robinson earned sacks last weekend for the Ravens and combined for 17 total yards tackled for a loss. Baltimore’s defense held the Colts to just 16 points through three quarters before giving up a garbage time score. The Raven defense can play hardnosed, competitive football long into the game meaning New Orleans will not be able to rely on too many late heroics and scoring spurts if they want any shot of getting their record up to .500 and avoiding an 0-2 start.

title: A look back at the history between the Saints and Ravens
summary: The New Orleans Saints will hit the road in Week 2 to take on the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium this Sunday. These two teams first met on September 29, 1996, in the Louisiana Superdome, with Baltimore coming away with a 17-10 victory. Since then, they have played one another just eight times, with […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - NOVEMBER 07: Kyle Hamilton #14 of the Baltimore Ravens makes the tackle against the New Orleans Saints at Caesars Superdome on November 7, 2022 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints will hit the road in Week 2 to take on the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium this Sunday. These two teams first met on September 29, 1996, in the Louisiana Superdome, with Baltimore coming away with a 17-10 victory. Since then, they have played one another just eight times, with the Ravens holding a 6-2 advantage in the all-time series. The last time they faced one another, Baltimore defeated New Orleans 27-13 in the Caesars Superdome on November 7, 2022. The Ravens controlled much of the game, with Lamar Jackson and Baltimore’s rushing attack proving difficult for the Saints to contain. New Orleans did not earn its first victory over Baltimore until 2018, when the Saints escaped M&T Bank Stadium with a thrilling 24-23 win that ended when then Ravens kicker Justin Tucker missed an extra point with 24 seconds remaining. The Saints enter Sunday’s matchup looking to bounce back after a heartbreaking 31-30 overtime loss to the Detroit Lions in Week 1. New Orleans fell behind 21-0 before mounting an impressive comeback, eventually forcing overtime and having multiple opportunities to get the upset. Despite three turnovers, quarterback Tyler Shough threw for 410 yards and three touchdowns, while Chris Olave finished with 10 receptions for 182 yards. The performance offered plenty of reasons for optimism despite the loss, especially after the Saints showed the resilience to battle back from a three-touchdown deficit on the road. Baltimore enters the matchup 1-0 after opening its season with a 41-23 victory over the Indianapolis Colts. The Ravens piled up 506 yards of total offense, led by Lamar Jackson’s 324 passing yards and Derrick Henry’s 144 rushing yards and three touchdowns. For the Saints, Sunday’s matchup represents another difficult early-season road test and an opportunity to build on the fight they showed in Detroit. Baltimore has historically had the upper hand in this series, but New Orleans will look to change that while earning its first victory of the 2026 season. No. 1 — Baltimore Ravens ( last week No. 8 ) 📈 7 spots The Ravens start the Jesse Minter era with a 40-burger against the Indianapolis Colts. Declan Doyle’s offense had over 500 yards, 200 of which came on the ground. The Ravens did this on the road. It appears that Zay Flowers — who had five catches for 150 yards and a touchdown — avoided major injury after leaving the game with a hamstring strain. Derrick Henry might still be running — he averaged six yards per carry. It was an old-fashioned Ravens kind of win that showcased the potential of John Harbaugh’s former squad, and they vaunted themselves to number one in my rankings ahead of their home matchup against the Saints. No. 2 — Buffalo Bills ( last week No. 5 ) 📈 3 spots The Bills went into Houston and defeated the Texans, 36-31. Josh Allen put the team on his back and willed them to victory — as he is one to do. He threw for 334 yards and rushed for two touchdowns, while connecting with new weapon DJ Moore for 100 yards and a score through the air. It’s even more impressive that the Bills did this with a short week ahead, as they host Detroit on Thursday Night Football. No. 3 — Seattle Seahawks ( last week No. 1 ) 📉 2 spots I hate dropping Seattle after a 13-10 win against the Patriots on Wednesday, but losing Sam Darnold and starting Drew Lock for the foreseeable future had an effect. Of course, though, the Seattle Seahawks remain a top-notch team due to their defense and the overall operation of Mike MacDonald. No. 4 — Los Angeles Rams ( last week No. 2 ) 📉 2 spots The Rams are looking to put the 27-7 beatdown by the 49ers behind them — Australia did not treat Sean McVay’s team well. They also lost Myles Garrett to a knee injury, and kind of just looked old. They host the Giants — a team with a ton of energy who is, in fact, no old at all — on Monday Night Football. They have extended rest and I expect them to be ready for the Giants, who aren’t an easy win anymore. No. 5 — Cincinnati Bengals ( last week No. 10 ) 📈 5 spots The Bengals defense forced four turnovers and harrassed Baker Mayfield all game. If the defense is improved and can remain opportunistic, look out for Cincinnati and the Joe Burrow led Bengals. Dexter Lawrence had three pressures in the game. No. 6 — Chicago Bears ( last week No. 11 ) 📈 5 spots The Bears scored 59 points against the Carolina Panthers and probably could have scored more. Now I am worried about the defense — they did surrender 37 points to Bryce Young — but Ben Johnson has Caleb Williams playing at a high level. Chicago is one of the most exciting teams in the sport, and they move up five spots in the rankings. No. 7 — Kansas City Chiefs ( last week No. 18 ) 📈 11 spots Yeah, I was too low on the Chiefs. I bought into the Kenneth Walker addition, but I didn’t see them commanding the trenches as well as they did in their 31-10 slaughter of Denver. Steve Spagnuolo is still excellent, and his defense made Davis Webb’s offense look inept. A team with a run first/defensive mentality with Patrick Mahomes at quarterback is incredibly scary. No. 8 — San Francisco 49ers ( last week No. 16 ) 📈 8 spots The 49ers punched their divisional rival in the mouth — looks like the extended week in Australia may have helped. Nevertheless, Raheem Morris has the now-healthy 49ers defense looking like a top-five unit, while the offense continues to thrive despite injuries. Brock Purdy is an underrated quarterback, and I expect to see another beatdown this week against Miami. No. 9 — Jacksonville Jaguars ( last week No. 15 ) 📈 6 spots Jacksonville easily handled the Cleveland Browns, beating them 34-10 as Trevor Lawrence threw four touchdowns. Liam Coen’s unit cruised to victory and will now face a tougher task in Denver, against a team that slid far down the rankings after their abysmal performance. No. 10 — Houston Texans ( last week No. 7 ) 📉 3 spots Houston faced Josh Allen and failed to contain the star quarterback in a back-and-forth battle. DeMeco Ryans still has a top-three defense in the league, despite allowing 36 points. I expect the Texans to bounce back, but the Bengals pose a tough test; at least Houston is home again. No. 11 — New England Patriots ( last week No. 3 ) 📉 8 spots The Patriots had one of the worst — most anticlimactic — opening games against a team that beat them in the Super Bowl. A.J. Brown was injured, Romeo Doubs disappeared, and Drake Maye played one of his career worst games. New England hosts Pittsburgh. No. 12 — Philadelphia Eagles ( last week No. 6 ) 📉 6 spots The Eagles won, but slid six spots down the rankings — my bias against Philadelphia or objective analysis of an offense that looks concerning? The latter! Sean Mannion struggled against the revamped Washington defense, and the offensive line did not look great. The Eagles won, 24-22, but it was in a very unconvincing fashion. No. 13 — Detroit Lions ( last week No. 13 ) SAME A failed two-point conversion by Tyler Shough and the Saints’ offense spared the Lions from a brutal overtime collapse. Shough, who was contained through the first three quarters, threw for over 400 yards, and the Lions could not cover Chris Olave through the game, who went for 182 yards. They’re ranked in the exact same spot as last week. No. 14 — Denver Broncos ( last week No. 4 ) 📉 10 spots Denver was dominated by the Kansas City Chiefs and now faces a hot Jacksonville team. The playcalling of Davis Webb is already in question, and the defense was gut-punched by Kenneth Walker. They dropped ten spots with that performance, but I expect them to stabilize. No. 15 — Minnesota Vikings ( last week No. 17 ) 📈 2 spots The Vikings continue to be a resilient team under Kevin O’Connell. Kyler Murray was injured in the first half, and Carson Wentz finished the game with an epic come-from-behind victory against Green Bay. The final score was 39-22, and Brian Flores’ defense turned it on in the second half, forcing a pair of turnovers and sacking Jordon Love four times. The Vikings will likely start Carson Wentz on Sunday against the Bears in Chicago. No. 16 — New York Giants ( last week No. 22 ) 📈 6 spots We heard all off-season about the run-first mentaltity centrailized around heavier personnel packages and under-cneter looks, and WOW was it effecitve against the Dallas Cowboys. The Giants ran the ball at will agaisnt Dallas, and limited Dak Prescott to just two possessions in the second half. Multiple 10+ play drives with four touchdowns, including three Jaxson Dart touchdowns through the air. The chapter of medocrity might be over. It’s a new and exciting time in New York for Big Blue. No. 17 — Dallas Cowboys ( last week No. 9) 📉 8 spots Dallas’ offense was sloppy against the Giants and their defense had several miscommunications. Still, it was the Giants commanding the trenches on offense that led to the poor defensive mishaps, for Christian Parker could not get his guys off the field. Sure, Dallas was a mess, but that doesn’t take anything away from the Giants. I expect that Dallas will see better days this season. Their defense has talent, but they’re not quite playing in unison yet. No. 18 — Green Bay Packers ( last week No. 14 ) 📉 4 spots The Packers were up 22-10 in the third quarter but Minnesota forced a fumble, interception, and a pair of turnover on downs in the fourth quarter that ended the game with a 39-22 Vikings’ win. The Packers will look to get right in their second consecutive road game against the Jets. No. 19 — Los Angeles Chargers ( last…

title: NY Giants news: Aaron Donald, ‘Pancake’ Patrick Ricard, more headlines
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories as the Giants hit the practice field for the first time this week to prepare for their clash with the Los Angeles Rams. Why NFL Projection Model is buying the Giants offense and selling Patriots panic | The Athletic Buying the Giants offense. Maybe the […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories as the Giants hit the practice field for the first time this week to prepare for their clash with the Los Angeles Rams. Why NFL Projection Model is buying the Giants offense and selling Patriots panic | The Athletic Buying the Giants offense. Maybe the Dallas Cowboys’ problematic defense isn’t any better than last year, but the New York Giants absolutely destroyed them from wire to wire Sunday night; it was the kind of performance that often predicts future success. Perhaps the most impressive aspect of the offense was quarterback Jaxson Dart’s play. Dart made some nice throws, took what the Cowboys gave him, and used his legs effectively. I’m not sure I was fully bought into the Dart experience within a Matt Nagy and Greg Roman offense, but the poise and accuracy he showed in prime time has me reconsidering that stance. Outside of Dart, the other reason the model likes the Giants more today than it did before the season is that they looked better than expected in the trenches. The Giants’ offensive line completely dominated the Cowboys’ front, delivering 0.7 EPA per dropback and a 51 percent success rate on the ground. The model still has concerns about New York’s defense, but it’s buying the offense being better than expected and believes the Giants will be a factor in the NFC playoff race. Playoff odds before Week 1: 14 percent • Today: 33 percent Skat mic’ed up "Let me eat!!!" 😤 pic.twitter.com/9aVT7wpl5V — New York Giants (@Giants) September 15, 2026 Francis Mauigoa impresses in NFL debut as Giants offensive line comes together | New York Daily News In fact, Mauigoa didn’t permit a single pressure on his 36 pass blocks, according to Next Gen Stats. Mauigoa also recorded a 75% run block win rate in Sunday night’s 28-20 victory at MetLife Stadium, contributing to a Giants offense that imposed its will against the Dallas defense. “Seeing him running to the ball, seeing him finish blocks, try to put guys in the dirt, that’s what you want for offensive linemen — especially at guard,” Giants fullback Patrick Ricard said Tuesday of Mauigoa. “To see that for the first game, it’s really encouraging. You want offensive linemen to set the tone for the whole offense. Me, seeing that, it makes me want to be doing that every play.” 2026 NFL offensive line rankings: Broncos retain top spot | PFF 22. New York Giants. Right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor was the Giants’ best pass-blocker in the win over the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday Night Football, earning an 83.4 PFF pass-blocking grade and allowing a 0.0% pressure rate. Rookie right guard Francis Mauigoa also didn’t allow a pressure, though he did lose pass-blocking reps that didn’t result in pressure, finishing his debut with an 82.4% PFF pass-block win rate. Why John Harbaugh’s fast Giants start did not come as a surprise to his greatest rival | New York Post Before John Harbaugh’s debut as the head coach of the Giants, one of his greatest combatants for nearly two decades predicted the pairing would turn out to be highly successful. And, perhaps, sooner than anticipated. “I think that the fix there is going to be quicker than maybe outsiders might realize. I’m not putting them in the Super Bowl, but I certainly expect those guys to be competitive and be competitive almost instantly.” John Harbaugh has already given the Giants something they haven’t had in years — hope | Yahoo Sports For a franchise that had won a total of 13 games the last three seasons combined, Sunday night was nothing short of an epiphany. With a single game, Harbaugh has swept away years of futility and instilled a mindset of expectation and self-respect that extends from the field to the stands and back. This is unfamiliar territory for the Giants and their fans as of late; the team hasn’t made the playoffs since the 2022 season. But before Big Blue Nation starts making February hotel reservations in Los Angeles, keep in mind that Dallas — particularly the woeful, overmatched Cowboy defense — deserves a Best Supporting Actor nomination for making the Giants look so good. If the Giants can in fact improve on their performance Sunday night — starting with a Monday night road game against the Rams — New York sports talk radio is going to be a lot of fun over the next few months. title: NY Giants add DL to 53-man roster, re-sign Dalen Cambre to practice squad
summary: The New York Giants juggled their roster on Wednesday, adding defensive line depth to their active roster. The Giants signed veteran defensive tackle Josh Tupou to their 53-man roster from the practice squad. Wide receiver/special teamer Dalen Cambre, who was waived on Monday, has been re-signed to the practice squad. Cambre was signed from the […]
full_text: Josh Tupou (94) with the Giants during preseason. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants juggled their roster on Wednesday, adding defensive line depth to their active roster. The Giants signed veteran defensive tackle Josh Tupou to their 53-man roster from the practice squad. Wide receiver/special teamer Dalen Cambre , who was waived on Monday, has been re-signed to the practice squad. Cambre was signed from the practice squad to the 53-man roster on Saturday to safeguard against the possibility Malik Nabers would not play. Nabers, of course, did play as the Giants defeated the Dallas Cowboys, 28-20. Cambre was inactive. Tupou, 32, is a 6-foot-3, 350-pound player in his ninth NFL season. He spent the last two seasons with Giants head coach John Harbaugh and the Baltimore Ravens. Tupou spent most of his time on the practice squad, but did appear in six games over those two seasons. Prior to joining the Ravens, Tupou spent six seasons with the Cincinnati Bengals. Overall, he has played 71 regular-season games with 23 starts.

title: Giants-Rams, Week 2 preview: 5 storylines, including Aaron Donald’s return
summary: The 1-0 New York Giants travel across the country to face the surpringly 0-1 Los Angeles Rams on Monday Night Football in Week 2 of the NFL season. Here are five storylines to pay attention to. Aaron Donald’s return? The future Hall of Fame defensive tackle, a nine-time First-Team All-Pro in 10 seasons, is back […]
full_text: Aaron Donald | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The 1-0 New York Giants travel across the country to face the surpringly 0-1 Los Angeles Rams on Monday Night Football in Week 2 of the NFL season. Here are five storylines to pay attention to. Aaron Donald’s return? The future Hall of Fame defensive tackle, a nine-time First-Team All-Pro in 10 seasons, is back with the Rams after a two-year retirement. The 35-year-old did not make the trip to Australia with the team. Could he make his return Monday night? “ We haven’t decided that yet ,” [Rams coach Sean] McVay said. “He’s going to continue to work his process and we’ll see what that looks like.” NFL Insider Ian Rapoport said there is “ very, very realistic chance ” Donald will be in uniform against the Giants. How much, and how well, Donald can play at this point are legitimate questions. Week 1 hangover The Giants are riding high after an upset victory. The Rams are facing questions after an unexpected — and unexpectedly large — season-opening loss, as well as the injury to star defensive end Myles Garrett . Does all of that psychology actually matter? “Maybe initially kind of – we’re all human, right? So, we’re all like, ‘Okay, what happened to this team?’,” said Giants fullback Patrick Ricard. “Like you look at the Rams. Like, you’re going to initially think they’re going to be pissed off, right? Like, they had to go to Australia, and they obviously didn’t win that game. So, I feel like they’re going to come back, and they have a vengeance and they’re going to be really just – so yeah, there is a little bit to it. “But I feel like at the end of the day all that really matters is, after a game get your bodies right, get recovered, start feeling good for the week, dive in on who we’re playing, kind of get the personnel, and then get the game plan from our coaches, and then just practice and execute those plays and learn the best we can. And then have a good week of practice and then just get ready to play.” A 2-0 start? Facing the Cowboys and Rams, two teams expected to be among the best in the NFC, looked like a difficult way to start the season. Entering that stretch, coming out 1-1 looked like it would be a victory for the Giants. It still might be considered that. Still, this game looks more winnable for the Giants than it did before the season started. The Giants remain 7.5-point underdogs , but that is down from an opening line of 9.5. The Giants’ victory over the Cowboys was not a fluke. They clearly earned it. The Rams are clearly not the unbeatable machine they were billed as before the season began. Los Angeles remains an outstanding team, should be favored Monday night, and probably wins the game. Still, I’m not going to tell Giants fans they shouldn’t dream a little bit. Big plays vs. efficiency The Giants were about as efficient on offense as they could possibly have been against the Cowboys. Jaxson Dart was 23 of 29, a career-best 79.3% completion rate. The Giants were 9 of 11 on third-down, 9 of 10 if you take out a game-ending kneel down. New York held the ball for 36:40. The Giants had three scoring drives of 10 plays or more, two of which lasted longer than eight minutes. What was missing? Explosive chunk plays, that’s what. The Giants had only one play of more than 20 yards, a 22-yard Dart run that turned into a 37-yard play thanks to a late hit by DeMarvion Overshown of the Cowboys. The Giants were successful going the long, hard way against the Cowboys. Over the course of the season, the Giants will need more big plays. “I don’t know if methodical would be our identity throughout the entire season,” Dart said after the game. “I think that that was just what was needed to win this game. We had success, we had the lead, and our coaches did an amazing job of just putting us in a great situation to capitalize on those moments and to really just be in control. “So, I think every single game is going to have a different thing that you have to adjust to, but that was kind of the key thing tonight: We were able to put really long drives together, execute on a high note, and then when we got down to the red zone, we were able to capitalize with a touchdown.” Running back depth chart Tyrone Tracy Jr. got a uniform against the Cowboys, with four-time 1,000-yard rusher Najee Harris inactive. Tracy had a costly fumble on his second — and final — carry of the game. Will those two switch places on Monday night?

title: NY Giants’ FB Patrick Ricard is the offense’s ‘secret sauce’
summary: The New York Giants talked … and talked … and talked as the season approached about being a physical football team. Even as the Giants were building the foundation of their offense, “we know it will be physical” was the answer you would get when asking what it might look like. We saw the physicality […]
full_text: Patrick Ricard | Getty Images The New York Giants talked … and talked … and talked as the season approached about being a physical football team. Even as the Giants were building the foundation of their offense, “we know it will be physical” was the answer you would get when asking what it might look like. We saw the physicality the Giants want to bring to the table during Sunday’s 28-20 victory over the Dallas Cowboys, with Dallas COO Stephen Jones even admitting “ they outphysicaled us .” The poster child for that physicality, and for the kind of football team head coach John Harbaugh wants the Giants to be, is 300-pound fullback Patrick Ricard . After nine seasons as a member of the Baltimore Ravens with Harbaugh, Ricard followed the coach to the Giants in free agency. Sunday, Ricard played 37 offensive snaps as the Giants ran 37 times for 165 yards (4.5 yards per attempt) and held the ball for 36:40. If you haven’t done the math, 37 snaps per game for 17 games would come out to 629 snaps. Ricard played a career-high 698 snaps for the Ravens in 2022, the only time he surpassed 600 snaps. He played only 274 snaps last season. “The jobs and the roles that he’s being asked to play are built into our offense,” Harbaugh said. “Not everybody has those, but a lot of people do. “There’s a lot of things that Pat can do that nobody else can do. Nobody in the world can do some of the things that Pat Ricard can do. And that’s good for us. That’s unique for us. So, it helps us be who we are. It builds into our team persona, our team identity. And we love that. We love that about him as a player.” Ricard’s job boils down to hitting guys on the other team. Hard. Clearing holes for running backs or keeping pass rushers off quarterback Jaxson Dart. He is forever trying to remind defenders why he has the nickname “Pancake Pat.” “Nobody in the world can do some of the things that Pat Ricard can do.” — John Harbaugh “Whatever the coaches ask for me to do to help his team win, I’m going to do,” Ricard said. “I mean, look, I was an undrafted defensive lineman. I played D-line, I played offense, I played both sides of the ball. I played special teams. Line me up in the backfield, on the line, in the slot, have me do this, that. Whatever it is, I’m going to try my best.” One thing Ricard’s job rarely includes is touching the ball. In 133 career regular-season games, Ricard has 11 carries and 49 pass receptions. He doesn’t care. He knows what he is good at. “I played defense for most of my life, so for me to play on offense, I (couldn’t) care less if I ever get the ball,” Ricard said. “For me, it’s all about, I want to impose my will on defenses, and I have the most fun when I’m pancaking people and I’m springing big blocks for my guys to have success, getting lots of points, getting a lot of first downs, winning.” “If the ball comes my way, cool. If not, then I’m not going to be getting in (Matt) Nagy’s face like, ‘I need the ball,’ or getting mad at Jaxson for not giving me the ball. It’s fine by me because these guys that are on my team, they’re playmakers, dynamic, and I feel like they would be better with the ball in their hands and me blocking for them. So, that’s what I’m cool with.” ‘Secret sauce’ Ricard played both ways for the Ravens in his first three NFL seasons, totalling 225 snaps as a defensive tackle. He has been a full-time fullback since 2020. “Early on, I didn’t play offense in college, so for me it was like they had to almost limit what I could do my first maybe couple years just because I was still learning the position and learning offense in general,” Ricard said. “But I feel like now it’s like I’ve been in – I’ve had (senior offensive assistant) Greg Roman as my run game coordinator, offense coordinator, and now being back in his scheme, it’s like there’s so much to build off of to where they can plug and piece me in any spots.” Ricard really has one job. Block people, and do it with authority. At this point in his career, he can do it from just about every spot or angle imaginable. Sunday, he was in a true fullback alignment 15 times, was an inline tight end seven times, in the slot 11 times and aligned as a wide receiver four times. “Motion me, shift me, to where – I’ve done it all to the point where I can execute it at a really high level to where I feel like that’s like what G-Ro (Greg Roman) said about me is like I’m like the spaghetti sauce on the offense,” Ricard said. “I’m like the secret sauce to where you put me in different spots to get the advantage, and I’m usually a mismatch of who I’m blocking because I’m usually bigger than them, to where I think it’s really an advantage for the offense. “And it’s a lot of fun. It’s a lot of fun to be in this offense, to be moved around a lot in motion and shift and be in different spots. It’s almost like Where’s Waldo on Sundays, and it can be a lot for a defense to defend.” The Giants’ way The smashmouth style that Harbaugh has brought back to the Giants is reminiscent of the Giants’ championship teams of the Super Bowl era. Those teams generally dominated the line of scrimmage. They were gritty, not pretty. They had physical defenses. They had physical run games. And, by the way, they featured fullbacks. The Bill Parcells teams had Maurice Carthon. The Tom Coughlin teams had Madison Hedgecock and Henry Hynoski. When I posted the ‘ Kudos and Wet Willies ’ after Sunday’s victory over the Dallas Cowboys, I did not included Ricard in the ‘Kudos’. BBV commenters let me know about the oversight. Ricard has been feeling the love from Giants fans. “I definitely felt it when I signed here and I’ve been around,” Ricard said. “But after this game, my social media has been flooding with just so much support from Giants fans just telling me how much they love how I play, MVP of the game, all this stuff. And I think it’s more of just how excited they are to have a fullback and the way I play. “I’m all for it, I love it. I’m (going to) continue to play hard and do whatever I can to help the Giants keep getting wins.” Pat Ricard has been impressed with the dedication of his Giants teammates and the organization as a whole: "NYC is right across the river, and guys would rather be in the locker room hanging out two hours after the game" pic.twitter.com/1HZtYXo5i7 — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) September 15, 2026 ‘Hungry and humble’ New head coaches always bring a handful of their favorite players from prior coaching stops to help ease the transition and build a culture. Ricard is, of course, one of several ex-Ravens now wearing a Giants uniform. Ricard has been impressed by his new teammates from the start. “I just see how hungry and how humble everybody is here,” Ricard said. “They just – they want – there’s so many guys here that want to prove themselves. They want to win, and you just see it with how they work, how they prepare, and how much they love each other. “I remember when I first got here for OTAs, just seeing how much the guys are cheering each other on in our running workouts and being there for one another and hanging out in the locker room two hours after we were done for the day. And I’m thinking, I’m like, ‘Wow, New York City is right across the river, right there, and guys would rather be in the locker room hanging out two hours after.’ So, I feel like that was just things I noticed right away, and I think it’s so important for a team to want to win and want to be crazed, loving one another and working hard.” Hungry and humble is actually a great way to describe Ricard. Hungry to deliver pain to opposing defenses and win football games, and humble about how good he has been at his job for a decade now.
author: Ed Valentine

title: NY Giants news: Looking ahead to the Rams
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to as the Giants get set to take a Los Angeles Rams coming off a tough loss in Australia to open the season. John Harbaugh’s next impact: Staying on Giants’ mistakes to beat Rams | New York Daily News “We understand that how […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to as the Giants get set to take a Los Angeles Rams coming off a tough loss in Australia to open the season. John Harbaugh’s next impact: Staying on Giants’ mistakes to beat Rams | New York Daily News “We understand that how you play this week is not gonna be good enough to win next week,” Harbaugh said Monday afternoon. “How we played [Sunday] night will not win the game next Monday night. It won’t be good enough. So we’ve got to improve.” “We’re putting the ball on the ground entirely too much,” Harbaugh said on Zoom. “It’s gotta change. We’ve gotta make the change on that. Every single ball carrier has got to make sure that it gets better. Sometimes as coaches we gotta drill it, we gotta teach it and we gotta make sure that we do it better. Because the ball was on the ground four times. That’s not even close to being acceptable as an example.” Ricard on the team staying away from distractions Pat Ricard has been impressed with the dedication of his Giants teammates and the organization as a whole: "NYC is right across the river, and guys would rather be in the locker room hanging out two hours after the game" pic.twitter.com/1HZtYXo5i7 — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) September 15, 2026 John Harbaugh effect: Five reasons Giants are different under Super Bowl winning coach | CBSSports.com 5. Harbaugh is rebuilding a broken culture. Coaching turnover and eight losing seasons over the last decade turned a proud franchise into a perennial bottom-dweller in the NFC East. That is a tough hole to climb out of. Reversing the year-in and year-out disappointment requires a strong culture, and Harbaugh is renowned for his ability to create one. It is already taking effect in New York. Harbaugh’s CEO approach, where he also reports directly to team ownership rather than general manager Joe Schoen, seems to be widely accepted in New York. And it might just lead the Giants back to the promised land. 2026 NFL season, Week 1: What We Learned from Sunday’s games | NFL.com What a way to kick off the Harbaugh era. Jaxson Dart was back, so too were Malik Nabers and Cam Skattebo, each of them making contributions to knock off the rival Cowboys in head coach John Harbaugh’s Gotham debut. Facing a franchise that popularized the triplets term, the Giants’ young franchise trio of Dart, Nabers and Skattebo proved to be the offensive catalyst. This was the start Harbaugh and the franchise needed and wanted. Their young guns were firing against a hated adversary. This wasn’t a pretty game. Too many penalties, too many fumbles, some drops. But for Harbaugh and New York, it was a beautiful result for the franchise’s new dawn. Why Malik Nabers’ mom wasn’t at Giants game for WR’s return: ‘He had to do this by himself’ | The Athletic “This game, Malik had to do this by himself,” Tonya told The Athletic on Monday. “He needed to go out there with no pressure from anybody and just perform… It worked out perfectly because if I had been there, I wouldn’t have been able to hide my emotion or my fear. He would have been able to sense that I was nervous or my anxiety was high, and I think I would have made him uneasy. So God’s timing is the best timing. And so this journey he needed to take by himself.” “We knew that it was his moment,” Tonya said. “For him to go out there, for him to decide that, ‘I’m ready,’ it took for him to trust this entire process. Trust the surgeon. Trust the surgery. Trust his workout and his recovery. He had to trust this entire journey for him to step out on that field and know that he was ready to play.” Presence and perspective for Malik Nabers in rousing NY Giants return | The Record Jaxson Dart took the last of three kneel-downs in victory formation, officially closing out Sunday night’s 28-20 triumph over the Dallas Cowboys, and he immediately knew where he was going with the football. Because the quarterback of the New York Giants knew what this meant to Malik Nabers, and Dart knows what Nabers means to him and this franchise, not just in this game, but going forward. title: New York Jets: Contextualizing Week 1
summary: It’s been an interesting few days. The Jets won their first game of the season on Sunday, and they did so in dominating fashion. Fast forward a few days and rightfully Jets fans don’t know what to do with themselves. This past Sunday marked only the second time the Jets have won their first game […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - AUGUST 14: Breece Hall #20 of the New York Jets runs during the game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on August 14, 2026 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (3Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images It’s been an interesting few days. The Jets won their first game of the season on Sunday, and they did so in dominating fashion. Fast forward a few days and rightfully Jets fans don’t know what to do with themselves. This past Sunday marked only the second time the Jets have won their first game of the season in the last eight years. And the other time they won a Week 1 game, Jets fans could barely enjoy it. That was the game where Aaron Rodgers tore his Achilles, and the fanbase was left watching in horror as he struggled to stand on the field. So even when the Jets won Week 1, there was an impending sense of dread that the season was already lost. For all intents and purposes, this was the first time in eight years I can confidently say that the Jets won their season opener and it actually felt like a win. And I can’t help but notice that a sizable portion of the Jets fanbase legitimately has no idea how to process this. The other day, on my way to work, I literally heard two Jets fans talking. One of them said, “I forgot what this feels like.” That pretty much sums it up. On one hand, you have a bunch of Jets fans who are overtly optimistic and excited. They are looking at what happened Sunday and thinking, maybe this team is actually good. Maybe this season could be different. On the other hand, you have another sizable portion of the fanbase that seems almost incapable of enjoying it. They’re waiting for the other shoe to drop. They’re prepared for disappointment because, quite frankly, that is what being a Jets fan has taught them to do. Not to get overtly psychological here, but I think there are actually two contrasting things happening. The first is cherophobia. Cherophobia is a psychological term used to describe an irrational fear of feeling happy or hopeful. One of the reasons people experience it is because of past negative experiences or trauma. As Jets fans, we know all about that. When you’ve spent years watching promising seasons fall apart, convincing yourself that things might finally be different only to have the team rip your heart out, eventually you start protecting yourself from the possibility of disappointment. And honestly, I understand it. But then there’s another psychological concept that I think is influencing the other side of the fanbase: the anchoring effect. The anchoring effect is a cognitive bias where people rely too heavily on the first piece of information they receive when making subsequent judgments or estimates. When it comes to estimating the Jets’ chances for the rest of the season, the only regular-season evidence we have right now is overwhelmingly positive. The Jets didn’t just win. They dominated. So naturally, that first piece of evidence becomes the anchor. Fans immediately start reaching for the most positive interpretation of what they just saw. If this is what the Jets look like, then maybe they can do this. Maybe they can do that. Maybe this team is actually capable of making a run. Where does this leave us this week? You have one group of Jets fans whose past experiences are telling them, “Don’t get too happy. You know how this ends.” And you have another group whose immediate experience is telling them, “Why shouldn’t we be excited? Look at what just happened.” Both reactions make sense. The problem, of course, is that neither one of those reactions necessarily tells us what the Jets actually are. It’s been one game. That doesn’t mean we should dismiss what happened Sunday. It also doesn’t mean we should extrapolate the entire season from it. I’m going to do my best to contextualize below what we just saw Sunday. What I think is realistic to get excited about and what isn’t. What Week 1 can tell us about a team and what it normally cannot. Here’s some things we do know: Week 1 Is Not Fundamentally Different Than Any Other Week This is something that I’ve heard a lot over the years. That Week 1 is particularly noisy and should be ignored more than other weeks. However, this isn’t really true when you look at the data. In other words, Week 1 doesn’t contain any less predictive value than using Week 2, Week 3, Week 6, Week 7, etc. The sample is obviously still small, but there isn’t something inherently different about the first game of the season that makes it uniquely unreliable. For starters, I want to preface this by saying that in any situation, looking at a one-week sample can lead to false conclusions. It’s a small sample. Former PFF data scientist Timo Riske outlines this in the thread below, which helps explain why Week 1 has probably developed a reputation for being more “fake” than any other week: With week 1 over, here is one thing I'd like to clarify: Looking at some basic team stats, week 1 is not lying more than other weeks *in retrospective*. When looking at how single week performance correlates to rest-of-season performance, week 1 doesn't stick out at all. — Timo Riske (@Timo_NFL) September 15, 2026 For Jets fans, I think this distinction is important because we are rightfully scared that we are being deceived by what we saw. For starters, most Jets fans remember that last year, the Jets’ offense looked significantly better in Week 1 than it did for much of the rest of the season. So naturally, there is going to be some skepticism that we’re watching the same thing happen again. But just because it happened last year doesn’t mean it is any more likely to happen this year. And that brings me to my second point. The Jets Didn’t Dominate In Flukey Ways If we’re going to look at the things that tend to hold steadier from week to week, I think you have to be at least a little more encouraged by the fact that the Jets dominated in some of the more stable metrics. I frequently cite EPA/Play and Success Rate. EPA/Play is incredibly useful and probably the gold standard in today’s NFL for analyzing offensive and defensive efficiency. However, EPA/Play can be volatile in small samples. One or two plays can have an enormous impact on a team’s EPA/Play in a single game. Over the course of a season, when you have several games in the sample, that volatility begins to stabilize. But in the short term, you can absolutely draw the wrong conclusions from it. Success Rate, for those who don’t know, is a little more measured. In the simplest terms, Success Rate is a metric that measures how consistently a team produces a productive outcome relative to the down and distance. Unlike total yards or yards per play, which can be heavily influenced by one explosive play, Success Rate essentially treats each snap as a binary outcome: Was the play successful or was it not? A play is generally considered successful if it gains: On first down, roughly 40% to 50% of the yards needed. On second down, roughly 60% to 70% of the remaining yards needed. On third or fourth down, 100% of the yards needed to move the chains or score a touchdown. Essentially, we are measuring how often a team stays on schedule rather than allowing one or two massive plays to dictate the numbers. And from a Jets perspective, they ranked really well on both sides of the ball. On first and second downs, the Jets ranked fourth in offensive Success Rate last week, led by a rushing attack that was successful on over 55% of its plays. Defensively, the Jets ranked 12th in Success Rate, led by a rushing defense that ranked sixth. Now, there is obviously no guarantee that any of this lasts. Like I said, it’s one game. But I feel a little more confident knowing that the Jets’ dominance wasn’t simply the result of weird turnovers, one major penalty, or one or two explosive offensive plays caused by a busted coverage. They were consistently successful. Which…

title: Eagles Film Review: A very good defensive performance against the Commanders
summary: The Eagles’ defense was very good against the Washington Commanders. It wasn’t an elite performance, and the final two drives left a slightly sour taste, but the unit held Jayden Daniels to 18 completions on 34 attempts for 164 yards and limited Washington to 4.4 yards per play. Given the number of new pieces in […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Zack Baun #53 of the Philadelphia Eagles tackles Jayden Daniels #5 of the Washington Commanders in the second quarter of a game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Eagles’ defense was very good against the Washington Commanders. It wasn’t an elite performance, and the final two drives left a slightly sour taste, but the unit held Jayden Daniels to 18 completions on 34 attempts for 164 yards and limited Washington to 4.4 yards per play. Given the number of new pieces in the secondary and how difficult Daniels was to defend, I came away impressed. However, this defense has an offense problem. The Eagles’ defense played 67 snaps while the offense ran only 53 and gained just 10 first downs. Washington possessed the ball for 10:02 in the fourth quarter alone and put together touchdown drives of 67 and 63 yards. You could see the defense tiring. Jalen Carter looked exhausted by the end, and the pass rush dropped off. This is becoming a familiar problem. The defense can play exceptionally well for long stretches, but asking it to keep returning to the field eventually has consequences. The advanced numbers tell an interesting story. The Eagles generated pressure on 47.4% of Washington’s dropbacks despite blitzing on only 23.7%, but Daniels was sacked just once. That matches up to the film. The rush affected him and remained disciplined, but it rarely arrived quickly. I think the Eagles were deliberately cautious because they did not want to create huge escape lanes for Daniels. Defense Jordan Davis picked up exactly where he left off last season. The Eagles did not completely dominate Washington’s running game, the Commanders finished with 132 yards on 32 carries, but Davis was consistently difficult to move. This is an excellent rep against a double team. He absorbs the initial contact, stays balanced, and then uses his quickness to work around the lineman and finish the play. That combination of size and movement is what makes Davis such a unique player. He is no longer simply occupying blockers as he was a couple of years ago. He is defeating them and making plays himself. Eagles' Defense Thread All22 vs. Washington. 1) Jordan Davis picked up where he left off last year. He made several excellent plays against the run. Watch how he handles the double team and uses his quickness to get around the center and tackle the RB. Lovely stuff. pic.twitter.com/u3YtwEEsmX — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 15, 2026 Marcus Epps’ return to the starting lineup was important to watch because the Eagles are relying on him to replace Reed Blankenship’s downhill presence. Vic Fangio asks his safeties to trigger quickly, fit the run and tackle in space. Epps reads this immediately, arrives in the backfield under control, and finishes the play cleanly. His timing is excellent. Communication issues will inevitably come in a secondary with new combinations, and we will get to that later, but Epps looked comfortable with the physical parts of the role. Nothing from this game made me think he cannot do what the Eagles need him to do. Which is a big positive! 2) It was good to see Marcus Epps coming downhill and making this play in the backfield early on. The Eagles are relying on Epps to replace Blankenship, and I didn't see anything this week that made me think he can't do that role effectively. His timing and finish here are… pic.twitter.com/BpPETBsBj1 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 15, 2026 Phew. Tariq Woolen’s Eagles debut was awesome. I knew he was good, but he played better than I expected. Washington tries to create a one-on-one deep shot to Dyami Brown here. Michael Carter does a good job from safety of pointing out the running back in the flat before helping against the crossing route, which leaves Woolen isolated outside, which is exactly what the Commanders want. Fangio is often seen as a passive coach, but he leaves his outside corners one-on-one routinely. It’s a big part of the scheme. Woolen makes it look easy. He stays balanced through the release, turns and runs without panicking (or looking stressed, at all), and then gets his head back toward the football. Corners with Woolen’s speed do not need to grab or play desperately when the ball goes downfield. He knows he can run with anyone. That athletic confidence showed up throughout the game. It was a huge upgrade on what we have seen in recent years at CB2. 3) Phew, beautiful rep by Tariq Woolen, who I thought was awesome. Michael Carter played at times in obvious passing downs, and he does a good job as the safety, pointing out the RB in the flat and helping out against the crossing route. It leaves Woolen one-on-one vs. Dyami… pic.twitter.com/GEz0St6zDF — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 15, 2026 I would love to see the Eagles’ short-yardage numbers since Vic Fangio arrived because this six-man front routinely wins on 3rd/4th and 1. The structure is simple but effective. The defensive line occupies every gap and prevents the offensive line from climbing cleanly to the second level. That keeps Zack Baun free, and few linebackers would be better suited to attack downhill in this situation. He was so so good in this game 4) I'd love to see numbers for the Eagles in short-yardage situations under Fangio over the past couple of years, but it feels like they are incredibly good when they use this 6-man front. The front keeps Baun clean, and he gets downhill fast, preventing the 1st down on 3rd and… pic.twitter.com/HIPJDejOp5 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 15, 2026 This might be my favorite Woolen rep from the game. The Eagles rotate into Cover 3, and Washington runs Dagger, a concept that uses a vertical route to clear space for a deep in-breaker behind it. Terry McLaurin is supposed to find the window between the underneath defenders and Woolen’s deep third. The receiver has the leverage advantage here, so this is a win for the offense on the whiteboard. However, Woolen recognizes the concept before McLaurin has even completed the route. You can see how eager he is to jump the route, even before McLaurin breaks inside. This is not simply an athletic win. It is preparation, awareness, and outstanding film study. Woolen was targeted five times and allowed one completion for one yard, although that completion was a touchdown attributed to him in coverage, which is very debatable. 5) Man, what an unbelievable rep by Woolen. The Eagles rotate to cover 3 and Woolen reads the Dagger coming from McLaurin before he runs it himself! This is pure film study and an understanding of what the offense is trying to do. This was a hell of a debut. pic.twitter.com/ZyxAF0xnJo — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 15, 2026 The pass rush was the most difficult part of this performance to evaluate. The numbers look fantastic. Nolan Smith led the defense with six pressures, while Jalen Carter, Jalyx Hunt, and Moro Ojomo recorded four each. The overall pressure rate was 47.4%, which sounds unbelievably good. Yet Daniels was sacked only once for a 1-yard loss, and the pocket didn’t consistently collapse around him. It’s hard to evaluate because Daniels held on to the ball and moves around a lot. I think some of the slow pass rush was intentional. Rushing Daniels is different from rushing a stationary quarterback. If every defender flies upfield searching for a sack, Daniels will step through the middle and is a huge rushing threat. The Eagles appeared focused on maintaining rush-lane integrity and forcing him to remain a passer. Daniels still escaped a few times, but holding him to five carries for 31 yards is a reasonable result. This play also shows why Fangio likes dropping an edge defender. Hunt falls into coverage while Baun rushes, which manipulates the protection and gives Carter a one-on-one against the center. Carter wins and appears to be held as Daniels escapes. This…

full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Cooper DeJean #33 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on against the Washington Commanders during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. It’s currently unclear if Carter is in jeopardy of missing Sunday’s game. The Eagles having to play without both DeJean and Carter sure wouldn’t be ideal. The Eagles listed one player under LIMITED PARTICIPATION: Jonathan Greenard. Hard to expect that Greenard will be playing until he starts fully participating in practice. Guessing Week 3 might be a more realistic target for him, especially since there’s an extra day leading into that Monday Night Football matchup. In the meantime, he’s ramping up for a return. title: Vic Fangio on Jalen Carter’s conditioning Week 1: “It wasn’t terrible”
summary: The Eagles are now moving on from their season opener, but DC Vic Fangio spoke on Tuesday about some of the issues the defense faced against the Commanders, on why Moro Ojomo’s stop was so impressive, and what he expects from Cam Ward and the Titans in Week 2. Fangio was asked about his overall […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - AUGUST 28: Philadelphia Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio looks on during the pre season game between the Philadelphia Eagles and the Cincinnati Bengals on August 28th, 2026 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Eagles are now moving on from their season opener, but DC Vic Fangio spoke on Tuesday about some of the issues the defense faced against the Commanders, on why Moro Ojomo’s stop was so impressive, and what he expects from Cam Ward and the Titans in Week 2. Fangio was asked about his overall takeaway from the Week 1 win, and he didn’t hold back. “Disappointed in their three scoring drives. There’s some scoring drives you give up where the other team just beats you. They’ve got good players and good coaches, too. But I think we could have played a little better in some of those instances from our just overall play, so that was a little frustrating.” Here’s what the DC had to say: On the 4th quarter struggles “The last two drives there, we just didn’t play well enough. The quarterback scrambling hurt us some. It wasn’t good the last couple for sure.” Fangio was asked about Cooper DeJean’s post-game comments about his eyes get bad and that’s what hurts him. The DC agreed that can happen at times, but also noted at other times, that quality has helped him. “[Cooper DeJean]‘s just got to make sure he can stay tight enough to his assignment and not let his vision get too skewed to where he gets out of position.” On Moro Ojomo’s big stop The DC also gave all the credit to Ojomo for sniffing out the play because it wasn’t something the Commanders had put on film prior to the game. “It was just a great play by him individually. Like he said, he saw the guard pull, so he immediately tried to cross the guy that was trying to block him, which he did successfully and made the play. Was a big play by him obviously, but to have the energy and the wherewithal to do that that late in the game was big.” Fangio later talked about about Ojomo’s play and how his instincts are both natural and something he works on. He also highlighted the effort Ojomo plays with and how that impacts things as well. “But [Ojomo] does have good instincts, but he gives great effort and he’s tenacious.” On Jalen Carter’s conditioning “ It wasn’t terrible. We did have a lot of reps, but a good bit of them came the last drive of the first half and then those last two drives. Those other drives were kind of shorter in duration, so it’s a little easier to play that many.” On preparing for the Titans Fangio was very complimentary of Titans QB Cam Ward, noting that the quarterback has very good arm talent, and he’s athletic and mobile. The DC said Ward is progressing well and thinks the QB will continue to improve in Tennessee’s offense. He also said that new Titans OC Brian Daboll does a good job of calling the game and has a good run-pass mix. Fangio expects Tennessee to take some shots in the passing game, but also get a mix of some quicker throws. “I think [Brian Daboll] does a good job of mixing it up, not just run and pass, but the types of run and passes, too.” Other player notables Fangio said that Jihaad Campbell “did fine” in the season opener, but said that there were plays he’d like back. The DC revealed that OLB AJ Epenesa got dinged up in the game against the Commanders, which is why OLB Arnold Ebiketie got more reps. He said that second-year safety Andrew Mukuba did a good job communicating on the backend, although Fangio added that the performance wasn’t perfect, but it was good. Fangio also said that the safety duo of Mukuba and Marcus Epps did fine, even though he noted that there were some plays that could have gone better from an assignment or execution standpoint. The DC said he’s very pleased with CB Riq Woolen ’s performance, and thought he had good focus and did a good job covering. He also explained that Zack Baun was able to participate in all of training camp, unlike last year, and Fangio highlighted that more practice tends to lead to better game performances. Still, the DC said he appreciates everything from what Baun was able to do on Sunday, and the LB played really well.

title: Eagles vs. Commanders: 14 winners, 5 losers, 5 IDKs
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles are 1-0 after beating the Washington Commanders to begin the 2026 season. It was a narrow win, yes, but it was an important one to avoid dropping a division game right off the bat. Time to hand out winners, losers, and I don’t knows. For even more analysis, check out my appearance […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Jalen Hurts #1 of the Philadelphia Eagles celebrates after a touchdown against the Washington Commanders during an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles are 1-0 after beating the Washington Commanders to begin the 2026 season. It was a narrow win, yes, but it was an important one to avoid dropping a division game right off the bat. Time to hand out winners, losers, and I don’t knows. For even more analysis, check out my appearance on the PHLY Eagles postgame show along with the legendary Brandon Graham and Bo Wulf! WINNERS JALEN HURTS My biggest takeaway from this game? Hurts looking good while carrying the offense. The box score: 14/25 (56%), 203 passing yards, 3 TD, 0 INT, 122.2 passer rating … 7 carries, 46 rushing yards*. Hurts converting 3rd-and-18 in the fourth quarter was a massive development. The offense ran 21 plays for just 67 yards and three points on their previous five drives. They needed a spark and he gave them one. The offense as a collective sure didn’t play a stellar game. But Hurts made big plays that were the difference in this win. His first touchdown pass to Dallas Goedert, which came on 3rd-and-goal from the 17-yard line, was thrown into a tight window up the seam. His touchdown pass to Dontayvion Wicks was a nice anticipatory ball. He showed admirable aggression by hitting Wicks deep while the receiver was running a clear out route. His completion to DeVonta Smith deep along the right sideline was a beauty. It’s always easier to feel better about your favorite NFL team’s outlook when the quarterback is playing well. This was an encouraging performance from QB1. *Hurts logged at least 46 rushing yards in just two out of 17 games played last year. Since 1950, three NFL quarterbacks have reached 6-0 in Week 1 games: Roger Staubach Johnny Unitas Jalen Hurts — Brandon Lee Gowton (@BrandonGowton) September 14, 2026 Jalen Hurts had an NFL-high 33% non-target rate in Week 1: 11 non-targets (5 scrambles, 3 throwaways, 3 sacks) on 33 dropbacks. Watching the film, he carried the offense (4 scrambles were nice gains, sacks not his fault) despite major protection issues which nullified the script. pic.twitter.com/bI3XJwAuZb — Deniz Selman (@denizselman33) September 16, 2026 MORO OJOMO With the Commanders in position to tie the game with a two-point conversion, Ojomo sniffed out Washington’s shovel pass to John Bates and sealed the deal by tackling the tight end short of the line of scrimmage. Shame that he doesn’t get officially credited for a TFL on that play since the NFL doesn’t count stats from two-point conversions. Ojomo also missed out on being credited with the sack that he created for Jihaad Campbell. No matter, though, because those numbers will come. Ojomo is very much poised for a big year ahead of being a free agent after this season. ZACK BAUN I’m not convinced that Baun gets proper credit for just how good he is. Locally? Probably. Nationally? Don’t think so. Baun finished fourth in offseason off-ball linebacker rankings based on league polling. He’s top two and I don’t think he’s very far behind Fred Warner at No. 1, if at all. Baun was a monster in this game. He logged a team-high 12 tackles (including one TFL, which came on a 3rd-and-1 to force a Commanders punt) and two pass deflections. The Commanders targeted Baun seven times in coverage. He allowed three catches … for negative two yards . He nearly made an impressive leaping interception along the sideline. The pick didn’t count, no, but it was still a high quality coverage rep to help prevent a reception. After Week 1, Baun leads all NFL defenders in “stops,” which are defined as tackles that constitute a failure for the offense by Pro Football Focus charting. Beast! JALEN CARTER Not the flashiest box score but Carter, who played the second-most snaps of any Week 1 interior defender, did make meaningful contributions to the Eagles’ win. First of all, his blocked extra point was huge. Washington would’ve been in a position to tie the game late with a relatively routine kick instead of a two-point conversion try otherwise. He combined with Baun to stop a Commanders 3rd-and-1 run for no gain to force a punt in the first quarter. Carter forced a fumble on the Commanders’ final drive. The Eagles didn’t manage to recover possession but that was just some bad luck. Had they received a more fortunate bounce, his punch out would’ve been viewed as a massive play. Carter also generated some disruption on the Commanders’ attempt to tie the game with a two-point conversion. I don’t know how much it mattered since Ojomo was in good position to stuff Bates … but Carter did get a piece of the Commanders’ tight end that might’ve slowed him down at least a little bit prior to making the catch for a loss. DALLAS GOEDERT For two years in a row now, the Eagles flirted with moving on from Goedert in the offseason. Thank Goedert they didn’t. The Eagles’ top tight end led the team in receiving with four grabs for 77 yards and two touchdowns. Dallas Goedert has scored 13 touchdowns in his last 15 games. — Brandon Lee Gowton (@BrandonGowton) September 14, 2026 SAQUON BARKLEY Barkley’s 15 carries resulted in 83 yards for a 5.5 average. His longest run of the day was a 42-yarder where he looked pretty explosive. Making his production even impressive was that only FIVE of his yards came before contact. According to my math sources, that means he gained 78 yards after contact. That’s a very flattering stat for Barkley. Speaks to his ability to create much out of nothing. Unfortunately, a much less flattering stat for the Eagles’ blockers. DONTAYVION WICKS If there was any doubt that Wicks is WR2, that should be over. His four targets resulted in 73 yards and a touchdown. His 64-yard reception marked the longest of his career, eclipsing his previous record of just 36 yards. Wicks deserves recognition for his effort on that big play because he was running a clear out route to create space for Goedert underneath. Not all receivers (I think we can think of one) put their best foot forward on that kind on play. Wicks also did a really nice job of tracking the ball in the air … while the Commanders’ defensive backs certainly did not. Wicks’ savvy route-running was on display when he got open for his touchdown reception. He cooked Mike Sainristil (or, as Hogs Haven referred to him , Mike StandRealStill … gottem). We’ll see how Wicks fares moving forward but, early on, the decision to trade for him is looking like a win. The Eagles only had to give up a 2026 fifth-round pick and a 2027 sixth-round pick in the deal with the Green Bay Packers. That’s value. DEVONTA SMITH Smitty’s six targets only resulted in three catches for 57 yards but that over-the-shoulder toe-tapping grab along the rights sideline was pretty sweet. JORDAN DAVIS The Commanders’ running backs gained 101 yards on 27 carries for a 3.7 average. Davis contributed to their lack of success on the ground, logging four “stops,” which was third-most on the Eagles. QUINYON MITCHELL and RIQ WOOLEN Terry was not so scary on Sunday: Terry McLaurin matched up against Quinyon Mitchell (9 snaps) or Riq Woolen (13 snaps): 1 target, 0 catches. — Brandon Lee Gowton (@BrandonGowton) September 14, 2026 In total, Mitchell was targeted three times, allowing two receptions for 15 yards. Woolen was targeted five times but allowed just one catch for one yard, which did happen to be a touchdown. Looked like Woolen and Marcus Epps had a miscommunication on that snap. It’s not difficult to feel pretty good about the Eagles’ outside cornerbacks right now. DARIUS COOPER Cooper, a wide receiver, finished sixth on the Eagles in tackles on Sunday. He logged four while playing special teams. That’s an impressive number! Consider that special teams coordinator Michael Clay recently noted…

title: Eagles in the community: Jalen Hurts, Jalyx Hunt make huge impacts
summary: The NFL is filled with players who are deeply committed to the communities in which they play, and the Eagles have a whole lot of guys like that on the roster. After their Week 1 game, QB Jalen Hurts and EDGE Jalyx Hunt both announced some hugely impactful initiatives for some high schoolers in Philly. […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Jalen Hurts #1 of the Philadelphia Eagles reacts as he runs with the ball off the field against the Washington Commanders following an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The NFL is filled with players who are deeply committed to the communities in which they play, and the Eagles have a whole lot of guys like that on the roster. After their Week 1 game, QB Jalen Hurts and EDGE Jalyx Hunt both announced some hugely impactful initiatives for some high schoolers in Philly. Jalen Hurts and his foundation announced a $600,000 donation to Northeast High School for a new HVAC system that will bring air conditioning into the often hot and uncomfortable conditions. Already this year, 52 schools without AC have had to close early due to the temperatures — that number is down to 52 from 118 when Hurts first committed to this initiative a few years ago. When speaking to the students about this six-figure donation, Hurts explained that education is so important, and the environment to do that important learning is critical to the work getting done. A comfortable space for students to learn is what every kid deserves. Jalen Hurts stopped by Northeast High School in Philadelphia to address the students after making an incredible donation 🥹 pic.twitter.com/n11ruRQ69h — NBC Sports Philadelphia (@NBCSPhilly) September 15, 2026 The next day, across town, Jalyx Hunt and his foundation announced the creation of three scholarships and an endowment at Little Flower Catholic High School for Girls. The scholarships are named after important women in Hunt’s life, his Mother, his Sister, his Grandmother, and his long-time friend. Two awards will cover two years of tuition, and two will cover four years, and the endowment will sustain the scholarships in the future. “This is longevity,” Hunt said, according to the Inquirer’s Olivia Reiner . “I’ve had a lot of talks with [Little Flower president Kristie] Dugan, and I just know that this is something that helps out a lot. A lot of people at this school require and need some sort of help to pay tuition, and if I can do that, I would love to do that.” Hunt has created a long-term connection with the students and staff at Little Flower HS back in 2024 when the Eagles defender wanted to support underfunded school sports teams. He helped the basketball team two years ago, and now he’s having an even bigger impact to a community he’s deeply committed to.

title: Zack Baun is NFC Defensive Player of the Week for the second time in his career
summary: Zack Baun was named NFC Defensive Player of the Week for his stellar performance in the Philadelphia Eagles’ Week 1 win over the Washington Commanders, according to an official league announcement. From the release: Baun recorded 12 tackles, two passes defensed and a tackle for loss in Philadelphia’s 24-22 win against Washington. Per Next Gen […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Zack Baun #53 of the Philadelphia Eagles reacts after a loss against the Washington Commanders during the second quarter at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Zack Baun was named NFC Defensive Player of the Week for his stellar performance in the Philadelphia Eagles’ Week 1 win over the Washington Commanders, according to an official league announcement. From the release: Baun recorded 12 tackles, two passes defensed and a tackle for loss in Philadelphia’s 24-22 win against Washington. Per Next Gen Stats, Baun was targeted six times in coverage, allowing three receptions for -2 yards, one of two defenders since the start of last season (Denzel Ward) to allow negative receiving yards on five-or-more targets in a game. This is Baun’s second-career Defensive Player of the Week award (Week 10, 2024). He becomes the third Eagles linebacker to win the award multiple times, joining Seth Joyner (three-time winner) and William Thomas (two). Additionally, Baun’s seven “stops,” which are tackles that constitute a loss for the offense, lead all NFL defenders (not just linebackers) after Week 1. Baun is a beast who deserves more national praise, so, it’s nice to see him recognized in this capacity. I’m just saying, Fred Warner has zero NFC Defensive Player of the Week awards since Baun became a full-time starter and earned two. Baun is the first Eagles player to win NFC Defensive Player of the Week since Cooper DeJean was honored for his Week 16 performance last season.

summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! In case you forgot, Zack Baun is really, really good at football. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! In case you forgot, Zack Baun is really, really good at football. Wild that the Eagles have a linebacker this good after years of them struggling to merely find competent players at the position. He isn’t just one of the best players at his position in the NFL … he’s one of the best overall defenders in the NFL. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Eagles film review: Zack Baun was a beast Week 1 vs. the Commanders – PhillyVoice Vic Fangio was asked on Tuesday what in particular he appreciated about Baun’s performance. “All of it,” Fangio told reporters. “He played really good. I think it’s a reflection that he played all camp, practiced all camp. Last year he missed most of camp with a back injury. When you practice, you play better.” Baun had a very good season in 2025 that meritoriously resulted in a Pro Bowl nod. Now fully healthy, he looks very much like the guy who finished fifth in Defensive Player of the Year voting in 2024. Eagles LB Zack Baun leads all NFL defenders in “stops” (tackles that constitute a failure for the offense) after Week 1 with seven. — Brandon Lee Gowton (@BrandonGowton) September 15, 2026 Eagles-Commanders Film Review: Offense did some good things but must improve – BGN It’s easy to look at the Eagles scoring 24 points, averaging six yards per play, and conclude the offense played well in the first game of the season. Unfortunately, I don’t think it did. The Eagles generated 318 yards, but 180 of them came on four plays. They finished with only 10 first downs, punted seven times, and had six possessions without earning a single first down. They also went three-and-out on three consecutive drives in the third quarter. Elite players made enough elite plays to win the game, but they showed little consistency. We saw this at times last season. The Eagles won games despite the offense failing to establish any rhythm, and the result often disguised the performance. That is not sustainable. However, it is Week 1. Sean Mannion is a brand-new offensive coordinator, and the Eagles are still working out what this offense should look like. I’m not panicking after one game. The important thing is whether Mannion recognizes the problems and adapts. Let’s get into the film. We are back, baby! Moro Ojomo was once defined by ‘potential.’ The Eagles are seeing something much bigger now – The Athletic Ojomo shares a position group with two of the NFL’s 10 highest-paid defensive tackles. Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis were first-round picks who signed lucrative contract extensions this offseason. Ojomo is “proud and happy” for his teammates. He also refuses to take a back seat. “I’m always trying to be the best,” Ojomo said this summer. “We have an extremely loaded room. Those guys know I’m not backing down from anything. The goal is always to be the best defensive tackle, and that’s the mindset. I want to make more plays, I want to have more sacks, I want to make more TFLs, I want to be the best in the room and the best in the league.” Ojomo’s talent is no secret in the Eagles locker room — or the NFL. Ojomo played 66 percent of the defensive snaps last season and finished second on the team with six sacks. On Sunday, he played 69 percent of the defensive snaps and thwarted the Commanders’ two-point conversion attempt to tie the game in the fourth quarter when he spun away from a block and upended the ball carrier on a shovel pass short of the end zone. Ojomo said he saw the guard pull and anticipated the play — “You can’t play indecisive,” he said — and the sequence was more than the right place at the right time. “I think part of it is due to his effort,” defensive coordinator Vic Fangio said. “His dogged effort plays a part in that, which he’s a little undersized as D-tackles go, and he needs to have all that stuff working for him. But he does have good instincts, but he gives great effort and he’s tenacious. They hadn’t shown that (play). Obviously, that was a special play they had cooked up for a 2-point play, and it was more of his reaction and instincts after the ball was snapped than anything pre-snap.” Download the SB Nation app today! Bowen: I have questions — Where have you gone, Landon Dickerson? And isn’t this really A.J. Brown’s fault? – PHLY Eagles This brings us back to A.J. Brown. General manager Howie Roseman ended up trading one of the top five players on his roster for nothing that will help this year’s team. Then he spent his first-round draft choice on a wide receiver, Makai Lemon. There is nothing you could possibly say that would convince me the Eagles would have drafted a wideout in the first round with a healthy, happy A.J. Brown in house. It would have been stupid. Roseman’s offensive line-building strategy was predicated on Dickerson and Jurgens (drafted 51st overall in 2022) being long-term bulwarks. The Eagles haven’t drafted an offensive lineman in the first two rounds since Jurgens. And they no longer employ offensive line coach Jeff Stoutland, noted developer of O-line talent. Given Lane Johnson’s alleged impending retirement (yes, fans of training camp practice reports, I am aware of third-round project Markel Bell, surely he’s headed for Canton once he actually plays), they are in danger of seeing the team’s foundation slowly crumble away. Jalyx Hunt wants to remain grounded as his NFL star rises. His support of Little Flower helps him stay connected. – Inquirer Jaaqua Hunt, a longtime teacher, has a favorite saying that she shares with her students and with her son Jalyx, the third-year Eagles outside linebacker — “blossom where you’re planted.” “You don’t have to originate in a place to become a part of that place,” she said. “So, take advantage of where you are.” Jaaqua said it’s become clear that Jalyx is listening. He isn’t native to Philadelphia. He was born in Memphis, Tenn., but he spent his adolescence in the Orlando area, then moved with his family back to Tennessee, then to Maryland, then to South Carolina, then back to Florida. In Philadelphia, though, Hunt has found a new home — and an extended family off the field. Hunt has an older sister, Jessica, and what he calls a “whole bunch of little sisters” in the hundreds of students at Little Flower Catholic High School for Girls in the Hunting Park section of North Philadelphia. His relationship with the school began in 2024, the year the Eagles drafted him in the third round out of Houston Christian, when he started a fundraiser for underfunded school sports programs.
